Critical commissioning and as-built deficiencies, outstanding TA endorsements.
New/revised engineering standards, obsolescence, skill gaps and technical authority succession.

blocks.t: An individual acting as the design author may provide technical evidence but should not be the sole independent verifier for a critical safety function. The TLC nominates appropriate reviewers for high-consequence departures and records unresolved disagreements, the risk position, responsible decision-maker and follow-up. Cost and schedule pressure is documented but cannot override minimum barrier performance.

Sample a complete evidence chain from MAH to SCE and PS, to inspection/work-order task, actual field result, defect disposition and current operational status. A second sample starts at a failed barrier test and follows its impairment control, repair, independent acceptance and hazard-study feedback. Findings in the chain reveal whether ONE navigation correctly represents the effective management system rather than merely the completeness of document metadata.

sections.title: Appendix Q — Records, ownership and ONE publication controls

rows: Asset, system, specification, drawing, technical deviation, project gate.
Hazard study ID, bow-tie, SCE, performance standard.
SCE ID, critical function, tests, MOC, associated safety study.
Equipment IDs, damage mechanism, approved scope, findings.
Function location, task code, due/actual, actual test results.
Condition, risk, deviation, remedy, restrictions and verification.
SCE, MAH, risk acceptance, expiry, compensating measures, restoration.
As-built documents, PSSR, competence, verification and closure.
Review date, finding, accountable owner, corrective-action evidence.

blocks.t: The approved Word source remains the authoritative policy and procedural requirement. ONE may display each section through IOGP expectation, asset, discipline, function, process and role views, while specialist engineering systems retain the detailed live asset data and records. Links to the SCE and anomaly registers should preserve the authoritative record identifiers and appropriate access restrictions; they are not licence to duplicate uncontrolled versions of asset data.

Every published cross-document integrity requirement shall retain its persistent heading bookmark and explicit OMS expectation tags so that changes in the parent document do not silently erase the traceable link to the controlling duty.

sections.title: Q.2 Minimum controlled data quality checks

blocks.t: Monthly checks include orphaned equipment IDs, missing performance standard revisions, unassigned TA ownership, task status without results, duplicate SCE references, expired deviations, missing as-built updates and overdue risk-action dates. Exceptions are routed to the owning system with due date and correction evidence; the ONE interface can report gaps but does not itself approve risk or technical change.

Maintain inspection and technical decisions for the equipment life and any longer period established by retention schedules or legal holds. Retired assets require a deliberate final record pack covering known hazards, changes, surveys, abandonment and remaining obligations. Temporary records on personal devices or email do not constitute the approved repository.
Can an independent auditor trace a major accident hazard to every credited barrier, an SCE performance standard and a recent verification record?
Does the SCE health report show actual test failures and impaired states, not only the percentage of scheduled jobs completed?
Are equipment tags, register entries, inspection circuits and CMMS task records uniquely linked and current?
When a new corrosion mechanism emerges, are all potentially exposed systems reviewed rather than only the failed item?
Does an integrity deferral carry a credible technical basis, the correct risk authority, dated compensating measures and expiry?
Has each significant MOC updated the inspection and maintenance strategy, barrier register and operational documentation?
Can operations demonstrate competent use of safe operating limits, bypass arrangements and return-to-service controls?
Are ageing, obsolescence and life-extension decisions supported by actual evidence and endorsed by the affected Technical Authorities?
Do technical reviews have a visible decision record, and are significant disagreements escalated without being erased?
Are contractor records, temporary equipment and partner interfaces covered by clear ACE accountability?
Do corrective-action closures demonstrate restored technical performance and an effective prevention of recurrence?
Does the ONE publishing layer consistently link section tags, roles, functions, processes and asset-control records to their approved sources?

Assessment outcome: each question is recorded as Conforming, Partially Conforming, Nonconforming or Not Applicable, with asset sampled, evidence reference, risk, corrective-action owner and verification date. Ratings do not replace the ACE Risk Matrix or formal conformance scoring methodology.

revisions.text: First approved issue; establishes ACE requirements for the asset integrity management standard.

docs.title: Inspection Management Standard
docs.author: Rochelle Mark — Inspection Engineer
docs.reviewers: Sophia de Souza — Materials & Corrosion Lead; Marlon Gonzales — Static Mechanical Lead; Allison Mitchell — Pipelines Lead; Marc Gomes — Maintenance & Integrity Manager
docs.applies: ACE pressure equipment, piping, tanks, Gulf of Paria pipelines and platform structures, land flowlines, CPF facilities and other integrity-managed fixed equipment
docs.subtitle: Risk-based inspection, written schemes of examination, asset-specific inspection controls, anomaly handling and technical verification.

blocks.t: This standard defines how ACE plans, performs, records and acts on inspection and examination across its operated assets. Inspection provides evidence of equipment condition and barrier fitness; it does not, by itself, certify equipment as safe for every possible operating condition. The parent Asset Integrity Management Standard governs safety-critical elements, performance standards, anomalies and verification; this document supplies the discipline-specific inspection controls.

The scope includes fixed pressure equipment, static mechanical equipment, piping, aboveground storage tanks, export and gathering lines, subsea pipelines, fixed offshore structures, marine loading interfaces, and associated integrity components at the CPF, Pommerac A, Chenet B, Sapodilla C, land leases and Point Lisas Shore Base where relevant. Well barrier inspection requirements are coordinated with ACE-WEL-STD-001, not substituted by this standard.
Each integrity-managed equipment item shall have an identified inspection strategy, an approved inspection scope and interval, a responsible owner and a traceable record of findings and disposition.
Inspection of safety-critical elements shall satisfy the applicable performance standard and any required independent verification before the element is accepted for service.

Equipment with unknown remaining integrity, missing critical inspection evidence or an unresolved defect shall be placed in a risk-controlled operating state until a competent engineering assessment permits continued use.

rows: Defines barrier requirements, anomaly system, fitness decisions and assurance.
Provides risk ranking and risk acceptance authority.
Integrates inspection activities into CMMS work planning, isolations and return to service.
Controls entry, access, isolations, permit requirements and concurrent work.
Controls repairs, rerating, inspection strategy changes with technical impact.
Maintains operating restrictions derived from inspection and anomaly evidence.
Controls inspection deferrals, impaired barriers and temporary alternative controls.

blocks.t: Inspection is delivered through an Operations organisation and governed through engineering Technical Authorities. The Inspection Lead owns method competence and programme adequacy, while the Maintenance & Integrity Manager ensures resources and executable work. The relevant discipline Technical Authority accepts engineering dispositions; the Area Authority controls local operation and access. These roles should not be collapsed into one generic “inspector” role in process maps.

rows: Accountable for asset integrity standards and discipline assurance.
Deliver inspection programme, CMMS mobilisation, budgets and overdue escalation.
Endorse WSE methods, intervals, competence and inspection quality.
Compile strategies, plan scopes, reconcile data, record anomalies and issue technical reports.
Sophia de Souza — Materials & Corrosion Lead
Corrosion mechanisms, material compatibility, degradation models and corrosion controls.
Pressure equipment and structural/fabrication assessment within discipline scope.
Pipeline integrity, in-line inspection, leak and defect assessment requirements.
Barrier assurance, anomalies, impairment and operational restrictions.
Rohan Ali; Roger Ramkissoon; Arjun Gittens; Luis de Verteuil — as applicable
Safe work access, operating restrictions, defect response and return to service.

blocks.t: The Inspection Lead shall approve the technical adequacy of each written scheme before scheduling, with endorsement by the relevant discipline Technical Authority for unusual, high-risk or novel damage mechanisms.
The Area Authority shall confirm operational readiness for inspection and acceptance of any resulting restriction or re-entry to service.
Figure 1. Cross-functional inspection process with distinct technical and operational gates.

The strategy considers degradation mechanisms, probability of failure, consequence of failure, available safeguards, historic inspection effectiveness and operational context. It sets examination methods, coverage, timing and required decision accuracy. Risk-based inspection (RBI) is a structured means of setting priorities; it is not a justification to omit statutory inspection or abandon an established performance standard.

rows: Pressure/temperature cycles, sour service, solids, water, external exposure, service changes.
Design case, operating trends, P&IDs, vessel data book.
General/local corrosion, erosion, SCC, fatigue, CUI, coating failure, mechanical damage.
Corrosion review, previous NDT, incident history.
Failure mode, leak scenario, occupancy, escalation, detection and isolation.
Risk Matrix, bow-tie, MAH / SCE register.
Accessibility, coverage limitations, method sensitivity and probability of detection.
Drawing, access plan, NDT procedure and inspection history.
Material verification, thickness variability, defect sizing and incomplete information.
Quality review, calibration records and engineering assumptions.
Scope, interval, action criteria, due date, owner and review trigger.
RBI worksheet, WSE and approval record.

blocks.t: RBI decisions shall explicitly document the damage mechanism, risk basis, inspection effectiveness, uncertainty, interval and responsible Technical Authority approval.
A risk-based interval extension shall not override a legal, regulatory, equipment-code or safety-critical performance requirement without approved, documented authority.

A major operating change, new damage mechanism, new corrosion data, incident, missed critical inspection or barrier impairment triggers review of the inspection strategy. RBI is periodically refreshed and when its underpinning assumptions no longer hold. A review can shorten, lengthen or change a technique depending on verified evidence and approval authority.
External framework: API RP 580 (Risk-Based Inspection) and, where adopted, API RP 581. The ACE Engineering Standards Register controls the applicable editions and scope.

sections.title: 4 Written schemes of examination and scheduling

blocks.t: A written scheme of examination (WSE) is the controlled technical instruction for examining an asset, rather than a bare CMMS due date. It defines what must be inspected, how effectively, against which criteria and with what response to an adverse finding. The WSE is linked to equipment identity, degradation groups, access provisions, inspection drawings and previous condition evidence.

rows: Unique tag, design dossier, boundaries and associated protective components.
Locations, inspection points, coverage/scan plan and exclusions.
Damage mechanisms, method qualification, expected sensitivity and limitations.
Acceptance criteria, hold points, engineering referral and notification thresholds.
Last inspection, due date, permissible window, next inspection trigger and priority.
Permit, isolation, confined-space, access, cleaning, marine or lifting constraints.
Author, Inspection Lead approval and relevant discipline endorsement.
Reports, photos, CML/TML data, anomalies, CMMS links and release decision.

blocks.t: The WSE shall be approved before work is dispatched and shall be available to the inspection team with the current equipment and isolation information.
Scheduled inspection tasks for safety-critical equipment shall be completed by their approved due date or deferred using the controlled deviation and barrier impairment process.
Deferral of a critical inspection shall require documented integrity risk assessment, alternative safeguards, technical endorsement, accountable approval and a time-bound revised due date.

Inspection activities are scheduled through CMMS and coordinated with shutdown plans and production windows. Work orders identify the WSE and record the executed revision. Work marked complete in CMMS without an accepted inspection report remains technically open until the inspection engineering review and any anomaly handover are concluded.

Method selection follows the expected failure mode and required confidence, not convenience alone. Inspection may use visual and dimensional checks, ultrasonic thickness measurements, phased-array or time-of-flight diffraction techniques, radiography, magnetic particle or penetrant examination, acoustic methods, corrosion monitoring, intelligent pigging or subsea surveys. The method, qualification and limitations are recorded in the WSE.

rows: Surface condition, coating, leaks, distortion, supports, external deterioration.
Access and visibility; does not reliably size internal loss.
Wall loss, corrosion rates, targeted grid mapping.
Material/geometry, surface condition, calibration and CML consistency.
Volumetric flaws and selected weld/thickness characterisation.
Qualified procedure, defect orientation and detection/sizing uncertainty.
Radiation controls, surface preparation and method-specific sensitivity.
Pipeline corrosion, geometry anomalies and suitable defect detection.
Tool capability, speed, cleanliness, validation digs and unpiggable segments.
Below-water members, risers, anodes, marine growth and seabed change.
Sea state, visibility, access, positioning and survey quality.

blocks.t: Inspection personnel shall work to an approved procedure, approved instrument calibration and the defined inspection hold points; any deviation in coverage or method shall be reviewed before acceptance.
Access and exposure risks for radiography, confined space, work at height, pressure systems and offshore lifting shall be controlled through the site Control of Work process.

Each accepted report shall retain the inspector identity and qualification, date, asset/tag, technique, calibration, coverage map, data, defect dimensions, acceptance assessment, reviewer and linked work order.

Independent review of safety-critical or high-consequence findings is proportionate to the consequences of error. Unexpected findings are not hidden by averaging away local defects or by assuming that unexamined areas have the condition of the measured sample. Inspection Engineering records uncertainty explicitly.

sections.title: 6 Pressure equipment, piping, relief devices and tanks

blocks.t: Fixed equipment at the CPF and offshore process facilities is grouped by equipment type, credible degradation and code basis. Pressure vessels, heat exchangers, separators, process piping, relief devices, tank farm assets and jetty transfer systems require inspection scopes appropriate to their function, design pressure/temperature, process fluids and damage history.

rows: Shell/head/nozzle thickness, welds, internals where accessible, supports, corrosion and pressure boundaries.
Static Mechanical TA plus Integrity Engineer for fitness and restrictions.
CML circuits, dead legs, injection points, small-bore vibration, CUI, supports and piping stress.
Static Mechanical and Materials & Corrosion for defects.
Tube bundle condition, shell integrity, fouling/corrosion and thermal/mechanical cycling.
Inspection + maintenance workpack and engineering disposition.
Bench test or in-situ evidence, set-pressure records, installation and seal integrity.
I&C / Mechanical interface, protection layer and safe return.
Tank shell/floor/roof, settlement, corrosion, seals, transfer line integrity.
Tank inspection standard and Area Authority operating constraints.
Performance standard, verification interval, test acceptance criteria and overdue rules.
Barrier impairment / technical deviation as necessary.

blocks.t: Inspection of in-service pressure vessels, piping systems and storage tanks shall follow the relevant approved ACE discipline practice and adopted code requirements.

The selection of API 510, API 570 and API 653 is governed by equipment scope, original construction basis, jurisdiction and the ACE Engineering Standards Register. Materials, piping or structural requirements that differ are resolved by the relevant Technical Authority rather than borrowing the most convenient clause from another code.
External technical references: API 510 (pressure vessels); API 570 (in-service piping); API 653 (aboveground storage tanks); and API 579-1/ASME FFS-1 for applicable fitness-for-service analysis.

ACE transports Gulf of Paria production through offshore pipelines and land production through flowlines and gathering stations. Inspections integrate pipeline inventory, route and environmental exposure, corrosion mechanisms, internal fluid condition, cathodic protection, third-party threats, spans, geohazards, crossings and operating history.

rows: External survey, CP potential/anodes, wall condition, seabed spans, marine interference and pigging data where feasible.
Pipeline TA → Offshore Operations Manager → Integrity Engineer.
Riser clamps and supports, splash-zone corrosion, flange joints, corrosion loops and mechanical loads.
Pipeline TA + Static Mechanical TA + OIM.
ROW patrol, leaks, corrosion coupons/monitoring, isolation points, external coating and crossings.
Wall thickness circuits, transfer loading, vibration, supports, valves and jetty interfaces.
Targeted NDT, corrosion modelling, excavations or alternative verification plans.
Pipeline TA-approved method and uncertainty record.

blocks.t: Each pipeline and flowline segment shall have an identifiable integrity threat assessment, approved inspection/surveillance plan, anomaly criteria and named owner.

In-line inspection indications shall be validated and dispositioned against the tool performance and applicable assessment method, with field verification where the uncertainty or consequence requires it.

Anomaly decisions should consider interacting defects and pressure cycling, not wall-loss depth alone. Where confidence is inadequate, the Pipelines Lead defines additional examination or operating restriction. If a new maximum allowable operating pressure is imposed, Operations updates the relevant operating-envelope controls under ACE-OPS-STD-001.

Fixed offshore structures include platform jackets, topsides supports, piles, risers and appurtenances at Pommerac A and unmanned wellhead structures. Onshore structures include CPF steelwork, pipe racks, foundations, loading jetty, tank supports and access systems. Inspections must distinguish safety-critical structural load paths from non-structural defects and include consequence-based priorities.

rows: Corrosion/paint, fatigue-prone weld details, deformation, bolts, joints, grating, handrails and load paths.
Structural TA assesses significance and inspection intervals.
Member condition, marine growth, pile/brace joints, scour, anode and CP status, corrosion defects.
Structural and corrosion TAs endorse survey response.
Support loads, grout/foundation state, vibration, anchors, settlement and weathering.
Structural TA and site Area Authority agree restrictions.
Piling, fenders, transfer support structures and load-bearing connections.
Structural TA, Logistics/Marine and CPF Area Authority.
Storm exposure, impact, fire, explosion, collision, significant vibration or abnormal movement.
Prompt integrity assessment and operating release gate.

blocks.t: Structural inspection programmes shall identify critical members, potential failure mechanisms, design load assumptions, inspection coverage and the decision threshold for engineering assessment.

For offshore fixed platforms, the engineering team uses the adopted structural integrity framework including API RP 2SIM where applicable. A defect or damage event can warrant immediate examination ahead of the scheduled programme. No report should declare a structure fit for additional loads or extended life solely from routine visual survey.
External reference: API RP 2SIM, Structural Integrity Management of Fixed Offshore Structures; current accepted edition controlled in ACE Engineering Standards Register.

sections.title: 9 Data, anomalies, fitness for service and impairment

blocks.t: Inspection data are managed as engineering evidence. Each measurement is connected to its asset, location, technique, equipment condition, inspection date, inspector, previous data and quality status. The asset register maintains history rather than replacing superseded records with the latest value. An anomaly exists when data indicate a deviation from the accepted condition or the assumptions used to justify operation.
Figure 2. Condition evidence and anomaly decision chain.
An inspection finding exceeding the WSE referral criterion shall be entered in the anomaly register and assessed by the relevant Technical Authority before technical closure.

Fitness-for-service, rerating, repair or temporary operating restriction decisions shall identify the analysis method, conservative assumptions, required approvals, limitations, expiry and verification evidence.

Anomaly records shall capture defect ID, asset tag, location, threat, severity and uncertainty, photographs and data, risk rank, interim controls, accountable owner, technical decision, due date and independent verification where necessary.

rows: Approve technical report and update remaining-life assumptions if relevant.
Document interval, method and acceptance trigger.
Area Authority informed of any restriction.
Prompt TA review, enhanced survey, interim controls and escalation.
Loss of critical barrier or unacceptable risk
Immediate make-safe response and controlled repair/alternative barrier assessment.
Stop affected operation until formally released.
Independent evidence of acceptance test, MOC updates and reinspection baseline.

blocks.t: A calculated corrosion rate or remaining life must retain original measurements and uncertainty bounds. The inspection engineer ensures the model fits the observed mechanism rather than adopting a smooth average through localised damage. For non-linear, episodic or unforeseen degradation, a technical review determines a more conservative sampling and monitoring strategy.

sections.title: 10 Inspector competence, contractor control and verification

blocks.t: Inspection competence covers both technical method qualification and knowledge of ACE hazards and equipment. Contract inspection service providers require prequalification, method statements, specified certification levels, equipment calibration and competence in the applicable sector. Independent reviewers must be appropriately qualified for the examination and decision they verify.

rows: Discipline qualifications, relevant experience, examination method awareness and ACE role authorisation.
Personnel method certification, method-specific experience, written practice and valid equipment calibration.
Method competence, degradation knowledge, assumptions and independently reviewable calculations.
Marine permits, ROV/diver competence, survey positioning accuracy and evidence-quality plan.
Code/method competence, engineering assumptions, peer review and sign-off authority.
Asset identifier, report completeness, retention and controlled publication checks.

blocks.t: Inspection contractors shall be evaluated for task competence and quality controls before mobilisation, and nonconforming results shall not be accepted as asset integrity evidence until technically resolved.
The Inspection Lead shall determine whether independent review is required by the decision risk and shall document the reviewer, scope and resolution of any technical differences.

Where external certification or qualifications are required by a selected code, ACE verifies the certificate status rather than relying on a résumé. Contract inspection evidence is ACE-controlled once accepted; the supplier’s document numbering can remain as a linked record, while the approved WSE and anomaly systems retain ACE identities.

Inspection performance is evaluated by condition evidence quality, closure of critical anomalies and implementation of the risk strategy, not only task completion counts. The programme is reviewed for inspection effectiveness, repeated defects, high-risk backlog, inaccurate assumptions and known blind spots. Management learns from anomalies that revealed previously unrecognised degradation.

Core measures: safety-critical inspections completed on time; overdue WSEs; high-severity anomalies awaiting technical disposition; ageing of approved deferrals; rejected inspection reports; verification effectiveness; and inspections that cause changes to risk or operating envelopes.

rows: WSE → CMMS work order → report → accepted result.
Scope and quality met, not just date completed.
Threat model → consequence → interval basis → TA approval.
Evidence supports decision and regulatory constraints.
Original data → risk assessment → TA decision → operational restriction.
Workpack → inspection/test → technical acceptance → Area Authority release.
Qualification → procedure → calibration → raw data → review.

blocks.t: The Inspection Lead shall periodically review programme effectiveness and report overdue safety-critical inspections and unresolved high-risk anomalies to the Maintenance & Integrity Manager and system owner.

Lessons from inspections should be fed back into corrosion models, inspection strategies, equipment design, approved discipline practices, operating envelopes and supplier requirements. ACE’s future process mapping should expose each handoff, the accountable role and the resulting controlled record.

sections.title: Appendix A — Written scheme and inspection record schema

rows: Controlled WSE ID, revision, site, asset tag, boundary and equipment hierarchy.
Material, design rating, fluids, limits, conditions and process hazards.
Equipment-specific inspection code/practice and adopted edition identifier.
Consequence, probability, degradation and detection uncertainty.
Surface, CML/TML points, welds, accessible boundaries and exclusions.
Qualified method, sensitivity, calibration, acceptance and referral thresholds.
Previous/next due, shutdown window, deferral rules and review trigger.
Author, Inspection Lead, discipline TA and applicability limits.
Person, qualification, method, readings, raw data, anomalies and photographs.
Action, risk, restriction, workpack, reinspection and verification.

blocks.t: Data lineage is essential. Measurements should remain attached to the original equipment and point identity, even if an asset tag is later renamed. A cross-reference to the re-tagging change allows ONE to publish a coherent history without losing the original inspection evidence.

sections.title: Appendix B — Technique selection and quality checkpoints

rows: UT thickness grid, profile mapping, appropriate corrosion monitoring.
CML geometry, calibration, repeatability and access.
Trend comparability, min thickness and uncertainty.
Targeted insulation removal, visual, UT or other qualified method.
Findings mapped to CUI circuit and repairs.
Appropriate surface/volumetric NDT and engineering analysis.
Crack orientation, sensitivity and examiner qualification.
Defect dimension uncertainty and FFS referral.
ILI, dig validation, coating survey and targeted NDT.
Tool suitability, cleaning and survey baseline.
Matching of tool signals to confirmed defects.
ROV/diver close visual, CP and dimensional measurements.
Member ID, location, condition and review decisions.
Tank floor scan, thickness, settlement and tank code examinations.
Tank safety, cleaning and code scope.
Defect location, extent and tank acceptance.

blocks.t: Method examples identify plausible approaches; the approved WSE determines the actual method and acceptance criteria for each item.

sections.title: Appendix C — Anomaly assessment and action register

rows: Unique ID, inspector evidence and immediate hazard notification.
Potential and actual consequence, barrier status, uncertainty and required response speed.
Relevant TA review, code/FFS method, restrictions and approved due dates.
Area Authority acceptance of shutdown/restriction, permitted operating conditions and handover.
CMMS/MOC workpack, contractor permits, qualified repair and QA evidence.
Reinspection/test evidence, technical approval, restored barrier status.
Asset history, WSE/RBI revision, KPI update and feedback to relevant practices.

blocks.t: A live anomaly register is a decision instrument. The state “closed” must indicate verified resolution or an explicitly approved permanent technical disposition, not merely that someone has issued a work request. A temporary barrier impairment remains open and traceable until permanent restoration or an approved alternative is established.

sections.title: Appendix D — Cross-functional process catalogue and references

rows: RBI refresh; annual plan; design or operating change.
Inspection Lead WSE approval; CMMS package and schedule.
Qualified report → QA review → accepted evidence.
TA engineering disposition → Area Authority restriction.
Approved corrective action or performance shortfall.
MOC / permit / test → technical acceptance → restart release.
New conditions, incidents, known method gaps.
Updated risk model, WSE, intervals and approvals.
Anomaly or integrity analysis changes allowable conditions.
Engineering decision → operating register / DCS / briefing.

blocks.t: ACE references: ACE-OMS-MAN-001; ACE-AIM-STD-001; ACE-RSK-STD-001; ACE-MNT-STD-001; ACE-COW-STD-001; ACE-OPS-STD-001; ACE-MOC-PRC-001; ACE-OMS-STD-002; ACE-WEL-STD-001; ACE-ENG-STD-901; ACE-DOC-STD-001 and ACE-DOC-STD-002.

External references: API RP 580/581 (risk-based inspection), API 510 (pressure vessels), API 570 (in-service piping), API 653 (aboveground tanks), API 579-1/ASME FFS-1 (fitness for service), API RP 2SIM (fixed offshore structures). Adopted editions and applicability are controlled by ACE’s Engineering Standards Register.

sections.title: Appendix E — Asset-specific inspection plans and access interfaces

blocks.t: Inspection planning is asset-specific. Shared ACE discipline practices provide consistent methods, but a CPF vessel, offshore riser and land lease flowline differ in degradation drivers, access risk, work windows and escalation contacts. The following table serves as the baseline interface specification when an asset-specific WSE is created.

rows: Corrosion circuits, pressure boundaries, supports, corrosion under insulation, barrier status.
Offshore crew, isolation, accommodation and marine logistics.
OIM + Inspection Lead + Static Mechanical TA.
Pommerac A risers and splash zone
Coating, CP, splash-zone corrosion, supports and fatigue-sensitive areas.
Over-water access, weather windows and dropped-object controls.
Normally unmanned structures, wellhead connections, riser and marine damage.
Vessel/crew mobilisation, platform access and simultaneous operations.
Offshore Operations Manager and discipline TAs.
Internal metal loss, subsea spans, external corrosion, CP and third-party risks.
Marine survey contract, pigging feasibility, operations interface.
Pipelines Lead and Offshore Operations Manager.
Flowlines, lease tanks, pump structures, crossings and external corrosion.
Road access, landowner/interface arrangements, production isolation.
Separators, compression, process piping, relief equipment and tank farm.
Turnaround scheduling, confined-space entry, cleaning and controlled isolation.
Plant Manager + Inspection Lead + relevant TA.
Tank bottom and shells, settlement, transfer connections, jetty structure.
Marine loading windows, tank entry, fire protection and environmental response.
Plant Manager + Structural / Static Mechanical TAs.
Handling and loading infrastructure, lifting structures, storage assets.

blocks.t: Inspection campaigns must identify which organisation controls each interface: contractor mobilisation may be owned by Supply Chain, access and worksite control by Operations, technical examination by Inspection, and engineering disposition by a discipline Technical Authority. The process map records these handovers as explicit decisions with evidence rather than treating all of them as a single inspection task.

sections.title: Appendix F — Corrosion monitoring and inspection data quality

blocks.t: Corrosion monitoring combines in-service measurements with process knowledge. ACE corrosion data may include thickness histories, corrosion coupons, probes, fluid chemistry, inhibitor performance, leak history and metallurgical evidence. Before calculating rates or changes in remaining life, inspection engineering verifies that readings refer to the same physical location, measurement technique, operating regime and material condition.

rows: Comparability is lost when measurement locations move.
Re-locate, map deviation and establish a controlled baseline.
Systematic bias can resemble metal loss or metal gain.
Quarantine suspect data; repeat calibrated measurement.
Coatings, scale and geometry affect signal quality.
Repeat with specified preparation and method.
Acoustic velocity and technique depend on material and shape.
Verify material and technique suitability before trending.
Data show unexpected gain or abrupt loss
Readings may reflect error, local attack or changed service.
Technical review and targeted confirmation; do not smooth away.
Point measurements may miss pits or cracking.
Increase mapping coverage or use another qualified method.
Fluid or pressure changes can invalidate old corrosion models.
Update damage mechanism review and risk assessment.
Supports audit, repeat examination and independent reassessment.
Reject incomplete handover pending recovery of evidence.

blocks.t: Corrosion rates or remaining-life estimates used to set inspection intervals shall retain the measured data, assumptions, uncertainty and a documented review by a competent integrity specialist.

A reported trend must not be converted to a new operating restriction by the Inspector alone. The Materials & Corrosion Lead and relevant equipment Technical Authority evaluate the condition, the Integrity Engineer records the anomaly, and the Area Authority implements any restricted envelope through the operating-limit process.

sections.title: Appendix G — Critical inspection deferral and return-to-service evidence

blocks.t: An approved inspection deferral is a controlled, temporary risk decision. It is not an alternative to planning or a mechanism to reset the compliance clock. The record links the affected barrier or equipment, unavailable inspection evidence, interim controls, technical endorsement, risk acceptance authority and expiry. Deferral closure requires verification that the intended inspection was completed and any defects have been addressed.

rows: Tag, SCE link, WSE/CMMS reference, last evidence and original due date.
Reason work cannot be done and which failure mechanisms are unverified.
Consequence, likelihood, alternative monitors, restrictions and residual risk.
Technical endorsements, risk approval, revised due date, review checkpoint.
Location, operating envelope impact, shift and contractor communications.
Inspection result, anomaly status, test, acceptance and formal release evidence.

blocks.t: Safety-critical inspection deferrals shall have a current authorised expiry and interim barrier assessment; once expired, the approved safe state applies until a new formal decision or completed examination resolves the condition.
The closing record shall retain proof that the inspection meets its intended WSE scope, or identify the residual items and the separate authority controlling them.

sections.title: Appendix H — Decision examples and scenario controls

blocks.t: Scenario — CPF separator wall-loss indication. An inspection campaign identifies a local thickness change at a nozzle transition on a CPF separator. The inspection report records the measurement grid, calibration, original condition and uncertainty. Inspection Engineering opens an anomaly. The Static Mechanical Lead determines whether more examination or a fitness assessment is required. The Integrity Engineer evaluates barrier impact. The Plant Manager controls whether the separator continues at a restricted envelope or is isolated pending repair. A later repair is accepted against a documented engineering requirement and a new baseline inspection.

Scenario — subsea pipeline survey. A Gulf of Paria pipeline survey detects a free span and coating anomalies. The Pipelines Lead reviews spans against the design and current environmental loading basis, and the Materials & Corrosion Lead evaluates CP/coating evidence. Inspection Engineering integrates survey coordinates and previous trends. If an operating pressure restriction or increased surveillance is required, the Offshore Operations Manager implements it under ACE-OPS-STD-001; the condition is tracked until verified closure, even if the survey contractor has completed its contract.

Scenario — land lease flowline leak history. Recurrent pinhole leaks on a Pawpaw gathering line indicate a possible damage-mechanism mismatch or inhibitor programme gap. Rather than repeating local repair without learning, the Inspection Lead and Materials & Corrosion Lead update the corrosion threat model, verify wall thickness and fluid conditions, and propose an appropriate inspection interval and monitoring plan. The Land Operations Manager controls line availability and permits; the Pipelines Lead endorses repair or replacement requirements. Completion records feed both the WSE and operating envelope.

Scenario — safety-critical inspection during shutdown. A high-priority CPF inspection is constrained by a delayed isolation. The Maintenance & Integrity Manager reviews the shutdown critical path with the Plant Manager. The Inspection Lead confirms whether the scope can be completed in the remaining access window, without losing detection effectiveness. An incomplete scope cannot be marked as full technical closure; a documented alternative strategy or approved deferral must be in place before restart.

revisions.text: Initial approved issue. Defines the mandatory ACE inspection and examination requirements.

docs.subtitle: The ACE process architecture, process ownership and the golden thread from mission to record.

blocks.t: This Practice sets out how ACE organises its work as business processes, and how those processes connect the company’s mission, vision and values to the records that prove work was done. It defines the ACE Process Architecture, the rules for owning a process, the choice between document types, and the traceability rules that let ONE show any requirement together with the process that carries it out.

Parent: ACE-LDR-POL-001 OMS Policy. The Practice applies to every ACE function and site (PAP, CHB, SAP, CPF, LND, PLB, HOF) and to contractors whose work is part of an ACE process. It is the parent of ACE-BPM-PRA-002 Process Modelling and Process File Practice and ACE-BPM-PRA-003 Process Ownership and Continuous Improvement Practice.

Business Process Management (BPM) is an OMS system. Its system owner is the Manager, Strategy & Planning, and its executive sponsor is the Chief Executive Officer. BPM supports OMS elements 1, 2, 3, 7 and 10.

Recognised practice applied: APQC Process Classification Framework (PCF), cross-industry and petroleum upstream versions; ISO/IEC 19510 Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) 2.0; ISO 9001 clause 4.4 (process approach); IOGP Report 510 Operating Management System Framework.

BPM separates the person who owns a process from the people who own its documents, its technical content and its workforce. These roles can be held by one person, but they are assigned separately so that each accountability is visible in ONE.

blocks.t: The BPM system owner shall maintain the ACE Process Architecture and the Process Register, and shall present their status to the Executive Leadership Team once a year.
Each function VP shall nominate the process owners for the L3 processes whose primary function is theirs.
The appointment of a process owner shall be approved in writing by the VP of the process’s primary function and recorded in the Process Register.

The golden thread is the unbroken line from why ACE exists to the record that shows a task was done. Every controlled document and every process sits somewhere on this line. ONE draws the line from the documents themselves: each document names its parent, each process names its governing Policy and parent Standard or Practice, and each step names the document sections, controls and records it relies on.

The BPM system owner shall confirm once a year that every corporate objective in the Objectives and Opportunities register (OMS-REG-001) is supported by at least one L3 process, and record any gap as an action (C-BPM-001).

ACE uses a five-level architecture in the style of the APQC Process Classification Framework. Levels 1 and 2 group the work. Level 3 is the unit of ownership: one L3 process is one Process document (PRS pair) with one process owner. Levels 4 and 5 sit inside the process: an activity is a step in its swimlane model, and a task is the procedure or work instruction that tells someone how to do the step.

blocks.t: A new L3 process shall only be added to the Process Register when it is placed under one L2 group in the architecture above (C-BPM-002).
A change to the L1 or L2 lists shall be approved by the BPM system owner after review by the OMS Manager and the affected function VPs.
A process with two owners has none. ACE therefore applies a strict one-owner rule at Level 3. The owner may delegate work but not the accountability.
Each L3 process shall have exactly one process owner, one primary function and one governing Policy, recorded in the Process Register (C-BPM-003).
A process owner shall hold a position at manager level or above in the primary function of the process.

Cross-functional processes still have one owner. The owner is taken from the function that carries the outcome. For example, the Management of Change process (ACE-MOC-PRS-001) crosses Operations, Engineering & Projects and HSE & Compliance, but its outcome — a safely implemented change — is carried by Engineering & Projects, so its owner is the Manager, Technical Excellence.

blocks.t: Writers choose the document type by the question it answers, not by its length. The test is simple: if a sentence describes a sequence of steps performed by named roles, it belongs in a Process or Procedure, not in a Standard or Practice.

blocks.t: A Practice shall not repeat the requirements of its parent Standard and shall not contain step-by-step role sequences.
Where a writer is unsure, the Information Management Lead and the BPM custodian decide the type before drafting starts. Changing type after approval needs a new document number.

Traceability is what lets ONE answer the questions auditors and managers ask: which process carries out this requirement, who owns it, and where is the evidence? It works only if the links are written into the documents at source.
Every Standard and Practice shall contain a table of the processes and procedures that implement it, showing each item as Current or Planned (C-BPM-004).
Every binding requirement in a Standard shall be carried out by at least one process step, or be marked in the Process Register as ‘direct’ where no process is needed (C-BPM-005).
Every L3 process shall trace up to its parent Standard or Practice and down to the procedures that perform its steps, and ONE shall flag any broken link as a gateway warning (C-BPM-006).

blocks.t: Example: ACE-AIM-STD-001 requires that SCE inspections are completed or formally deferred. ACE-AIM-PRA-001 sets the deferral rule (C-AIM-004). ACE-AIM-PRS-001 carries it out in a deferral step owned by the Inspection Lead, and the evidence is the deferral record in ONE. Opening the requirement in ONE shows all four, and the process owner who answers for them.

The Process Register (ACE-BPM-REG-001) is the master list of ACE processes. It is a controlled register file in the repository (registers/BPM-REG-001.csv). ONE reads it to draw the process architecture, the process library and the coverage matrix.

blocks.t: The Process Register shall be reconciled with the document register every quarter so that every Current process has an approved PRS pair at the same revision (C-BPM-007).
Changes to the Process Register shall be made only by the Practice custodian and shall be recorded in the register’s change log with date, change and approver.

blocks.t: ONE shows the register as a three-ring wheel: L1 categories on the inner ring, L2 groups in the middle and L3 processes outside. Each process tile shows its owner, status, maturity and the number of controls it performs. Selecting a tile opens the process reader (swimlanes) defined in ACE-BPM-PRA-002. A coverage matrix shows OMS systems against document layers, so gaps in the Process layer are visible.

Many organisations already hold process maps in a modelling tool, a spreadsheet or a quality system. ACE’s architecture is built so that those maps can be brought in rather than redrawn. The architecture codes, the PRS number and the role names are the keys; any tool that can export them can feed the Process Register.

blocks.t: This Practice sets how ACE describes a process so that people can read it and ONE can draw, check and later simulate it. It defines the Process (PRS) document pair, the modelling conventions, the fields of the process file, the links from steps to documents, controls and roles, and how the ONE process reader displays the result.

Parent: ACE-BPM-PRA-001 Business Process Management Practice, which defines the process architecture and the one-owner rule. This Practice applies to every L3 process in the Process Register (ACE-BPM-REG-001) at all sites.

Recognised practice applied: ISO/IEC 19510 Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) 2.0 — a small subset only; SIPOC analysis as used in ISO 9001 process documentation; APQC Process Classification Framework levels.

A Process is controlled as a pair of files with the same number and revision. The Word process description is the controlled source of the narrative — purpose, ownership, scope and what each step means. The process model file carries the structure — lanes, steps, gateways and links — in a form ONE can read. Neither is complete without the other.

Every exclusive gateway branch carries a label (for example ‘Major’, ‘Minor’) so the reader and later the simulation know which condition sends work down which path.

docs.subtitle: What process owners do, how processes are measured, reviewed and improved, and how maturity is assessed.

blocks.t: This Practice sets what a process owner does, how process performance is measured, how processes are reviewed and improved, and how process maturity is assessed and shown in ONE. It makes sure that ACE processes get better over time rather than simply being written down.
Parent: ACE-BPM-PRA-001 Business Process Management Practice. The Practice applies to every L3 process in the Process Register (ACE-BPM-REG-001) and to everyone appointed as a process owner.
Recognised practice applied: ISO 9001 clause 10.3 (continual improvement); Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle; capability maturity concepts as used in process maturity models.
Four roles touch every process. They are often confused, so this Practice separates them clearly.

rows: Design, performance and continuous improvement of the end-to-end flow

blocks.t: The process owner shall be accountable for the design, performance and continuous improvement of their process across every function it touches.
The process owner shall report process KPIs to the VP of the primary function at least every quarter.
Line managers shall release staff for process reviews and shall implement the process changes approved for their teams.

blocks.t: Each process owner shall complete process owner training within 60 days of appointment, and the training record shall be held by Learning & Competence (C-BPM-040).
Every L3 process has at least four KPIs, one in each family below. Process owners may add more. KPIs come from records the process already creates, so measuring them adds no extra work in the field.

blocks.t: Every L3 process shall have at least one KPI in each of the four families, with a target, defined in its PRS description (C-BPM-041).
KPI values shall be calculated from process records and shall state the period and the sample size.
Each process is reviewed at least once a year. A review is also triggered when something happens that suggests the process may not be working as intended.

Each process owner shall hold an annual process review that covers KPIs, control health, linked incidents and audit findings, open actions and maturity, and shall record the outcome in ONE (C-BPM-042).
A trigger review shall start within 30 days of any of the triggers in the table below (C-BPM-043).

blocks.t: Review records shall list attendees, the evidence reviewed, decisions and actions, and shall be retained for five years.
Not every improvement needs the same level of control. The route depends on what is being changed.

blocks.t: A change that alters roles, controls or systems in a process shall be made through ACE-MOC-PRC-001 and not by document revision alone (C-BPM-044).
After a process change, the process owner shall confirm that the people in each affected lane have been briefed before the revised process becomes effective (C-BPM-045).

Maturity describes how well a process is defined, controlled and improved. Process owners self-assess every year. The OMS Manager uses the results in the OMS maturity assessment (ACE-OMS-MAN-001, Part C.4).

A process shall not be assessed above Level 2 unless its KPIs have been measured for at least one full year.

docs.owner: Sasha George — VP Supply Chain Management

docs.applies: All ACE activities, sites, employees and contractors
docs.subtitle: How ACE moves people and materials safely, chooses and manages contractors and suppliers, and builds local content.

blocks.t: This policy sets ACE's commitments for moving people and materials safely to and from its sites, and for buying goods and services from capable contractors and suppliers, with a preference for Trinidad and Tobago companies and nationals.

It applies to marine and aviation movements between the Point Lisas Shore Base (PLB) and the offshore installations (PAP, CHB, SAP), to road movements to the CPF and the land leases (LND), to the shore base warehouse, and to every contract and purchase made by any ACE function. Its parent is ACE-LDR-POL-001. Tender and contract award value limits are set by ACE-FIN-POL-001, which also applies to the processes listed here.
Each commitment names the ACE values it serves, as set in ACE-LDR-POL-001 section 1. The steps that deliver the commitments are in the governed processes and implementing documents in section 6.

In line with our value Safety above all, every person who travels offshore is on the manifest, has completed the required induction and offshore survival training, holds the competence their role needs and is fit for work. Personnel on board (POB) at every installation and on every vessel and helicopter is known at all times.

No person shall board a helicopter or vessel for an ACE offshore installation unless they are on the approved manifest and have passed the pre-boarding checks of induction, competence and fitness for work.
Personnel on board shall be recorded and reconciled for each installation, vessel and flight at every departure and arrival.

In line with our value Safety above all, all cargo is declared on the manifest, dangerous goods are identified, packed, marked and documented to the applicable dangerous goods rules, and lifting equipment and cargo carrying units are within their certification. Undeclared or uncertified cargo does not travel.

sections.title: 2.3 Transport decisions belong to the competent person

blocks.t: In line with our values Safety above all and Integrity in everything, the weather and sea-state limits for vessel and helicopter movements are set by the Marine Lead and by the helicopter operator, and the master or pilot decides whether a movement goes ahead. These limits are never overridden to keep a schedule, and anyone may stop a movement under the stop work commitment of ACE-LDR-POL-001.

In line with our values Safety above all and One team, one way, when a flight or a vessel is oversubscribed, seats and deck space are allocated in a fixed order, the same at every site. The order is set in section 4.2 and is the decision point in the trip planning process when demand exceeds capacity.

sections.title: 2.5 Contractors selected and managed by risk

blocks.t: In line with our values Safety above all and One team, one way, the risk of the work, not its value, sets how much assurance a contract receives. Contractors are risk-rated before procurement, pre-qualified where the rating requires, bridged into ACE arrangements before mobilisation and monitored through the contract (ACE-CON-STD-001). ACE stays accountable for work it delegates.

In line with our value Care for people and places, ACE prefers Trinidad and Tobago suppliers, contractors and nationals wherever they are capable of meeting our safety, technical and quality requirements, and helps local suppliers become capable. Local content is a scored criterion in every tender evaluation; the targets are set in section 4.4.

In line with our values Safety above all and Integrity in everything, critical items are inspected and traceable to their manufacture, test and certification before they are accepted. Nonconforming supply is identified, segregated and kept out of use until it has a recorded disposition.

docs.title: Contractor and Supplier Management Standard
docs.owner: Sasha George — VP Supply Chain Management
docs.author: Rhea Sookram — Contracts Manager
docs.approver: Sasha George — VP Supply Chain Management
docs.reviewers: Gillian Modeste — Procurement Manager; Christina Bain — HSE Manager; Terrence Henry — Quality Lead
docs.applies: All ACE functions, locations, suppliers, contractors and subcontractors within contracted scope
docs.subtitle: Risk-based contracting, supplier assurance and worksite interfaces from selection to verified close-out.

blocks.t: This standard sets ACE requirements for acquiring, directing and assuring contractor and supplier services and materials. It applies from the first definition of a contract need through sourcing, selection, mobilisation, execution, acceptance and retention of records. It covers third parties at Pommerac A, Chenet B, Sapodilla C, the Gulf of Paria pipelines, the Tamarind, Pawpaw and Soursop leases, the Central Processing Facility (CPF), Point Lisas Shore Base and Head Office.

ACE retains accountability for safety, operating integrity, environmental protection and contractual performance when work is delegated. The risk of the work—not its contract value—determines the depth of HSE, technical and quality assurance. The work owner controls field interfaces; Supply Chain controls the sourcing and commercial process. Discipline Technical Authorities remain accountable for technical standards.
A contract owner shall be nominated before a request for sourcing is issued and shall maintain an approved scope, risk screen, delivery acceptance criteria and performance measures.
Any contractor working at an ACE-operated location shall comply with ACE Control of Work requirements or an ACE-approved documented bridging arrangement.
Interfaces: ACE-RSK-STD-001 Risk Management Standard; ACE-COW-STD-001 Control of Work Standard; ACE-MOC-PRC-001 Management of Change Procedure; ACE-AIM-STD-001 Asset Integrity Management Standard.

A contract is a managed obligation covering services, labour, equipment hire or supply of goods. An ACE purchase order may be the commercial instrument but does not remove the need for risk screening and technical acceptance. Where a prime contractor engages subcontractors, the prime remains accountable for its chain; ACE retains the right to inspect competence, control measures and records for each material subcontractor.
Subcontracting of safety-critical tasks, marine activities, well interventions or regulated work shall receive documented contract-owner approval before the subcontractor mobilises.

The contract owner screens reasonably foreseeable personnel, process safety, environmental, technical, commercial, cyber and logistics exposures using the one ACE Risk Matrix. The contract category is based on the highest credible uncontrolled or residual exposure, criticality of deliverables, duration and interfaces. Contract risk class guides assurance effort; it does not replace task risk assessments, HAZOP, permit-to-work or acceptance of operational risk.
The contract risk screen shall identify the highest material exposure, assumptions, proposed barriers, interface owners and recommended risk class before procurement begins.

Where the scope could affect a major accident barrier, safety-critical equipment, well containment or an unmanned offshore installation, the relevant Technical Authority shall review the screening assumptions.

rows: Routine offsite services or standard goods with low exposure
Basic eligibility and specification checks; receiving inspection; completion review
Recurring work with ACE site access or managed technical interfaces
HSE pre-qualification, named supervisor, mobilisation evidence and scheduled field verification
Hazardous work, offshore marine interfaces or safety-critical tasks
HSE and technical pre-qualification, formal bridging, hold points and monthly performance review
Complex work with multiple barriers or major-accident exposure
High-level approval, multidisciplinary assurance plan, leadership oversight and independent verification

blocks.t: Figure 1. Contract assurance intensity follows the ACE risk-screen decision.

The classification is revisited when incident history, duration, subcontracting, equipment, logistics route or interface complexity changes. The contract owner initiates an MOC when the change falls within ACE change-control criteria; contract variation alone does not replace MOC.
A contract risk classification shall be reviewed at award, before mobilisation and following a material change, major incident or adverse assurance finding.

Pre-qualification establishes whether the provider can safely and consistently deliver the scope. The Contracts Manager coordinates the process. HSE & Compliance examines management arrangements and leading indicators; the technical discipline examines methods, equipment and competent personnel; Quality checks inspection and manufacturing arrangements where relevant.
Contractors performing Medium, High or Very High risk work shall pass HSE pre-qualification before award, in accordance with the OMS Manual.

rows: Registration, insurance, statutory permits, ownership and restrictions
Risk assessment, incident data, leadership practices, emergency capability, subcontractor control
Role matrix, training and verification for safety-critical roles, supervisors and assessors
Method statements, calibration, traceability, inspection plans, previous technical outcomes
Capacity, spare equipment, transport, supply route and business continuity

blocks.t: A qualification can be accepted, accepted with pre-award conditions, or declined. Material weaknesses involving legal eligibility, barrier protection or unqualified safety-critical personnel prevent qualification until corrected. A condition may be allowed only where a specified control can be fully verified before mobilisation.
The Contracts Manager shall record the pre-qualification decision, named reviewing authorities, unresolved actions and any conditions that must be met before award or mobilisation.
Do not treat a low tender price or a contractual indemnity as a substitute for competent personnel, adequate barriers or valid permits.

Tender packages should state the deliverables, ACE sites, work boundaries, interfaces, technical specifications, measurable acceptance criteria, required records and the risk-specific assurance approach. The evaluation plan is agreed before responses are opened and captures any mandatory pass/fail conditions separately from weighted scoring. For a hazardous contract, a low commercial price cannot override a failed mandatory HSE gate.
Tender evaluation shall use written, pre-established technical, HSE, delivery and commercial criteria proportionate to contract risk.

rows: Evidence of pre-qualification and risk-specific controls
No award while mandatory HSE gate fails
Conformance with specification, critical materials and engineering exceptions
Capacity, logistics approach, subcontractors and applicable commitments
Whole-life pricing, payment, contract conditions and uncertainty allowances

blocks.t: The award recommendation records the qualified bidders, evaluation findings, clarifications, conflicts of interest, risk screen and selected commercial instrument. Approval is by the delegated authority recorded in ACE procurement governance. Technical or HSE endorsement is evidence supporting the decision, not a substitute for the commercial approval.
The approved tender evaluation, award recommendation, signed agreement, risk screen and contractual scope shall be registered in the controlled contract record.

Before work starts, the contract owner and Area Authority test readiness rather than relying solely on corporate certificates. A mobilising supplier must demonstrate named competent personnel, maintained equipment, approved lifting and transport arrangements, valid site access and a clear method for escalating unsafe conditions. For offshore deployments this includes vessel, weather and personnel-transfer interfaces; for CPF or land operations it includes road, process isolation and emergency assembly interfaces.

The contract owner shall complete a documented mobilisation readiness review, including contractor personnel, equipment, training, supervision, emergency arrangements, permits and work boundaries, before the first work release.

High-risk contractors shall demonstrate that worksite supervision and the applicable permit-to-work, isolation, simultaneous-operations and emergency-response controls are established before arrival at the workface.

rows: Roster, critical competencies, medical/fitness where applicable, inductions
Inspection status, load tests, calibration, certification and preservation
Method statement, task assessment, permits, isolations, SIMOPS boundaries
Manifest, transport plan, vessel and loading interfaces, receiving arrangements
Contacts, alarms, muster, medevac interface and incident notification

blocks.t: A bridging document explains how equivalent contractor controls meet ACE expectations, who has authority to stop work, which rules prevail at interfaces and where evidence is retained. It is limited to differences that require management; it is not a second management system. Any proposed departure from a mandatory ACE requirement is processed under the deviation standard rather than described vaguely as “contractor practice”.
The Area Authority and relevant HSE or Technical Authority shall endorse a risk-based contractor bridging arrangement before the affected operations begin.
Figure 2. Lifecycle stage gates and controlled handovers.

The contract owner ensures the contract scope translates to safe daily instructions, and the Area Authority retains operational control of the location. The performing authority provides task-level supervision and checks crew understanding. Where multiple contractors, ACE operations and marine activity coincide, SIMOPS reviews establish the boundaries, priorities, communications and suspension criteria.
The Area Authority shall control work release, permit coordination, simultaneous operations and the response to unsafe conditions at the ACE location.
Contractor supervisors shall verify that the applicable work permits, isolation certificates, toolbox briefings and hold-point approvals are in place before task execution.

Field verification concentrates on controls with the largest potential consequences: line breaking, lifting, confined spaces, hot work, marine transfers and barrier impairments. Observed deviations are recorded with action owner and target date; the contract owner follows up contractor corrective actions. ACE personnel and contractors have the duty to stop unsafe work without awaiting a contract change.
Work involving an ineffective or unavailable critical barrier shall stop until the impairment is assessed, compensating controls are approved and the Area Authority releases the work.
A material change to contractor personnel, methods, technical scope or worksite interfaces shall be screened against the Management of Change Procedure before implementation.

Performance assurance combines lagging results and leading evidence of control effectiveness. For contracts rated High or Very High, ACE holds a formal review at least monthly; Medium contracts are reviewed at least quarterly; Low contracts are reviewed at completion or at intervals set by the contract owner. A major incident or repeated defect triggers an immediate extraordinary review.
Contract owners shall conduct and record performance reviews at the frequency specified for each contract risk class.

rows: Critical work orders completed against planned critical work
Escalate overdue or ineffective barrier checks
Permit verification defects per sampled permit
Accepted lots / inspected lots and recurring NCRs
Inspection hold points or supplier development

blocks.t: The performance meeting decides whether the contract continues, requires recovery, needs tighter oversight, moves to formal contractual remedy or should be considered for suspension. Repeated process-safety deficiencies must be surfaced to the relevant technical owner and HSE. Lessons learned are shared with the contracts and supplier qualification teams to inform future sourcing decisions.
Each performance review shall retain the scorecard, significant findings, corrective actions, contract decisions and evidence of closure in the controlled contract record.

Supplier quality requirements scale with the service or material consequence. Items contributing to a safety-critical element need an identified technical specification, approved manufacturer or equivalent evaluation, documented inspection/test points and traceability sufficient for intended service. Receipt at the Point Lisas Shore Base, land lease or CPF is a new quality gate rather than automatic acceptance.
Safety-critical equipment and materials shall be accepted against documented technical requirements and verified evidence of manufacture, inspection, test and traceability.

rows: Datasheet, specification, MTC or certificate, inspection/test results, serial and traceability
Inspection certificate, calibration where required, dimensional/functional checks
Purchase-order match, damage inspection, quantity verification

blocks.t: A receiving or fabrication nonconformance is uniquely logged, physically identified when possible, and controlled to prevent unintended use. Disposition options include return, rework, repair, concession or rejection. A concession that alters a technical specification or safety barrier requires Technical Authority review and, where appropriate, an OMS deviation or MOC.
Nonconforming safety-critical items shall remain segregated or positively controlled until technical disposition and release are recorded.

Contract completion is both a commercial and operational event. The contract owner checks that technical deliverables are accepted, work areas reinstated, permits closed, temporary materials removed, punch items risk-assessed and as-built documentation or data transferred to ACE repositories. Final payment approvals do not, by themselves, demonstrate safety or quality close-out.
The contract owner shall obtain operational and technical acceptance of the agreed deliverables before recording contract closure.

rows: Permit closure, isolation release, reinstatement and housekeeping
Inspection packs, as-built documents, test evidence, material certification
Final scorecard, NCR closures, improvement actions and vendor record

blocks.t: The final evaluation is retained against the supplier record and made available to future evaluation teams. The evaluation distinguishes contractor-caused performance issues from failures of ACE scope definition or site readiness. Where a recurring failure is systemic, the owner commissions a cross-functional review and updates requirements or qualifications accordingly.
The final supplier evaluation, acceptance records and open-item ownership shall be stored with the contract close-out record for the period specified by the Document and Records Management Standard.
Figure 3. Interface responsibilities supporting the accountable contract owner.

rows: Sasha George — VP Supply Chain Management
System owner; escalates significant supplier and commercial exposure.
Controls sourcing and contract administration; maintains contract record and close-out.
Runs procurement evaluation process, fairness, qualification trail and award documentation.
Reviews contractor HSE capability, serious findings and risk-based assurance.
Defines inspection and supplier-quality evidence for procured goods and services.
Manages logistics, receiving, material movement and marine/shore base interfaces.
Controls the operational worksite, permits, isolations, SIMOPS and work release.
Endorses technical specifications, equipment deviations and technical dispositions.

blocks.t: The system owner uses risk-based sample checks and management review to test whether the process is working, not simply whether documents exist. Reportable trends include unqualified high-risk awards, mobilisations missing hold-point evidence, repeat permit observations, overdue safety-critical supplier NCRs, and contract close-outs with unresolved operational actions.

The Contracts Manager shall maintain an auditable trail linking screening, pre-qualification, tender evaluation, approvals, execution assurance, supplier quality and close-out records to the unique contract reference.

docs.author: Adrian Rodriguez — Permit to Work Coordinator (Offshore)
