docs.title: Operational Document Publishing Standard
docs.owner: Marvin Williams — VP IT, Data & Knowledge
docs.author: Ryan Ramsaran — Technical Writer / Procedures Specialist
docs.approver: Marvin Williams — VP IT, Data & Knowledge
docs.reviewers: Sanjay Jagessar — Information Management Lead; Marissa Bobb — OMS Manager; Paul Gomes — Document Controller
docs.applies: All ACE functions, assets, sites, projects, staff and relevant contractors
docs.subtitle: Mandatory Word authoring, semantic structure, OMS tags, metadata, automated gateway and ONE publication rules.

sections.title: 1 Purpose and the controlled publishing model

blocks.t: This Standard defines how ACE prepares Word documents so that the approved source can be reliably interpreted, tested and displayed by ONE. It establishes a common authoring contract between document owners, authors, Document Control, the OMS Manager and the publishing software. The contract is based on Word styles, content controls, stable heading identities, document properties and evidence of approval.

The core principle is source authority: approved Microsoft Word documents remain the controlled instructions. ONE reads their structure, exposes the sections that support each OMS expectation and supplies additional routes through functions, business processes, roles and document relationships. Displayed excerpts or generated web pages are derived representations; they do not replace the approved source.
Only a numbered Approved Word revision that has passed the publishing gateway shall enter the current ONE views.
The publishing process shall retain enough information to trace each displayed requirement and section to the exact document ID, revision and heading or paragraph from which it was taken.

rows: Approved ACE Word template and controlled reference sources
Named author creates a well-structured draft
Draft Word source, comment log and relevant technical basis
Reviewed source, endorsement and approval evidence
Submitted Word source, OMS register and rules catalogue
Accepted gate report and exact authorised source
Published Word source and controlled metadata
Parser builds section records and navigation
Current web representation, approved source link and communications
Users receive the correct revision and change notice

blocks.t: The DOC system is owned by Marvin Williams, VP IT, Data & Knowledge. Sanjay Jagessar, Information Management Lead, controls numbering and publication acceptance. Ryan Ramsaran, Technical Writer / Procedures Specialist, supports authors with structure and style. Paul Gomes and Allison St. Hill perform central document-control functions. Marissa Bobb, OMS Manager, maintains framework mapping and conformance rules. Shalini Mungal, Data & Applications Manager, supports implementation and data governance.

Operational system owners remain accountable for their content. A web developer cannot approve a new operating requirement by correcting extracted text; errors discovered in publication are corrected in the controlled source, revalidated and republished through the documented route.
Information Management Lead: Owns the content-control schema, publication rules, exception register and release decision following gateway acceptance.
OMS Manager: Controls the expectation register and approves interpretation of framework tags and coverage logic.
Technical Writer: Maintains author guidance, template quality and consistent use of Word meaning styles across document classes.
ACE-OMS-MAN-001, One Management System Manual, Part D — enterprise source of the document standard.
ACE-DOC-STD-001, Document and Records Management Standard — numbering, status, repository, records and retention.

sections.title: 2 ACE Word templates and document anatomy

blocks.t: All controlled OMS documents begin with an ACE-approved Word template, not a blank file that imitates its appearance. The master template contains the reusable style definitions, structured metadata controls, cover elements, page headers and footers, section levels and document references. Type-specific variants may suppress unnecessary content while preserving required controls.

Manuals, policies, standards, procedures, plans, work instructions, registers, forms and technical specifications may have different body layouts. A form might use a compact instruction block and structured fields; a technical specification may add discipline schedules and drawings. They still carry the same controlled identity, OMS tag mechanism and approval status.

rows: ONE identity; company name; controlled title; ID; revision; status; effective date
Owner, custodian, author, review, endorsement, approval, class, scope
Issue, change description and decision date
Named decision authorities and evidence reference
Numbered Word headings, semantic paragraphs, native tables/figures
Controlled document IDs, external references if relevant
ID, revision, current-source notice and page marker

blocks.t: The ONE visual identity uses the ACE-approved wordmark, segment symbol, teal, orange and dark-navy accents, with consistent information hierarchy. Branding is part of document recognition and reinforces that a task instruction belongs to a coherent management system. Visual consistency does not replace coded Word styles: a visually large bold paragraph is not a Heading 1 unless Word assigns that style.

A change in corporate branding or template version is coordinated by the Information Management Lead. Re-styling an approved issue without changing the recorded revision is not a permitted publication path when it changes section interpretation, document content or displayed obligations.

Authors shall retain the defined Word style names and content-control tags. A style may be visually adapted only through an approved template revision that preserves its semantic identifier and parser contract.

sections.title: 2.3 Required front matter and framing sections

blocks.t: Every controlled document carries the appropriate purpose, scope, definitions or abbreviations, governing references, approval information and revision history. Short documents may combine framing material where the template permits, but they do not omit evidence of authority or source identity.

The document owner verifies that scope includes affected assets, roles, contractor interfaces and exclusions. A document controlling an operational task identifies prerequisites, steps or rules, hold points, verification, records and recovery actions as appropriate to its type. A technical document also identifies the applicable standards and equipment or design basis.
The approved document title, document-control table, Word core properties and custom document properties shall describe the same controlled object and revision.

The only supported document outline levels are Word Title, Heading 1, Heading 2 and Heading 3. Numbering is written in the heading text, such as “5 Semantic paragraph styles”, “5.2 Applying requirement styles” or “5.2.1 Approval gates”. A heading is a navigable structural boundary, not merely an attractive line of text.

Title identifies the document. Heading 1 begins a major section; Heading 2 a section beneath it; Heading 3 a subsection beneath Heading 2. Authors avoid skipped levels and do not use Normal style with enlarged type to create a pseudo-heading.
A document shall use the approved outline styles and logical nesting. Heading text shall include the appropriate section number except for approved front matter and appendices.
Each heading intended for ONE navigation shall contain a unique persistent bookmark or equivalent section identifier that remains stable when the heading text is edited.

ONE deep links are anchored to section identities rather than page numbers or visible title strings. The preferred identity is a unique Word bookmark located at the beginning of the heading paragraph. It may contain letters, digits and underscores and may not be duplicated within the source. The section identifier should be recorded independently of the displayed numbering so inserted sections do not invalidate links.

When a section is renamed without changing its meaning, retain its bookmark. When the subject is fundamentally replaced or split, the owner identifies a new stable section ID and records a predecessor relationship or redirect. Reordering sections changes their document position but not their controlled identity.

rows: Do not recycle an old section ID

blocks.t: A reader determines each heading’s section as the content that begins at that heading and ends immediately before the next heading at the same or higher outline level. A Heading 1 section includes the nested headings beneath it as content; each Heading 2 or 3 also has its own logical child section. Extraction must preserve the difference between document ownership, outline containment and explicit OMS tags.

The parser records the original order of paragraphs, lists, figures and tables. It does not infer a new heading from page breaks or bold formatting. Repeated section titles at different locations are permitted if their bookmark IDs differ. A missing or duplicate bookmark on a navigable heading is a gateway failure.

Page numbers are useful in printed documents but unstable across devices. ONE links to documents, sections and controlled items by document ID, revision and structural identifier. Generated table of contents content may be used for Word readers, but the portal builds its own navigation from Word headings. An author may introduce an Appendix without using Heading 4 or higher.
No external sidecar file is required from authors to define heading structure; the identity and structure live in the approved Word document.

OMS expectation tags link a document or section to the numbered expectations of the IOGP 510 framework adopted by ACE. The visible control sits immediately beneath the Title or the corresponding heading, displays “OMS”, and stores a comma-separated list of expectation numbers in most-relevant-first order. The official control carries a machine-readable association with the heading bookmark.

Tags are numbers only: “7.1, 1.7, 7.4” is valid. “E7.1”, ranges, commentary, duplicate values and unknown expectation numbers are invalid. Authors may assign any number of valid expectations or leave a section untagged where a linkage would be misleading.
An OMS tag list shall contain valid expectation numbers from the controlled ACE OMS expectation register, separated by commas and without duplicates.
The tag control for a heading shall reference that heading’s stable identifier; a free-text note resembling an OMS tag shall not be treated as a controlled tag.

rows: Valid numeric IDs, unique and ordered by relevance
E prefix not permitted in stored tags
Ranges do not identify discrete expectations

sections.title: 4.2 Tag relevance, document scope and heading scope

blocks.t: Title tags state which expectations the whole approved document supports. Heading tags describe their own section. The ordered list is qualitative relevance: first means strongest association, not a separate approval ranking. Multiple tags are appropriate for cross-functional work where an action genuinely contributes to more than one expectation.

A heading tag applies to the section bounded by the next same-level or higher-level heading. Child headings do not automatically inherit the tag as an explicit tag on the child; the system may show them within their parent section while retaining their own explicit associations. The distinction prevents false claim inflation in coverage and gap reporting.

rows: Parent section explicitly linked to two expectations
Child is explicitly linked only to 7.4
No explicit tag; remains visible in ancestor outline

sections.title: 4.3 Controlled expectation register and mapping decisions

blocks.t: The OMS Manager maintains the expectation register, including valid identifiers, descriptions, current framework version and element ownership. The register is used for gateway validation and coverage reporting. The parser must not silently treat a newly typed number as valid or guess a nearest matching expectation.

Where an ACE-specific management framework contains longer hierarchical identifiers, the system can support a separate controlled namespace, but that namespace must not be mixed into the IOGP 510 mapping without an explicit configured scheme. For the documents covered by this standard, IOGP-style expectation IDs are the default.
OMS Manager: Resolves disputed expectation mappings, maintains the authoritative register and authorises controlled mapping changes.
Document owner: Proposes the actual expectation relationships and verifies that the document genuinely delivers those obligations.

ONE can identify whether an expectation has mapped documents and which sections state how it is addressed. This is evidence of documented coverage, not proof of operational implementation. Conformance requires review of actual work practices, records, barriers, performance and assurance evidence. The portal must preserve that distinction in labels and dashboards.

An untagged section is not automatically a failed document. An invalid control, malformed tag, duplicate or missing required title metadata is a structured-data failure; a suspicious omission may be a reviewer warning.

Word semantic styles identify the function of a paragraph independently of its visual formatting. A standard can show requirements, accountabilities, controls, approvals, records and procedural steps in their original order. ONE uses those styles for focused reading, filtering and assurance checks. Authors apply styles in Word; they do not manually label every paragraph in external metadata.

Only author-approved meaning styles are interpreted as normative markers. Standard Word Normal and List Bullet are used for explanation and non-mandatory context. Bold, underline, colour and font size alone never change a paragraph’s semantic classification.

rows: Duty attached to a named function or role
Authorisation, hold point, release or sign-off

blocks.t: ACE mandatory wording uses the modal verb reserved for binding requirements. A mandatory sentence is written as an independently understandable paragraph with the ODS.Requirement style. Avoid hiding several unrelated obligations in a single paragraph or table cell; this improves understanding, review and automated identification. “Should” describes a recommendation unless another controlled rule makes the action mandatory.

A gateway scanner examines plain paragraphs, tables and relevant text runs for mandatory wording. It flags mandatory wording in Normal or other unsuitable styles for review. False-positive handling is documented, for example where a quotation or definition uses mandatory terminology without creating a new ACE obligation.
Authors shall mark each mandatory requirement using ODS.Requirement, or the designated more-specific semantic style where the controlled rule catalogue permits it.

A responsibility names the accountable function or role; a personal name may be included as a current holder but does not replace the role. An approval gate describes the decision authority and evidence required before proceeding. Record requirements state what is captured, where it is retained and who owns its integrity. A risk control refers to barriers or specified actions, including how impairment or failure is handled.

The same underlying fact may be mentioned in narrative and a structured paragraph, but the mandatory statement is kept singular and clear. For instance, the Plant Manager’s approval may be shown as an approval requirement; the Plant Manager’s ongoing oversight may also be marked as a responsibility.
Document owner: Assigns clear role names to duties and validates their accuracy against the ACE organisation register.
A document release gate shall show its approver and necessary endorsement evidence before Document Control publishes the issue.
A completed review and gateway report shall be retained in the document issue pack linked to the approved revision.
Work involving a safety-critical element shall identify the controlling barrier and the method used to authorise any impairment or deviation.

sections.title: 5.4 Steps, warnings, references and non-normative text

blocks.t: ODS.ProcedureStep is applied to one logically ordered action; the sequence is clear even when the web reader places each step in a card or compact task list. ODS.Warning is reserved for critical personal-safety attention and does not replace hazard assessment. ODS.DocumentReference carries a controlled document number or a clearly named external source, preferably with its relevant section.

Standard documents may also use ODS.Note, ODS.PerformanceIndicator, ODS.ExternalStandard and ODS.Definition where defined in the corporate style catalogue. These additional styles assist clarity and may be adopted by the parser with an explicit supported-style definition; they do not create a new document level or bypass the core requirements.
1. Read the applicable controlled instruction and verify the document ID and revision.
2. Confirm the responsible role, required approvals and work prerequisites.
3. Perform the specified task and capture the required completion evidence.
Where the status or authenticity of a safety-critical instruction cannot be established, stop the affected task and request a verified controlled issue.

sections.title: 5.5 Style consistency within lists and tables

blocks.t: Native Word tables may contain normal text, quantities and instructions; the reader must preserve cell relationships and header rows. A mandatory statement inside a table cannot be made optional merely because it is not a stand-alone paragraph. Document owners are encouraged to use a structured meaning paragraph outside complex tables for important controls and to provide unambiguous labels in tables.

Requirements expressed in images alone are inaccessible to the semantic gateway and difficult to search. Pictures can illustrate plant and diagrams, but the governing obligation and safety response appear in actual Word text.

The approved Word file contains controlled document properties that reconcile to the visible cover and document-control tables. The DOC register may add system-managed fields for workflow and audit. Publishing uses the properties embedded in the approved source; the portal does not depend on a manually maintained separate mapping spreadsheet for every revision.

rows: MAN, POL, STD, PRC, PLN, GDL, WIN, FRM, REG, SPC
Valid and consistent on cover and table

sections.title: 6.2 Metadata fields for function, process, role and assets

blocks.t: ONE also supports contextual links to the organisation structure and business process map. ACE functions, departments, roles and locations are sourced from controlled organisational registers. Authors select the relevant references; they do not invent role spellings or abbreviations that create a second parallel taxonomy. A document may have one primary function and multiple supporting functions.

Process references describe actual workflows—such as MOC, permit to work, preventive maintenance, incident investigation and design handover—and may be attached to the document or sections where appropriate. Role references can be inferred from clearly marked ODS.Responsibility paragraphs but require validation against the role register before being displayed as official role obligations.

rows: Registered role, not just person name
Controlled site code and asset identity where applicable
Registered process identifier or governed process name
Controlled document ID with relationship type

blocks.t: Word content controls provide visible text for editors and machine-addressable values for the gateway. Each control has a stable tag name. The title OMS tag control is associated with the title bookmark; heading tags are associated with their respective heading bookmarks. The gateway compares these controls with the register and detects contradictions among file properties, cover, approval table and current issue.

If a person changes the displayed revision but not the custom properties, the mismatch is not silently resolved by the reader. Document Control returns the source for correction and re-approval where necessary. No one outside the controlled process edits an already approved Word source.
The controlled metadata fields in Word and the document-control register shall agree for the identifier, revision, status, title, owner, issue and effective dates, classification and applicability.

sections.title: 7 Tables, figures, document references and links

blocks.t: Authors use real Word tables for structured information, not screenshots of spreadsheet ranges or tables pasted as bitmaps. Headings, row labels, units and notes are included in actual text so they can be read, searched and interpreted. Figures may be images, diagrams or drawings, but must have an appropriate caption, document context and explanatory text when they carry important safety or operating meaning.

For a schedule of protective equipment or alarm settings, the author states the governing requirement in text, provides units, references the technical baseline and identifies how the current value is controlled. The publishing system reproduces a faithful view of the table and clearly links it to the approved source.
Tables used to define acceptance limits, authorisation levels or equipment data shall show headings and units and shall remain native Word tables in the approved source.

A reference to an ACE-controlled document uses its complete current identifier and meaningful title. Where a specific section matters, the reference includes the section or stable bookmark. Relationship types include implements, governing standard, supporting form, work instruction, record source, supersedes and technical basis; these relationships help ONE build document networks.

External standards are cited by publisher, report or standard number and edition where known. IOGP Report 510 provides ACE’s OMS framework. A reference to ISO/DIS 29501 identifies a draft standard under development and must not be represented as proof of certification or adoption of a completed ISO publication.
ACE-DOC-STD-001, Document and Records Management Standard — controls the source repository, register and document life cycle.
ACE-RSK-STD-001, Risk Management Standard — governing risk assessment and Risk Matrix (as registered and issued).

A stable deep link resolves first to document identity and current revision, then to the named section. If an approved revision supersedes an earlier issue, ONE directs ordinary users to the current issue while permitting authorised reviewers to inspect historical material with clear superseded labelling. A missing section or broken reference produces a visible problem, not fabricated replacement content.

The portal’s excerpt must not reorder operating steps in a way that changes meaning or omit a prerequisite, approval or warning that the source requires. For complex layouts, a reader opens the whole approved document rather than presenting a misleading fragment.

The gateway is a deterministic quality check with accountable human review. It validates the structure and metadata of the exact Word file that has received approvals, tests controlled expectation values against the register, and records a report tied to the revision. It does not certify the technical adequacy of procedures or substitute for a competent reviewer.

Validation results are grouped as blockers, errors, warnings and information. A blocker prevents acceptance when the file cannot be safely interpreted, including corruption or ambiguous identity. An error breaches a mandatory machine-readable rule and prevents normal publication until corrected or formally excepted where the rule permits. A warning is reviewed and acknowledged; information is recorded for reporting.

rows: Missing ID, title, revision, Approved status or metadata conflict
Draft code or missing required decision
Unsupported/skipped style, duplicate or missing navigable bookmark
Correct control; OMS Manager resolves mapping
Apply appropriate semantic style or justify exception
Broken current-document target or mismatched ID
Unreadable content, unsupported restricted material exposure
Block current display; use secure representation
Dropped tables, missing warning or failed section extraction
Hold publication until output is faithful

blocks.t: 1. Load the submitted approved Word package, calculate its source identity and compare document number, revision and approval evidence to the register.
2. Parse Title and Heading 1–3, collect stable bookmark IDs and confirm outline structure and headings match their tag controls.
3. Read custom properties and visible document controls, validate mandatory values and resolve taxonomies against current controlled registers.
4. Check semantic paragraph styles, including mandatory-wording detection, role names, decision gates and record requirements.
5. Inspect native tables, figures, controlled references and security classification for reliable extraction and permitted display.
6. Produce a rule-level report containing location, rule ID, severity, observed content, expected condition and proposed owner of correction.
7. Document Control confirms approval status, reviews warnings and exceptions, and records the final accept/reject decision for the exact revision.
8. Release only the accepted source to current ONE publication and reconcile the previous revision, links, notifications and cached views.

A document that fails a mandatory check is returned to the author with enough detail to correct the Word source. The author does not repair a failure by editing only the published web representation. The same validated source is resubmitted after correction and any relevant re-approval, so the report reflects the content actually issued.

An exception may be accepted only where a rule explicitly permits one, the responsible Document Controller records the rationale and compensating control, and the Information Management Lead accepts the residual risk within delegated authority. The OMS Manager reviews exceptions affecting expectation mapping. Exceptions do not excuse absent operational approval or a source whose meaning cannot be safely presented.
No document with a blocker, unresolved mandatory error or absent required approval evidence shall be released as a current Approved ONE instruction.
Each gateway execution shall retain document and revision identity, file fingerprint, rule-set version, findings, accepted exceptions, reviewer, final decision and publication result.

The demonstration programme contains deliberate faults in controlled test copies to show detection of missing tags, invalid or duplicate expectation numbers and unstylised mandatory text. A test file is kept apart from current Approved documents, marked for validation use and never issued for operational direction. The expected failures become repeatable software regression tests.

The approved maintenance standard and incident standard are not intentionally published with defects. The gateway must detect seeded faults in separate QA fixtures before the release of a code change; passing a test suite does not permit the gateway to relax document controls.

rows: Error or reviewable rule violation under rule catalogue
Approval absent for an Approved standard
Valid heading with no OMS tags
Valid approved document with unique headings and exact properties
Pass; eligible for Document Control decision

blocks.t: Gateway rule definitions, schema versions, expectation registers and role vocabularies are maintained under controlled change. A change to parser behaviour is tested against representative manuals, standards, procedures, work instructions, tables, site documents and known defective fixtures. Results are compared with the expected outputs before new gateway code is enabled.

A false negative that suppresses a requirement or warning is treated as a publication quality incident. The Information Management Lead may suspend affected extracts and route users to the approved source while the error is corrected. The software release record preserves the rule set and parser build used for each published document.

sections.title: 9 ONE web views and publication acceptance

blocks.t: The OMS wheel presents the ten IOGP 510 elements grouped Lead (1–4), Control (5–8) and Learn (9–10). A user selects an element and expectation to see the ACE documents explicitly tagged to it, then opens a relevant document or section. Results display document ID, title, revision, status, owner and section context, with a link back to the approved Word source.

Coverage and gap views distinguish “has mapped controlled content”, “awaiting documentation” and “needs operational assurance”. Counts must avoid double-counting a child section as separately tagged through its parent. The mapping view can be filtered by the exact source revision and validity of the register.

The function view follows the ACE organisation structure and shows documents owned or used by Operations, Engineering & Projects, HSE & Compliance, Wells, Supply Chain, IT, Data & Knowledge and other functions. The process view follows approved cross-functional workflows such as risk assessment, MOC, control of work, maintenance, project handover and assurance; it does not merely replicate department folders.

The role view is assembled from validated role metadata and styled responsibilities and approval gates. For example, a CPF Plant Manager may see local operating responsibilities, MOC readiness gates, incident and maintenance interfaces, and relevant site plans. A Technical Authority sees the standards and endorsement points within their discipline. The same approved source may appear in several views without being copied or reapproved.

sections.title: 9.3 Document network, search and current-source access

blocks.t: The document network links governing policy, standards, procedures, work instructions, forms, registers and relevant technical source documents using typed relationships. Search accepts title, document ID, system, OMS expectation, role, site and keywords from approved text. Results are filtered to current approved issues by default, with an explicit historical view for authorised users.

Every web excerpt carries source provenance and a clear link to the complete controlled Word file. A user should not need to determine manually which of several similar PDFs is current; Document Control determines and records the current source, while ONE makes it easy to find.

The publishing service respects the repository’s access controls and the sensitivity of source metadata. It must not expose privileged content through search snippets, cached indexes or links merely because a document has a matching OMS tag. Where a user’s access is restricted, only permitted metadata is shown and the source remains protected.

Current-source checks are performed when new revisions are released. Cached excerpts are invalidated or version-bound so users cannot be directed to an obsolete revision without warning. If the application cannot confirm current status, it presents the uncertainty and the repository link rather than asserting that the extract is current.
Where the publication view is unavailable or out of synchronization, users shall confirm the approved issue in the controlled repository before carrying out safety-critical work.

Document Control accepts a publication when the source and issue pack are valid, required tags and bookmarks parse correctly, all critical meaning and tables are displayed faithfully, navigation points to the right headings and the current revision is unambiguous. Site and operating owners verify that critical procedures are findable by the people who need them.

Quality indicators include successful gateway first-pass rate, link health, broken-bookmark count, metadata consistency, current-revision fidelity, time to publish after approval, unresolved rule exceptions and the percentage of sampled role-based obligations that resolve to the correct source. These are monitored for systemic improvement rather than treated as certification scores.

A test copy of the same instruction is deliberately given a nonexistent OMS tag and an unstyled mandatory statement. docs.title: Emergency, Crisis and Business Continuity Standard
docs.author: Jenelle Paul — Emergency Response & Security Manager
docs.custodian: Jenelle Paul — Emergency Response & Security Manager
docs.reviewers: Shane Bain — Emergency Response Coordinator; Rohan Ali — Plant Manager - Central Processing Facility; Roger Ramkissoon — Offshore Installation Manager; Ricardo Gittens — Communications Manager
docs.applies: All ACE operated assets, offices, marine interfaces, contractors and critical business functions
docs.subtitle: Integrated site response, incident escalation, oil spill preparedness, crisis coordination and recovery of critical services.

blocks.t: This standard establishes ONE requirements for readiness, response, escalation, recovery and learning following events that threaten people, the environment, assets, communities or continuity of ACE operations. It applies to the Central Processing Facility (CPF), Pommerac A, unmanned Chenet B and Sapodilla C, the Gulf of Paria pipelines, Tamarind, Pawpaw and Soursop leases, Point Lisas Shore Base, Head Office and activities performed by contractors on ACE’s behalf.

A site emergency concerns immediate protection of life and limitation of consequences. An incident becomes a wider crisis when its consequences or demands exceed site capacity or require enterprise decisions, external engagement or sustained business recovery. ACE prepares for both in one framework; this standard sets minimum corporate controls while site plans specify arrangements and contact details appropriate to each location.
Each ACE-operated manned site shall maintain an approved and exercised emergency response plan appropriate to its credible scenarios and interfaces.
Protection of life, safe isolation and prevention of escalation shall take precedence over production, asset recovery and commercial objectives during an emergency.
Controlling interfaces: ACE-OMS-MAN-001; ACE-RSK-STD-001; ACE-PSM-STD-001; ACE-COW-STD-001; ACE-INC-STD-001; ACE-AIM-STD-001; ACE-DOC-STD-001.

Offshore response may depend on weather, crew transfer, marine rescue and remote assistance. Land operations may require remote-site access, public road control and communication with nearby communities. The CPF carries processing, storage, gas delivery and jetty interfaces. Contractors and mutual-aid providers must understand which command structure applies and how initial notification is made.
The emergency planning basis shall identify credible consequences, the site’s initial response capability, external dependencies, evacuation constraints and scenarios requiring escalation.

The Area Authority or designated site incident commander controls the immediate scene and has authority to suspend work, isolate systems, muster personnel and direct site response within competence and safe access. The Incident Management Team (IMT) provides specialist resources, cross-site coordination and information management. The Crisis Management Team (CMT) provides strategic decisions on wider exposure, customers, communities, reputation and business continuity. Escalation adds support; it does not automatically transfer tactical scene command.
Figure 1. Three response layers and the direction of escalation.
Every emergency response plan shall identify a primary and alternate incident commander, the succession arrangement, deputies, activation contacts and the authority to request external support.

rows: Alarm, rescue within capability, isolation, muster, initial incident information
Offshore Installation Manager; Plant Manager - Central Processing Facility; Land Operations Manager

blocks.t: The incident commander maintains an accurate picture of employees, contractors and visitors; security and administration support reconciled headcounts and access control. Contractor site supervisors have immediate muster and personnel accountability duties within ACE command. Marine providers, field medical support and specialised responders retain professional control of their equipment and techniques while coordinating through ACE’s agreed incident plan.
The Area Authority shall account for all personnel in the affected area and ensure contractor rosters and visitors are included in muster and evacuation decisions.

Planning is based on major accident hazard studies, process-safety barrier information, site risk registers, credible environmental releases, occupational emergencies, marine transport exposure and significant external disruptions. Scenarios are defined by initiating event, escalation potential, safe response actions and resource needs. A site plan may group scenarios that share response methods but must preserve scenario-specific safety controls.

Each asset scenario register shall link its emergency response scenarios to applicable hazard studies, barrier controls and operational interfaces and be reviewed following significant change or incident.

blocks.t: Activation is consequence- and capacity-based. Any event involving imminent life threat, a possible major accident escalation, significant uncontrolled environmental release or a need for external emergency responders prompts immediate assessment for IMT activation. Potential sustained loss of critical operations, serious public exposure or high-consequence cross-site impacts prompts CMT consideration. Classification is reviewed as information changes; do not delay protective action pending a formal severity code.

blocks.t: The plan is a usable field instrument. It must identify the boundaries of the site and activity, command succession, alarms, notification trees, muster and personnel accounting, protective actions, response resources, isolation and shutdown interfaces, evacuation and medical arrangements, assembly locations, communication fallbacks and hand-over arrangements. Maps and contact lists are maintained as controlled annexes with owners and review dates so they can be changed without silently changing command requirements.
Site plans shall specify practical initial actions for each credible scenario, including actions that must not be attempted without competent personnel or suitable equipment.

rows: How to raise alarm, contact duty officers, request response and escalate

First actions, isolation points, exclusion zones, rescue limitations and refuge/evacuation
Location, capability, inspection status and deployment method for response equipment
Emergency-service, mutual-aid, marine, medical, regulator and community interfaces
Scene transfer, safe reinstatement criteria, records and post-event review

blocks.t: A plan that exists only online is inadequate during a loss of electricity or telecommunications. Each location retains accessible approved copies in emergency positions and tested offline contact information. Emergency equipment and communication alternatives have accountable inspection owners; failures are logged, prioritised and compensated according to risk. Operational changes affecting access, evacuation, alarms or response capability trigger immediate review.
Where a critical response resource is impaired, the Area Authority shall evaluate the resulting risk and implement approved temporary controls or restrict the affected activity.

Oil spill planning covers land leases, flowlines, Gulf of Paria infrastructure, the CPF tank farm, marine transfer activities and transport interfaces. Plans identify credible release locations, initial containment and isolation capability, access routes, surveillance, recovered material handling and escalation to external response capability. Coastal or marine impacts are managed with attention to weather, currents, access restrictions, fisheries and community communication.

The spill response plan shall define the site’s immediate containment capability, mobilisation triggers for external support and responsibilities for operational, environmental and public-facing coordination.

blocks.t: Spill-event records support response control and regulatory reporting. The incident log records detection time, estimated and updated quantities, source, containment measures, environmental conditions, resource deployment, communications and decision rationale. Estimates are revised transparently as evidence improves. Notifications follow the legal requirements register and authorised communication chain rather than a generic timeline in this standard.
Spill response records shall include the incident chronology, response decisions, notifications, surveillance data, waste-transfer evidence and restoration close-out.

The Emergency Response Coordinator maintains a risk-based exercise schedule for sites, responders, contractors and relevant business functions. Exercises range from alarm or muster tests to scenario drills, tabletop coordination and combined field exercises. Objectives are stated before execution: time to raise alarm, account for people, transfer command, request resources, communicate clearly and demonstrate critical tactical actions.
Each manned site shall run drills at the frequency specified in its approved plan, including at least one major emergency exercise each year, as required by the OMS Manual.

rows: Alert chain, response contacts, redundant communications

blocks.t: Observers record both good practices and failures of preparedness, including performance under degraded communications or unavailable responders. Findings are graded by potential consequence and assigned to action owners. A revised plan is trained, reissued and communicated through document control. Significant open findings require interim controls and are tracked until verified closed.
Lessons from drills and real emergencies shall be recorded and relevant plans updated within 90 days, consistent with the OMS Manual.
Exercise records shall retain objectives, participants, observer evidence, achieved results, findings, action owners, due dates and verification of closure.

Emergency planning identifies parties that may be affected or needed: nearby lease communities, port or marine parties, emergency services, regulators, landowners, partners, utility suppliers and customers. Contact routes, authority to notify and backup contacts are maintained outside individual staff devices. Where a response might affect public roads, marine movements or neighbouring property, planned coordination is included in exercises.
The Emergency Response & Security Manager shall maintain verified external response contacts and pre-agreed support interfaces relevant to the credible emergencies for each site.

blocks.t: An agreement with a third party is useful only if the capability, mobilisation route and point of contact are current. Exercises include representative interface testing where practical. The lead maintains an inventory of mutual-aid arrangements, service capabilities, notification paths, limitations, cost authorities and periodic verification dates.
Mutual-aid arrangements shall be registered with capability, response limitations, activation contacts, agreement owner and the date of the last verification.

The CMT focuses on decisions beyond the incident scene: enterprise priorities, wider stakeholder and financial impacts, external messaging, resource allocation and preservation of business capability. The team maintains a factual common operating picture with clear confidence levels for unconfirmed information. The crisis lead assigns decisions to named owners, and the IMT supplies operational updates without creating parallel conflicting command channels.
Figure 2. Immediate response and successive activation decisions.
Every activated IMT or CMT shall maintain a dated decision log recording current facts, assumptions, decisions, action owners and next review time.

The Communications Manager coordinates public and media statements with the crisis lead and applicable legal and regulatory obligations. Initial statements focus on confirmed protective information, people and response status; technical causal claims are held until supported. Families and directly affected communities should not learn essential confirmed information through uncontrolled public channels. Social-media monitoring helps identify rumours but is not treated as incident evidence without confirmation.
Personnel shall not disclose personal casualty details, speculative incident causes or unapproved technical information through public channels.

blocks.t: The business impact analysis (BIA) identifies critical outcomes, dependencies and tolerable disruption before plans are written. Critical processes may include production and safe shutdown, gas delivery to the Gas Buyer, crude storage/loading, marine logistics, financial payments, personnel communications and critical IT/OT services. Each function defines the consequences of service loss, minimum service level, recovery time objective, recovery point objective where data loss matters, and the roles and suppliers needed to recover.
Owners of critical business functions shall maintain a documented BIA that defines service priorities, essential dependencies and recovery objectives approved by the responsible function head.

blocks.t: Continuity strategies may use alternate locations, manual fallback, reserve staff, spares, alternate communications or staged restart. Each strategy is assessed for safety, cyber and operational risks; it cannot bypass permit-to-work, technical integrity or the deviation process. Recovery is declared complete only after critical controls, information integrity, staffing and service quality are verified by accountable owners.
Figure 3. Continuity planning and improvement feedback loop.
Recovery actions that change plant, controls, competence or procedures shall be reviewed under the applicable MOC, Control of Work and technical assurance requirements before return to service.
Each critical function shall exercise or verify its continuity arrangements on a risk-based schedule and retain evidence of recovery objectives achieved or missed.

blocks.t: Emergency assurance combines equipment readiness, completed drills, exercise quality, availability of role alternates, open critical findings, notification effectiveness and recovery test outcomes. Dashboard indicators use clear numerator, denominator and coverage, and show overdue actions separately from closed actions. Independent assessments test a sample of plans against actual capabilities and observed site behaviour.

The Emergency Response Coordinator shall retain approved plans, call-tree tests, exercise reports, response logs, mutual-aid reviews, emergency equipment readiness and action close-out evidence in controlled records.

docs.title: Safety Instrumented Systems Specification
docs.author: Ian Laquis — Instrumentation & Control Engineer
docs.reviewers: Akilah Noel — Fire & Gas and Safety Systems Lead; Damian Daniel — Process Safety Lead; Michelle de Verteuil — Process Engineering Lead
docs.applies: ACE process facilities and related projects including Pommerac A and Central Processing Facility where SIFs are installed
docs.subtitle: Functional safety engineering requirements for safety instrumented functions, lifecycle evidence and operating interfaces.

sections.title: 1 Scope, functional safety basis and applicability

blocks.t: This specification defines ACE minimum engineering and management requirements for safety instrumented systems (SIS) and safety instrumented functions (SIF) serving process facilities. It links hazard analysis to safety requirements, design, verification, validation, operations, maintenance, management of change and independent assurance. It applies to new systems, significant modifications and the controlled assessment of existing systems across ACE-operated facilities.

The principal application sites are the Central Processing Facility and Pommerac A, including relevant process shutdown functions, transmitters, logic solvers, field interfaces and final elements. The specification also applies to unmanned facilities where safety functions exist under the engineering scope. A protection device is classified as a SIF only when its role and integrity requirement have been established through a documented hazard and risk assessment.

Each safety instrumented function shall have an identified hazardous scenario, an allocated risk reduction requirement, a current safety requirements specification (SRS), a named technical owner and a documented verification and operating-test basis.
A generic example of a shutdown loop must never substitute for the approved asset-specific safety basis, device details, trip setpoints, proof-test procedure or operating authorisation.

ACE-PSM-STD-001 — Process Safety and Hazard Study Standard; ACE-RSK-STD-001 — Risk Management Standard; ACE-AIM-STD-001 — Asset Integrity Management Standard; ACE-ENG-STD-901 — Engineering Standards Framework and Technical Authority Standard.

rows: Specific instrumented safety function that prevents or mitigates a defined hazardous event.
The sensors, logic solver, final elements and associated elements used to implement a SIF.
The approved technical description of each SIF, including required behaviour and testable acceptance criteria.

Planned test intended to expose dangerous undetected failure modes covered by the accepted method.
Functional safety assessment, conducted with independence suitable to the risk and assessment stage.
Basic process control system; not automatically credited as a safety-independent protection layer.

blocks.t: Non-SIS safety systems, conventional alarm functions, mechanical protective devices and fire-and-gas arrangements remain subject to their own governing standards. Interfaces and interdependencies are considered where they may affect a claimed independent protection layer or safety function.
IEC 61511-1:2016+A1:2017, Functional safety — Safety instrumented systems for the process industry sector — Part 1: https://webstore.iec.ch/en/publication/61289
IEC 61511-2:2016, Guidelines for application of IEC 61511-1; IEC 61511-3:2016, Guidance for determination of required safety integrity levels (IEC publications).
IEC 61508 series, Functional safety of electrical/electronic/programmable electronic safety-related systems (IEC publications).

The IEC standards are external governing references adopted through the ACE engineering standards process. The disciplined edition review and acceptance route is defined in ACE-ENG-STD-901. Where an edition is revised, the impact on installed systems, supplier evidence and required competence is assessed before formal adoption.
An engineering design basis shall identify the relevant IEC 61511 parts and accepted editions, ACE technical supplements, legal requirements and any approved exceptions for the facility.

blocks.t: The process owner, technical owner and Area Authority hold distinct decisions. A recorded endorsement of a SIF design does not itself authorise field implementation or return to service.
Figure 1. The SIS lifecycle links hazard definition through technical delivery and operational assurance.

The SIS lifecycle passes through hazard definition, allocation, design, procurement, integration, verification, validation, operations, change and decommissioning. Each handover retains a clearly identified owner. The engineering approval process and the site operating process are linked through the controlled handover package.

blocks.t: The project and asset teams shall complete the defined technical and operating handovers before responsibility for a SIF is transferred or its operating condition is changed.

ONE links this specification to several business processes rather than forcing the document into one workflow. The SIF development process begins with a risk-analysis requirement and ends with the technical handover; a separate Operations-owned work process controls proof testing and bypass activities. They share the same SIF identity and approved SRS as the common traceability reference.

blocks.t: A SIF arises from a structured assessment of hazardous process scenarios. HAZID/HAZOP establishes credible causes and consequences, while an appropriate protection-layer assessment identifies the risk-reduction gap. The selection of a SIF, the target SIL and the assumptions about independence are recorded in the hazard-study package.
The assigned target SIL, demand assumptions, independent protection layer credits, operating mode and safe-state objective shall be traceable to the approved hazard and risk study.
A control loop, alarm or operator response shall not be credited as an independent protection layer without documented assessment of independence, effectiveness and common-cause vulnerabilities.
Figure 2. Hazard-to-test traceability; every claim of protection requires a design and verification record.

rows: Scenario, initiating event, consequence and process boundary
Independence, response, common cause and demand assumptions

Measured response and achieved coverage relative to design

blocks.t: The SRS is the unambiguous, testable reference against which the SIF is designed, assessed, validated and maintained. It records functional and integrity requirements without delegating acceptance criteria to general procurement narratives. Each requirement has an identifier and a method of verification or validation.

A SIF shall not be released for detailed implementation until the SRS has been technically endorsed by Instrumentation & Control and the process safety and process engineering inputs have been resolved.

blocks.t: A change to a trip point, voting architecture, final element, proof-test interval, permissive, bypass logic, reset rule or credited device shall be assessed against the SRS and processed through the applicable management of change controls.

The reviewer confirms that updated calculations and test cases remain consistent with the hazard assumptions and documented performance standard. Superseded SRS revisions remain accessible in the controlled repository but are not used to authorise new work.

SIS design covers the input subsystem, logic solver, final elements, communications where used, utilities and human interfaces necessary for the safety action. The design basis evaluates systematic capability, random hardware failures, diagnostic coverage, common-cause effects, architectural constraints, environmental suitability and testability in the selected standard.

Design verification shall demonstrate that the complete SIF, including sensors and final elements, satisfies the approved functional and integrity requirements under the defined operating and fault conditions.

Separation from the basic process control system, power dependencies, shared impulses, air systems, communication links, maintenance activities and physical routing must be considered. Independence is demonstrated through an engineering assessment of the actual architecture, not only by the product certification of a logic solver.
A single shared component or service that can defeat both the control function and a credited protective layer requires explicit assessment and documented mitigations.

sections.title: 8.1 Managing tests, exceptions and punch-list items

blocks.t: Test exceptions are classified by their effect on safety function, documented with the accountable person and given a corrective action. An unresolved finding affecting SIF integrity is handled through the approved risk and deviation controls; a general punch-list close-out approval does not replace barrier impairment authorisation.

Operations controls the safe use of the installed safety function. Maintenance & Integrity delivers approved preventive and corrective activities and maintains the associated CMMS history. The I&C Technical Authority maintains the functional safety acceptance basis, including the proof-test assumptions, limits and verification requirements.

The proof-test interval and required coverage shall be derived from the approved SIF integrity assessment and equipment failure assumptions; routine calendar defaults do not substitute for that assessment.

Proof-test records shall identify SIF and device identifiers, procedure revision, actual conditions, test steps performed, acceptance criteria, recorded results, defects, restoration, technician and verifier.

blocks.t: No test is complete until temporary bypasses, forced values, simulation equipment and override arrangements have been removed or placed under explicit approved impairment control, and protection is confirmed restored.

The approved test procedure defines personnel responsibilities, protected equipment boundaries, safe test prerequisites, restoration evidence and criteria for stopping the test. Where an intrusive test can initiate an actual shutdown, it is planned and authorised under the site Control of Work arrangements.

An inhibited or bypassed safety function is an intentional reduction or alteration of the available protection. Such conditions require documented reason, risk assessment, compensating measures, accountable approval, effective monitoring and prompt restoration. Permanent departures are controlled as design changes rather than recurring temporary permits.

Any SIF bypass or inhibit shall be recorded against the affected SIF identity, scope, risk basis, start time, responsible Area Authority, permitted duration, compensating measures and restoration verification.
Do not bypass or suppress a credited safety function solely to maintain production or avoid an operational inconvenience.

sections.title: 11 Management of change, competence and contractor assurance

blocks.t: SIS change may be initiated by project modifications, failures, supplier obsolescence, plant operating changes, periodic integrity review or hazard reassessment. The process is multi-functional: Operations owns field readiness; Process Safety owns the hazard basis; Engineering owns design adequacy; I&C owns technical specifications; Document Control preserves the issued records.
SIS design, proof-test and change activities shall be performed and verified by people with documented competence appropriate to the safety function, equipment and decision being made.

Third-party systems integrators and suppliers are controlled through ACE contractor and supplier management. Supplier assessments include evidence of functional safety competence, quality processes, documented test coverage, relevant certifications and access to the controlled source/configuration records.
ACE-CON-STD-001 — Contractor and Supplier Management Standard; ACE-PPL-STD-003 — Competence Assurance Standard; ACE-ENG-STD-901 — Engineering Standards Framework and Technical Authority Standard.

blocks.t: Functional safety assessments address the lifecycle stage, scope of hazard and SIF requirements, completeness of independent review, resolution of material findings and suitability of arrangements for operation and maintenance. The assessor’s independence and qualifications are chosen to match the risk and applicable external standard, with decisions documented before the next relevant gate.
A formal functional safety assessment shall be planned and recorded at the lifecycle stages required by the adopted IEC 61511 framework and by the asset-specific functional safety management plan.

Decommissioning is integrated with the hazard assessment and asset isolation plan, including any temporary protective arrangements during removal.

docs.subtitle: Discipline engineering standards, technical authority, governance and controlled interfaces with ACE business processes.

blocks.t: This standard governs the development, selection, application and assurance of engineering standards at Acme Caribbean Energy Limited (ACE). It defines how professional discipline requirements are connected to accountable organisational roles, how technical decisions enter business processes, and how controlled documentation provides evidence that the intended outcomes have been achieved.

It applies to engineering undertaken for ACE operated facilities, brownfield changes, projects, wells, subsea facilities, electrical and instrumentation systems, materials, corrosion, maintenance and specialist services. It includes work delivered by contractors and engineering service providers.
Each engineering scope shall identify its governing ACE engineering document, applicable external codes, appointed Technical Authority and the business process through which the work is accepted.

The current approved ACE standard takes precedence over an uncontrolled local copy; conflicts between ACE requirements and a mandatory legal requirement shall be referred to Legal & Government Affairs and the responsible Technical Authority before work proceeds.

ACE-OMS-MAN-001 — ONE Management System Manual; ACE-AIM-STD-001 — Asset Integrity Management Standard; ACE-DOC-STD-001 — Document and Records Management Standard; ACE-DOC-STD-002 — Operational Document Publishing Standard.

The document hierarchy and the process architecture serve different purposes. The hierarchy says which rules apply; the process defines who moves a business outcome through a sequence of decisions and handovers. An engineering practice or specification can be used in several processes without being the process itself.
Figure 1. Standards, accountable business processes and work instructions are separate but traceable layers.

The Technical Leadership Council (TLC) holds a coordinated catalogue for 32 disciplines, each with a discipline lead. Standards, specifications and supporting practices are linked to their discipline blocks and to the controlled ONE repository.

The discipline lead shall maintain an applicability matrix for the discipline, recording the selected external standards and editions, ACE supplements, relevant legal requirements, applicable assets and documented exceptions.

sections.title: 2.2 Standards, practices, specifications and technical guidance

blocks.t: An ACE standard defines mandatory minimum engineering expectations. A discipline practice explains how accepted engineering principles and industry codes are applied within a particular ACE discipline. A specification defines measurable technical performance and design requirements for a system or item. A guideline explains acceptable approaches without creating a new mandatory requirement unless explicitly invoked by contract or an approved specification.

blocks.t: A technical standard or practice shall not duplicate an operational procedure; it shall identify the controlled processes and procedures that implement its technical requirements.

The selected edition, technical basis, contract applicability and owner are documented in the discipline standards register. Relevant regulatory conditions, licence requirements, partner obligations and contractual requirements are reviewed before adoption. New editions enter ACE only following an impact assessment rather than by automatic replacement.
The responsible Technical Authority shall approve the selected edition and any ACE-specific supplements before an external standard is declared governing for design or operation.
The standards register shall retain standard number, edition, title, adoption status, applicability, owner, last technical review, supersession and approved deviation reference.

ACE operates two complementary lines of accountability. Solid-line managers direct personnel, budgets and daily priorities. Discipline leads retain their line position in their home function but have a technical dotted line to the VP Engineering & Projects through the TLC. This allows technical standards to remain consistent across the assets and functions using them.
Figure 2. Functional delivery and cross-functional technical authority converge through controlled decisions and records.
Dev Jaggernauth — VP Engineering & Projects: sponsors the Technical Authority framework, chairs the TLC and confirms the appointments of discipline leads.
Elena Farfan — Manager, Technical Excellence: administers the discipline catalogue, TLC secretariat, technical approvals and engineering standard review programme.
A Technical Authority: defines the discipline requirements, endorses technical changes, reviews technical risk and provides written decisions within the delegated authority.
The appointment register shall record each discipline, named lead, designated deputy, competence basis, decision scope, limits of delegation and escalation route.

Where a technical decision concerns the lead’s own design, a peer reviewer or an independent specialist is assigned according to the risk and novelty of the decision. Commercial or project schedule pressure is not a valid basis for bypassing technical endorsement.

docs.author: Nadine Cooper — Environmental Specialist
docs.reviewers: Rohan Ali — Plant Manager - Central Processing Facility; Christina Bain — HSE Manager; Jenelle Paul — Emergency Response & Security Manager; Rawle Sandy — Counsel, Regulatory & Licensing; Sophia Hosany — VP Operations
docs.applies: All ACE activities, sites, employees and contractors
docs.subtitle: How ACE complies with its permits, cuts flaring, prevents and responds to spills, manages waste and reports its performance.

blocks.t: This policy sets ACE's commitments for protecting the environment it works in: complying with its permits, cutting flaring and venting, preventing spills, managing waste and discharges, and reporting its environmental performance openly.

It applies to all ACE sites and activities, on land and in the Gulf of Paria, including drilling, production, the CPF, the export jetty, marine and road transport, and contractors working for ACE. Its parent is ACE-LDR-POL-001.
Each commitment names the ACE values it serves, as set in ACE-LDR-POL-001 section 1. The steps that deliver the commitments are in the governed processes and implementing documents in section 6.

sections.title: 2.1 Comply with permits and licence conditions

blocks.t: In line with our values Integrity in everything and Care for people and places, ACE meets every condition of the permits and licences issued by the environmental regulator and the energy ministry. Each permit condition has an owner and is monitored, and an exceedance is reported to the regulator as the permit requires.

In line with our value Care for people and places, ACE will end routine flaring by the end of 2030. Until then, routine flared volume falls by at least 15% a year against the 2025 baseline. Gas is not vented except where needed for safety. Flaring limits are part of the operating envelope (ACE-OPS-STD-001).

sections.title: 2.3 Prevent spills and respond by tier

blocks.t: In line with our values Safety above all and Care for people and places, ACE prevents loss of containment through its integrity and operating commitments, and when a spill happens responds at the tier in section 4.1, using the capability tiers of the oil spill plans (ACE-EMR-STD-001 §5).

In line with our value Care for people and places, waste is managed by the hierarchy of avoid, reduce, reuse, recycle, then safe disposal through licensed contractors, and every discharge to air, water or land stays within its permitted limits.

In line with our values Integrity in everything and Learn and improve, ACE measures its emissions, discharges, spills and waste, reports them at the frequencies in section 5.2, and uses the results to set its environmental objectives.

blocks.t: The tier sets the response branch in the emergency process and is set by the volume, where the oil goes and the resources needed. Where a spill meets more than one row, the higher tier applies.

blocks.t: Any spill of Tier 2 or Tier 3 shall be reported to the environmental regulator within 24 hours, or sooner if a permit requires.
Any exceedance of a permit limit is reported to the VP HSE & Compliance within 24 hours and recorded as an incident under ACE-INC-STD-001, and the regulator is notified in the time the permit sets.

docs.title: Financial Control and Delegation of Authority Policy
docs.author: Sherma Isaac — Planning & Budgeting Manager
docs.reviewers: Krishna Jagessar — Financial Controller; Nicole Lange — Head of Internal Audit & Risk Assurance; Melissa Mitchell — JV & Partner Accounting Lead; Sasha George — VP Supply Chain Management; Sharda Bissoon — VP Legal & Government Affairs (General Counsel); Karen Jack — VP Business Development & Markets
docs.applies: All ACE activities, sites, employees and contractors
docs.subtitle: Who may commit ACE's money and within which limits, how duties are separated, and how partner costs and revenues are accounted.

blocks.t: This policy sets how ACE controls money: who may commit it, within which limits, how duties are separated, and how partner costs and revenues are accounted. The Delegation of Authority schedule in section 4 is the condition on every approval step that commits or changes money in an ACE process.

It applies to every function, site and employee, to every commitment of ACE funds or of joint-venture funds that ACE manages as operator, and to revenue from gas and crude sales. Its parent is ACE-LDR-POL-001.
Each commitment names the ACE values it serves, as set in ACE-LDR-POL-001 section 1. The steps that deliver the commitments are in the governed processes and implementing documents in section 6.

sections.title: 2.1 No commitment without budget and authority

blocks.t: In line with our value Integrity in everything, ACE commits money only when there is an approved budget for it and the person approving holds the authority for that value under section 4.1. Spending outside the budget needs the higher approval set in section 4.2.
No purchase order, contract, variation or other financial commitment shall be issued until it has been approved by a person holding the delegated authority for its value.

In line with our value Integrity in everything, the person who requests a commitment is never the person who approves it, and no one person controls a transaction from start to finish. In ONE this is checked on the process maps: an approval step is never in the same lane as the step that raised the request.
The approver of a financial commitment shall be a different person from the requester, and shall hold a position above the requester.

sections.title: 2.3 Partner costs and revenues are accounted as agreed

blocks.t: In line with our values Integrity in everything and One team, one way, ACE accounts for and reports joint-venture costs and revenues exactly as the joint operating agreements require, bills partners on time and answers their audit requests openly.
In line with our value Integrity in everything, ACE invoices gas and crude sales only from allocation volumes approved under ACE-HMA-POL-001, and corrects invoices when measurement is corrected.
In line with our value Integrity in everything, financial records are complete, accurate and kept in the approved systems, so that every figure can be traced to its approval and its source document.

docs.owner: Karen Jack — VP Business Development & Markets
docs.author: Navin Sookdeo — Metering & Measurement Lead
docs.reviewers: Rohan Ali — Plant Manager - Central Processing Facility; Vidya Rajkumar — Crude Loading & Custody Transfer Coordinator; Michael Fernandes — Hydrocarbon Accountant; Melissa Mitchell — JV & Partner Accounting Lead; Anushka Seepersad — Partner Relations Lead; Dev Jaggernauth — VP Engineering & Projects
docs.applies: All ACE activities, sites, employees and contractors
docs.subtitle: How ACE measures and allocates what it produces, delivers product to contract quality and honours its nominations.

blocks.t: This policy sets ACE's commitments for measuring and allocating the oil and gas it produces, for the quality of the sales gas and crude it delivers, and for meeting its nominations to customers. Accurate measurement is the basis of revenue, royalty, partner statements and trust with the Gas Buyer and partners.

It applies to custody-transfer and allocation metering at the offshore installations, the CPF, the land leases and the export jetty, to gas deliveries to the Gas Buyer, to crude export cargoes, and to the people and systems that calculate allocation. Its parent is ACE-LDR-POL-001.
Each commitment names the ACE values it serves, as set in ACE-LDR-POL-001 section 1. The steps that deliver the commitments are in the governed processes and implementing documents in section 6.

In line with our value Integrity in everything, custody-transfer and allocation meters are calibrated, verified and proved at the intervals in section 4.3, by competent people, and the records are kept so that any figure can be traced to the meter and the calibration behind it.

sections.title: 2.2 Allocation is approved, documented and auditable

blocks.t: In line with our values Integrity in everything and One team, one way, ACE allocates production to wells, fields and partners by one approved, documented method. Partners can see the method and the data behind their statements, and any change to the method is agreed with partners and made through Management of Change.

In line with our value Integrity in everything, a measurement error is never hidden or absorbed. Above the threshold in section 4.1, the Gas Buyer and partners are told within the stated time, the volumes are corrected, and the correction is shown in the next statement.
A mismeasurement above the threshold in section 4.1 shall be notified to the Gas Buyer and affected partners within 24 hours of discovery.

In line with our values Integrity in everything and Care for people and places, sales gas and crude meet the quality set in the sales contracts. Off-specification product is not delivered without the buyer's written agreement; otherwise delivery is stopped or the product is diverted until it is back in specification.

In line with our value Integrity in everything, ACE delivers what it nominates. When a shortfall is expected, the Gas Buyer or the crude lifter is told in advance, at the threshold and time set in section 4.2, so that they can plan around it.
