docs.title: Incident Reporting and Investigation Standard
docs.author: Christina Bain — HSE Manager
docs.reviewers: Damian Daniel — Process Safety Lead; Edward Low Chew — HSE Auditor; Rohan Ramkissoon — Knowledge Management Specialist
docs.applies: All ACE personnel, facilities, projects, contractors, operated assets and activities within ACE operational control
docs.subtitle: Reporting, classification, investigation and verified learning from incidents, near misses, barrier failures and unsafe conditions.

sections.title: 1 Purpose, scope, duties and governing principles

blocks.t: This standard establishes the ACE process for reporting, responding to, classifying, investigating and learning from undesired events. It makes the incident record the common link between an event at the worksite, the affected hazards and safeguards, the risk register, the corrective-action system and verified change to operations.

The purpose is not simply to generate an investigation report. ACE must recognise weak signals before loss escalates, protect people and evidence after an event, understand how technical and organisational controls behaved, and establish whether improvements actually prevent recurrence. A high-quality investigation preserves uncertainty and distinguishes observed facts from interpretations.
All ACE incidents and near misses shall be reported within the shift in which they occur, whether or not injury, loss or production interruption resulted.

Applies at Pommerac A, Chenet B, Sapodilla C, Gulf of Paria pipelines, Tamarind/Pawpaw/Soursop leases, the Central Processing Facility (CPF), Point Lisas Shore Base, Head Office, associated marine and road transport under ACE control, wells, workovers and capital projects. Events involving contractors and visitors are included.

It covers occupational injury and illness events, fire and explosion, releases of hydrocarbons or other substances, loss of containment, transport and security events, process-safety demands, integrity anomalies with immediate loss potential, environmental releases, near misses, unsafe conditions, and verified breaches of mandatory controls. Technical failure analysis under Asset Integrity, MOC and Maintenance remains relevant and must be linked to the incident record.

Governing: ACE-OMS-MAN-001; ACE-RSK-STD-001; ACE-PSM-STD-001; ACE-AIM-STD-001; ACE-MNT-STD-001; ACE-COW-STD-001; ACE-MOC-PRC-001; ACE-DOC-STD-001; ACE-DOC-STD-002. Planned related standards: ACE-INC-STD-002 Lessons Learned and Action Tracking; ACE-PRF-STD-001 Performance Measurement and KPI.

sections.title: 1.3 Accountable roles and safeguarding of independence

rows: Make safe where authorised; summon assistance; promptly notify supervisor or control room; preserve known facts and identify witnesses.
Area Authority (OIM / Offshore Operations / Land / CPF)
Lead immediate response and local investigation; protect the site and evidence; approve safe restart when technical conditions are met.
Manage event registration, classification challenge, investigation level, action discipline and corporate incident data quality.
Challenge major-accident potential, barrier status, process safety classification, technical failure hypotheses and return-to-service criteria.
Plan scope and evidence; test competing explanations; maintain factual record; produce findings and causal model.
Translate verified findings to lesson alerts, targeted role communications, search tags and cross-site dissemination.
Own this system; oversee significant cases and escalation; assure investigation quality, timeliness and systemic learning.
Determine statutory notification, preservation and privilege obligations and authorised external disclosures.
Independently sample case quality, overdue actions, management controls and effectiveness evidence.

blocks.t: The Area Authority leads the local investigation and first response, while the HSE Manager coordinates classification and the Process Safety Lead challenges the technical barrier conclusions on significant events.
Life safety, medical response and control of continuing hazards take precedence over investigation activity.
Report observed facts early; imperfect early information is better than waiting for certainty.
Evaluate actual and credible potential severity independently; an event with no injury can expose a major accident scenario.
Separate individual performance from enabling system conditions, without concealing wilful misconduct or serious control breaches.
Preserve unsuccessful hypotheses and evidence conflicts where they affect the conclusion; a single narrative is not presumed correct.
Use one incident reference to connect response, assessment, investigation, actions, lessons and closure.
Incident investigations shall not compromise emergency response, personnel safety, regulatory duties, evidence integrity or mandatory restrictions on restarting plant.

rows: Injury, occupational illness, hydrocarbon loss, fire, dropped object causing impact, environmental release, vehicle collision.
Activate local response, notify control room and register event.
Dropped object narrowly missing worker; failure of two independent protective layers without release; vessel almost contacts platform.
Stop exposure; assess credible potential and preserve data.
Unplanned primary containment loss; relief or ESD demand; failed SCE proof test; impaired fire/gas detector coverage.
Protect barriers and contact Process Safety Lead.
Uncontrolled ignition source, missing isolation label, suspect lifting gear, damaged walkway or hazardous leak path.
Control hazard and enter observation / incident system.
Mandatory test bypassed, overdue significant barrier verification, non-reporting of required measurement.
Contain exposure and evaluate escalation and legal duty.

blocks.t: 1. Stop work and raise alarm where necessary; protect people, initiate emergency response and isolate or evacuate only within competence and site procedure.
2. Notify the supervisor, Area Authority or control room immediately; report time, precise location, people affected, current hazard and measures already taken.
3. The supervisor records preliminary facts and sets an event reference within the shift; oral reporting does not replace the controlled electronic entry.

4. Where major-accident potential, injury, loss of containment, fire or public exposure is plausible, the Area Authority notifies the HSE Manager and other required functional leads without waiting for classification consensus.

5. Protect evidence, identify witnesses, capture time-stamped plant/control data and record the initial condition before restoration or clean-up changes the scene, except where immediate safety demands otherwise.
6. The Incident Coordinator reviews completeness and assigns provisional actual/potential classification and next assessment owner.

The receiving supervisor shall acknowledge every report and ensure an incident entry exists by the end of the reporting shift, including where the event occurred during contractor activity or outside normal office hours.

Initial records shall include event time and discovery time, shift, asset/location, reporter, supervisor, asset/equipment IDs, persons affected, event class, immediate controls, photographs or data references, witnesses, notifications, and any uncertainty in the account.

sections.title: 2.3 Protective actions and return to work

blocks.t: The Area Authority determines whether operations can safely continue pending investigation. For potential major-accident events, the current status of credited barriers must be assessed explicitly, including other simultaneous impairments and planned work. Where evidence is incomplete, maintain the controlled safe state until a competent technical decision is recorded.

Restoration of equipment, clearing alarms or restoring production does not close the incident. The investigation may remain open while a controlled, risk-assessed interim operation is authorised; the authorising route is the Risk Management Standard, Asset Integrity Standard, MOC and relevant deviations process.

Return to service following a material barrier failure shall require documented Area Authority release and Technical Authority acceptance of the applicable repair, verification or compensating measures.

Classification requires two separate judgments: actual consequence supported by observed outcome, and credible potential consequence had a realistic additional safeguard failed or exposure differed. Use the approved ACE 5×5 Risk Matrix and describe the evidence for severity and likelihood instead of relying only on the coloured result.

Choose the highest relevant consequence across people, environment, assets, business continuity and reputation. Consider the full credible sequence, not an arbitrary worst imaginable outcome. Re-score following material new evidence and keep the original classification trail.
Incidents shall be investigated at the level determined by actual and credible potential severity using the ACE Risk Matrix; classification shall never be lowered solely because harm did not occur.

rows: Injury or release facts, instrument trends, damage, exposure and verified event chronology.
Initiating event, exposure route, available safeguards, barrier failure combination and credible consequence.
Existing bow-tie, hazard study, SCE standard, task risk assessment and operating envelope.
Current barrier state, deferred tests, temporary mitigations, area status and risk acceptance reference.
Area Authority, HSE Manager and relevant Technical Authority/Process Safety Lead for material cases.

sections.title: 3.2 Process safety events and barrier indicators

blocks.t: Process-safety event classification follows the approved ACE metric definition and recognised industry reporting criteria; different measures such as Tier 1 and Tier 2 loss-of-primary-containment events, Tier 3 challenges to protective systems, and Tier 4 operating-discipline indicators must not be interchanged. Classification requires physical event data, substance, quantity and threshold applicability from the governing reporting standard.

Where a threshold is uncertain, record “classification pending technical verification”, keep the event open for technical review and do not assume a non-reportable tier. The Process Safety Lead maintains the boundary between process safety reporting and personal safety statistics.

The event file shall retain any tier-assessment worksheet, material identity, release duration and estimation method, applicable metric definition/version, barrier demands and Technical Authority review.

The Incident Coordinator logs every classification change with date, reason and evidence reference. An affected operational manager may challenge the technical basis, but may not unilaterally alter the released classification. Material disputes are escalated to the VP HSE & Compliance; independent review is available through Internal Audit where assurance independence is affected.

Data quality review may discover duplicate events or linked incidents. The cases are reconciled through an audit trail rather than silently deleted, preserving original report numbers, evidence and any already communicated obligations.
A change to an externally reported classification shall receive Legal & Government Affairs review before amended regulator, partner or customer communication is issued.

rows: Control room or supervisor; Area Authority; HSE; medical responder.
Area Authority; HSE Manager; Process Safety Lead; relevant Technical Authority; VP HSE & Compliance.
Shutdown / barrier status, incident level and technical investigation scope.
Area Authority; HSE; Environmental Lead; Legal/Government Affairs as required.
Containment, sensitive receptors and regulator/partner notification.
Emergency lead; CEO via executive escalation; HR; Legal; Head Internal Audit as warranted.
Crisis response, independent investigation and preservation.
Area Authority; owner function; commercial or JV interface manager.
Operational continuity and contract notification review.

blocks.t: Regulatory thresholds, report formats and deadlines differ by event, licence, statute, authority and operating location. The Legal and Regulatory Compliance function owns the current obligations register and determines notification requirements with HSE and the relevant asset owner. No fixed statutory deadline is implied by this standard where the duty comes from another instrument.

For matters involving partner facilities, Gas Buyer sales-gas delivery, marine operations or public impact, the responsible contract or stakeholder owner confirms agreed notification routes while maintaining the formal incident record. Statements to the media, customers or external parties are coordinated through Communications and authorised management.

The designated regulatory owner shall record each assessed reporting obligation, its legal source, responsible signatory, actual notification date/time and evidence of submission or documented determination that no external notification was required.

If potential seriousness is high but an event description is incomplete, escalate on the plausible consequence, clearly marking the classification provisional. Delayed escalation while waiting for final root cause is not acceptable. The Incident Coordinator updates management as material information changes and records the time, recipient and content of each substantive correction.
Do not disclose personal medical details, protected witness material or legally privileged advice through general lesson bulletins or unrestricted incident dashboards.

rows: Low actual and low credible potential, bounded control issue, no significant barrier failure.
Area Authority delegate with HSE review and action record.
Medium/high potential, repeat event, significant injury, failed control or multiple interfaces.
Area Authority leads or delegates competent lead; multidisciplinary participation and HSE challenge.
Very High credible potential, serious harm, major accident, complex barrier breakdown or independent scrutiny need.
Independent team appointed by VP HSE & Compliance with Process Safety and discipline specialists; Audit independence assessed.

blocks.t: The table provides a method-selection guide; the actual and potential risk determines escalation. A repeat cluster of lower-severity incidents may warrant a major systemic inquiry. The investigation plan fixes scope, terms of reference, leadership, evidence controls, technical experts, reporting cadence and decision gates. External specialist participation may be required for metallurgical, automation, human-factors or marine evidence.
Investigation leaders and analysts shall be competent for the event hazards and shall declare conflicts that could compromise independent conclusions.
1. Appoint team leader and record scope, event reference, actual/potential severity and mandatory technical participants.
2. Establish key causal questions, time boundaries, evidence sources, interview plan, site access and preservation requirements.
3. Document roles for fact gathering, data custody, analysis, recommendations, legal/regulatory coordination and report approval.
4. Hold an initial barrier and evidence review before prematurely narrowing the likely cause.
5. Agree progress milestones and exception escalation, including resources needed to protect evidence quality.
An investigator shall not independently approve the effectiveness of a corrective action that the same investigator owns or executed.

Interview witnesses promptly in a non-coercive setting, explain the purpose and permitted information use, capture their own observations before sharing a compiled chronology, and distinguish first-hand perceptions from information learned afterward. Witnesses may correct their statement. Avoid leading questions and pressuring teams to reach a predetermined explanation.

If substance impairment, deliberate conduct or potential criminality is relevant, coordinate the evidence and employment processes with Legal and Human Resources without confusing disciplinary procedure with the factual incident investigation. Preserve medical confidentiality and protect reporters from retaliation for good-faith safety disclosures.
Interview material shall identify participant, interviewer, date/time, location, consent/acknowledgment where applicable, method, corrections and restricted-access classification.

Evidence is assigned a unique identifier and maintained with custody details and context. Sources may include failed components, maintenance records, permit and isolation documents, shift logs, P&IDs, CCTV, DCS/SCADA trends, alarm and ESD event logs, inspection findings, weather/sea state, contractor records and contemporaneous photographs. The investigation lead determines which time synchronisation uncertainties or sensor limitations could distort chronology.

For digital evidence, preserve read-only original exports when practical, record source system and extraction method, restrict editing and maintain recoverable copies. For samples, record who collected them, packaging, conditions and transfer history. Emergency controls may change the scene; document those changes rather than treating missing original condition as proof it did not exist.
Every material item of investigation evidence shall have a source, collection time, custodian, authenticity/quality limitation and secure repository reference.

Construct the time sequence from independent sources: equipment condition and alarms before the event; work planning and control; initiation; detector and operator response; safeguard success or failure; consequences; and recovery actions. Where sources conflict, state the discrepancy and test it.

The analysis identifies immediate causes, failed or absent barriers, degraded conditions, design/maintenance/operations interactions, management-system decisions, competency and supervision factors, and latent contributors. It should test alternative hypotheses against evidence, not simply assign a root-cause label. Record why rejected hypotheses were inconsistent with the facts.

rows: What changed, who or what detected it, how did the system respond and which facts have uncertain timing?
Which safeguards were expected, available, tested, relied on, bypassed, impaired or defeated?
Which mechanism, failure mode, operating demand or environmental condition enabled the event?
Were workload, interfaces, procedures, competence, supervision and incentives consistent with safe action?
Which specific controlled requirement failed to prevent, detect or mitigate the path, and why?
Could the same weakness exist at CPF, Pommerac A, other platforms, land leases or contractors?

blocks.t: For an event related to a major-accident hazard, revisit the relevant bow-tie and SCE performance standard. Identify each prevention, detection, isolation and mitigation layer and the reliability of the evidence used to credit it. A barrier marked “available” in a system register may have failed to perform under actual demand conditions.

If the analysis finds a missing hazard scenario, weak proof-test scope, flawed isolation boundary, unsupported ALARP claim or repeated anomaly, revise the risk assessment, maintenance/inspection strategy, performance standard or MOC plan as appropriate. Do not solve systemic weakness exclusively with an awareness briefing.
Barrier-related investigation recommendations shall identify the owner of the technical performance standard and the field verification needed to demonstrate restored effectiveness.

The final investigation report shall contain summary and impact; actual and potential classification; verified chronology; evidence and limitations; barrier analysis; causal model and alternative hypotheses; contributory OMS control weaknesses; actions with owners and evidence; cross-site applicability; and outstanding uncertainties.

The HSE Manager shall confirm classification and reporting quality and the affected Technical Authorities shall review conclusions involving their technical safeguards before the report is accepted for close-out.

Recommendations are translated into actions which change a technical barrier, operating process, competence, management control or assurance practice. A conclusion such as “operator should pay more attention” is not an adequate preventive action unless the analysis identifies a specific controllable error trap and objective effectiveness test.

Select controls using the hierarchy of elimination, engineering prevention, protective functions, administrative safeguards and competence where appropriate. Link each action to its originating finding, risk rating, impacted site or equipment, due date, accountable owner and success criterion. Use a single corporate action system to connect incidents, audits and hazard studies.
Each significant corrective action shall have a unique identifier, accountable owner, due date, proposed control change, acceptance evidence and an independent effectiveness-verification method.

rows: Incident ID, finding ID, causal explanation, affected risk / barrier and source report.
Affected equipment/sites, deliverable, relevant procedure or drawing, simultaneous actions/dependencies.
Risk and action owner, Technical Authority endorsement, MOC/deviation reference where needed.
Approved drawing/revision, proof test, observation, training competence or inspection result.
Verifier independent from implementer, sampling period, objective measure, result and reopen decision.

sections.title: 7.2 Prioritisation, overdue actions and temporary controls

blocks.t: Actions arising from Very High or High risks require expedited planning and executive visibility consistent with the Risk Management Standard. Delay can occur because of design, procurement or shutdown constraints but does not cancel the exposure. The owner documents compensating controls, additional monitoring and decision authority before any extension.

The corporate action owner may request an extension but must not approve their own increased residual risk. A formal change to a performance standard, barrier status or operating limit follows the relevant deviation/MOC process and updates the register and site team.
A critical action whose due date has passed shall remain open and visible until an authorised extension and current risk disposition are recorded; it shall not be re-dated to conceal lateness.

sections.title: 7.3 Evidence of effectiveness and formal closure

blocks.t: Completion means the control has been implemented; effectiveness means that field evidence indicates it prevents or detects the identified failure mode. The verifier reviews work orders, test results, user observations, monitoring data or a repeat challenge at a reasonable operating exposure. If verification fails, reopen the action and reassess residual risk.

A close-out notice identifies who approved the conclusion, the exact evidence, linked document revisions and any change to investigation lessons. Report closure and action closure may occur at different times; both statuses remain transparent in ONE.
Closure of significant actions shall be verified by someone independent of the action owner and retained in the controlled action system.

A lesson states the event mechanism, failed or successful safeguard, who else could face the same exposure, and the practical check or action needed. Use sufficient technical context to be credible without disclosing unnecessary personal details. A short alert and a detailed technical annex may serve different audiences.

The Knowledge Management Specialist assigns affected locations, functions, activities, equipment classes, role groups and applicable OMS expectations. Lessons from a Gulf of Paria platform are screened for offshore fleet exposure and comparable CPF or land systems, including common vendors and maintenance strategies.
Rohan Ramkissoon, Knowledge Management Specialist, manages the distribution and feedback process for incident lessons and keeps the link to the investigation and corrective actions.
1. Identify duty holders and assets affected by the hazard, not only the original investigation team.
2. Select channel: controlled revised procedure, toolbox talk, shift briefing, competence assessment, technical bulletin or engineering standard revision.
3. Record delivery, recipient roles, queries and required field actions. A message opened or read is not by itself evidence of changed practice.
4. Verify at a sample of affected sites that the intended change was implemented and is understood.
5. Document external industry relevance and required approval before any wider sharing.
Lesson records shall retain event and action references, approved wording, audience/asset scope, issue date, method, responsible communicator, field confirmation and follow-up.

The approved incident report remains in its controlled records repository with appropriate security; ONE may show expectation coverage, associated requirements, lessons and summary links to authorised users. Where a lesson changes mandatory work, the source Word document is revised under ACE-DOC-STD-001 and ACE-DOC-STD-002 with numbered heading tags and a controlled effective date.

Tagging an incident finding to an OMS expectation helps discovery and coverage analysis but does not itself prove conformance, effectiveness or closure. Audit evidence must connect the tagged requirement to implementation and verified results.

rows: Incident ID, type, date/time/shift, reporter and employer, asset/site, equipment and work activity.
Actual and potential harm, risk-matrix rationale, process-safety tier if applicable, classification reviewer.
Structured chronology, witness and data references, photographs, custody, system limitations.
Immediate controls, emergency activation, status, all management and external notifications.
Technical barrier status, relevant OMS expectation, causal findings, MOC and risk-register links.
Owners, due dates, proof of completion, independent verification, lesson audience, close-out status.
Events entered within originating shift / reportable events discovered; record late recognition separately.
Investigations accepted by due date / those due; show severity and overdue age.
Repeated event mechanisms per asset/equipment exposure; link to prior action effectiveness.
Counts with exposure context, classification shifts and leading barrier checks.
Significant actions independently verified / significant actions ready for verification.
Tiered criteria and denominators from approved metric definitions; avoid mixing tiers.

blocks.t: The HSE Manager reviews incident data monthly with Operations and Process Safety; material findings and trends are reported to the VP HSE & Compliance. Quarterly OMS reporting aggregates incidents, audit outcomes, barrier impairment and risk-management actions, ensuring weak indicators from different systems are assessed together. The annual trends review examines each OMS element and proposed preventive changes.

Monthly performance evidence: reporting compliance, investigation cycle by level, overdue actions, recurrence, process-safety leading/lagging indicators, classification revisions and cross-site lesson verification.

sections.title: 9.3 Retention, controlled access and periodic assurance

blocks.t: Investigation reports and supporting evidence for asset events are retained for life of asset plus ten years under the OMS Manual retention schedule. Personal and legally sensitive supporting material has need-to-know access and legal holds override ordinary disposal. Audit sampling tests completeness, timeliness, classification decisions, action quality, independent verification and accessibility from the controlled records system.

This standard is reviewed at least every three years or earlier following significant legislative change, serious incidents, audit concerns, new business activities or approved OMS changes. The governing Word document remains authoritative; ONE presents controlled views.
Incident investigations and HAZOP reports shall be retained for life of asset plus ten years, subject to longer applicable legal, contractual or hold requirements.

blocks.t: Trace each action to a specific investigation finding and approved risk decision.
Identify an implementer, accountable owner and independent effectiveness verifier.
Describe the physical, procedural or organisational control to be changed and its technical endorsement.
Specify evidence that shows implementation and a separate test of effectiveness.
Retain all due-date changes and associated risk decisions.
Verify changes to documents, training/competence, risk register, SCE register and maintenance strategy.
Record applicability screening for similar equipment and sites.
Do not close failed verification as complete; reopen and escalate.

sections.title: Appendix F — Worked example: CPF compression protective trip

blocks.t: Scenario: During compression at the CPF, a protective shutdown function is demanded by a high-pressure transient; the final element responds slowly, while a separate operator intervention prevents containment exceedance. No injury or release occurs. The event is reported as a high-potential near miss and a protective-barrier challenge, not dismissed because production resumed.

Evidence includes the trip setpoint and alarm trends, instrument calibration records, valve as-found travel profile, proof-test specification, maintenance work orders, prior bypasses and operators’ shift notes. The analysis tests instrument impulse-line fouling, control logic timing, mechanical stiction and the testing method, distinguishing established evidence from plausible causes.

Potential corrective work includes an engineering disposition by the Instrumentation Technical Authority, affected SCE performance-standard review, revised proof-test coverage and interval through MOC, and cross-site screening for the same valve actuator. The investigation remains linked to a separate release-to-service decision and an independent effectiveness check of the revised testing regime.
The worked example demonstrates classification and evidence logic only; the live event record determines the applicable risk level, protective response and authorised release.

sections.title: Appendix G — Worked example: Point Lisas lifting near miss

blocks.t: Scenario: A lifting sling component falls into an isolated laydown area at Point Lisas Shore Base, narrowly missing a contractor as a boundary is being moved. Record the event as a near miss and assess realistic worst exposure, including whether exclusion zones and banksman control were effective.

Review lifting plan, sling certification, inspection evidence, rigging geometry, work permits, exclusion barrier location, toolbox talk and supervision arrangement. An instruction to “be careful” is not adequate if the equipment choice or lift control creates predictable exposure. Reassess contractor competence and interface roles, revise the lifting standard or work pack when supported, and verify change in the field.

docs.title: OMS Policy — Health, Safety, Environment and Operating Integrity
docs.author: Marissa Bobb — OMS Manager
docs.reviewers: George Habib — VP HSE & Compliance; Sharda Bissoon — VP Legal & Government Affairs (General Counsel); Sophia Hosany — VP Operations; Dev Jaggernauth — VP Engineering & Projects; Nicole Lange — Head of Internal Audit & Risk Assurance
docs.applies: All ACE activities, assets, sites, employees and contractors
docs.subtitle: ACE's mission, vision and values, and the leadership commitments for safe, responsible and reliable operations across ACE.

blocks.t: ACE operates one integrated management system for health, safety, environment, operating integrity and business performance. ONE sets the common expectations; accountable leaders provide the people, standards and resources necessary to meet them. We measure our performance through the health of our controls as well as our results.

This policy states why ACE exists, what it aims to become and the values that guide how we work. It is the top of the ACE golden thread: every other ACE policy names the values below in its commitments, and every process traces to a policy.
Our mission: to produce oil and gas from Trinidad and Tobago's land and the Gulf of Paria safely, reliably and responsibly, creating lasting value for the country, our partners and our people.
Our vision: to be the most trusted and best-run independent energy operator in the Caribbean.

No production, schedule or cost target justifies putting people or essential barriers at risk. In practice this means we stop work when a risk is not controlled, keep safety-critical equipment working and never knowingly exceed a safe operating limit.

We are honest, do what we say and follow the rules when no one is watching. In practice this means accurate reports and records, conflicts of interest declared, approvals given only within authority, and problems reported rather than hidden.

sections.title: 1.4 Value: Care for people and places

blocks.t: We look after our workforce, our neighbours and the environment we share, on land and in the Gulf of Paria. In practice this means preventing pollution, minimising flaring, listening to communities and fishers, and answering their concerns.

Staff, contractors and partners work to one management system and one set of rules at every site. In practice this means one risk matrix, one document hierarchy, one way of controlling work, clear roles, and processes that each have a single owner.

We learn from every incident, audit, idea and result, and turn lessons into lasting change. In practice this means reporting openly, closing actions with evidence that they worked, and improving processes and standards by revision and Management of Change.

This policy applies to every ACE activity: offshore production in the Gulf of Paria, the Central Processing Facility, land leases, wells, pipelines, marine and shore-base services, and work delivered by contractors on our behalf. No production, schedule or commercial objective takes priority over protecting people or maintaining essential barriers.

It covers all sites (HOF, PLB, PAP, CHB, SAP, CPF and LND), all functions, and every employee and contractor. The other ACE policies listed in section 6.3 sit under this policy and apply its values to their own subjects.
Each commitment below is an outcome ACE commits to, and names the values it serves. The steps that deliver it are in the governed processes and the implementing documents in section 6.
In line with our values One team, one way and Integrity in everything, our leaders own ONE and are seen to lead it.
The Chief Executive Officer shall own ONE, set the company direction and require each Executive Leadership Team member to demonstrate accountability for the controls in their area.
Every system and OMS element shall have an accountable owner, an approved set of requirements and a means of verifying implementation.
Vice Presidents and managers provide visible leadership, evaluate risk and act on concerns raised by employees, contractors and neighbours.

We lead by visiting the work, listening to the people who do it, checking the condition of critical barriers and correcting what is not working. Silence or an absence of reported problems is not evidence that risk is controlled.
In line with our value One team, one way, ACE runs its business through one system, not through separate programmes.
ACE activities shall be governed through ONE rather than disconnected HSE, integrity, maintenance or quality programmes.
System owners shall use the common ACE Risk Matrix, the approved document hierarchy and the ONE reporting and assurance arrangements.
A policy sets direction; standards describe requirements; procedures and work instructions describe how a job is performed. The current approved source is the ONE document repository.

sections.title: 2.3 Protect people and prevent serious harm

blocks.t: In line with our value Safety above all, hazards are understood and controlled before work starts.
ACE shall identify hazards before work, assess credible consequences, select effective prevention and recovery barriers, and verify that those barriers are available.
Work involving major accident hazards shall be supported by appropriate hazard studies, competent personnel, operating limits and effective emergency arrangements.

In line with our values Safety above all and Integrity in everything, anyone at ACE can stop work that is not safe, and is supported for doing so. The control that delivers this is in the Control of Work Standard (ACE-COW-STD-001).
Everyone has authority and a duty to stop or suspend work when conditions cannot be made safe.
Stopped work restarts only after the hazards are controlled and the responsible Area Authority releases it.
Anyone who identifies an uncontrolled hazard or a failed critical barrier shall stop the affected work, make the situation safe where competent to do so, and inform the supervisor or Area Authority.
We encourage reporting and professional challenge. No one is expected to continue a job solely because a schedule, budget or superior demands it.

sections.title: 2.5 Plan, permit, supervise and hand back work

blocks.t: In line with our values Safety above all and One team, one way, work is done the same controlled way by staff and contractors at every site.
ACE shall assign critical tasks to competent people, communicate current procedures and ensure that work is planned, permitted, supervised and handed back safely.
All employees and contractors shall follow the current approved requirements relevant to their role, attend required inductions, and act within their competence and authorization.
Do not bypass a safeguard or improvise around a mandatory procedure. Escalate the conflict and obtain an approved solution before proceeding.

In line with our value Safety above all, every ACE system is operated within its approved operating envelope. Operating limits are set, known by the people who run the plant, and changed only through Management of Change.

Excursions beyond operating limits are reported, assessed for their effect on safety-critical equipment and major accident barriers, and corrected. A safe operating limit is never knowingly exceeded to meet a production or sales target (ACE-OPS-STD-001).

sections.title: 2.7 Maintain the integrity and reliability of assets

blocks.t: In line with our values Safety above all and One team, one way, our assets are kept fit for purpose for their whole life, and the equipment that prevents or limits a major accident is known, owned and proven to work.
Safety-critical elements shall have defined performance standards, ownership and planned inspection, maintenance and testing.

Known impairments, overdue safety-critical tasks and changes affecting technical integrity shall be risk-assessed, escalated and managed using the approved deviation and management-of-change arrangements.

An overdue or impaired safety-critical element is never deferred silently: it is either restored on time or held under an approved, time-limited deviation with compensating measures (ACE-OMS-STD-002).
ACE manages wells, platforms, subsea and land pipelines, the CPF, tank farm and jetty on a life-cycle basis; reliability and safe operation are treated as connected outcomes.

In line with our values Safety above all and Integrity in everything, each engineering discipline has an appointed Technical Authority who owns its technical standards and endorses designs, changes and deviations.

Technical Authorities are appointed in writing, are competent for their discipline, and give their technical judgement independently of production, schedule or cost pressure. Their endorsement cannot be replaced by a line manager's approval (ACE-ENG-STD-901).

sections.title: 2.9 Meet legal, environmental and stakeholder obligations

blocks.t: In line with our values Integrity in everything and Care for people and places, ACE knows its obligations and meets them.
ACE shall identify and comply with applicable laws, licence conditions, permits, contractual obligations and adopted engineering and industry standards.
Operations shall prevent pollution where practicable, control emissions, discharges, spills and waste, and respond promptly to events that affect communities or the environment.
Legal & Government Affairs supports interpretation and monitoring of obligations; operational owners remain accountable for their implementation.
We will engage respectfully with communities and customers, respond to material concerns, and protect the quality of our sales gas and crude.
In line with our value Learn and improve, events and concerns are reported openly and used to make our barriers and methods better. How improvement is managed is set by ACE-OMS-POL-001.
Incidents, near misses, equipment anomalies, deviations and concerns shall be reported accurately and used to improve barriers and methods.
People shall promptly report incidents and near misses, cooperate with investigations and raise concerns about procedures that cannot be followed as written.
The table names the policy owner and the owners of the processes this policy governs. Process owners are as recorded in the Process Register (ACE-BPM-REG-001).

rows: Owns this policy and ONE; approves Level 1 policies; leads the Executive Leadership Team in acting on OMS performance.

Accountable for safe operation within limits, control of work and maintenance delivery at all producing sites.

Accountable for well integrity from design to abandonment.

Area Authorities control activity at their locations, coordinate simultaneous work and confirm the condition of plant before release or restart.
Technical Authorities define and assure technical requirements, assess proposed changes and deviations, and challenge decisions that could weaken critical barriers.

This policy sets no financial or risk-band thresholds of its own. Risk acceptance, deviation periods and change classes are set by ACE-RSK-POL-001; financial limits are set by ACE-FIN-POL-001. The decision rights below are fixed by this policy.

blocks.t: An approval to operate with a deviation shall never replace a legal permit or authorize action outside an absolute safety limit.
Every OMS objective shall have a measurable target, an accountable owner, a review date and an evidence source.

Performance reporting shall include leading indicators for barrier health, overdue corrective actions, competence and control-of-work verification, alongside incidents, losses and environmental outcomes.
Tier 1 and Tier 2 process safety events. Target: zero Tier 1 and no more than two Tier 2 per year (objective OBJ-26-02).
Safety-critical element inspections and tests completed on time. Target: 100% (objectives OBJ-26-03 and OBJ-26-06).
Safety-critical element deviations past their expiry date. Target: zero at any time.

Measures include safety-critical maintenance compliance; impairments overdue; high-risk actions overdue; incident investigation closure and effectiveness; legal compliance status; and corrective actions verified effective.

Objective IDs are those in the Objectives and Opportunities register (OMS-REG-001). They are renewed each year in the annual OMS plan under ACE-OMS-POL-001; the headline indicators above stay the same.

This policy has no review cycles of its own beyond those below. The arrangements for assurance, management review, process review and continuous improvement, and their frequencies, are set by ACE-OMS-POL-001.
ACE shall conduct planned self-checks, independent assurance and management review to test whether ONE requirements work in the field.
The Executive Leadership Team shall review management-system performance at least annually and commission improvements where results or evidence indicate weaknesses.
The Chief Executive Officer shall review and re-approve this policy at least every three years, or sooner following a material change to ACE's operations, risk profile or obligations.
The OMS Manager maintains the policy and coordinates conformance evidence; the CEO and ELT act on review outcomes.

This policy is the governing policy of the L3 processes below. Numbers are given where the process is in the Process Register; the others are candidates from the process inventory. The L1 1 Explore & Develop processes are governed here for now, until a reserves and resources policy is written. As the OMS Policy, this policy also applies to every other ACE process.

docs.owner: Sharda Bissoon — VP Legal & Government Affairs (General Counsel)
docs.author: Winston Daniel — Senior Counsel, Contracts & Commercial
docs.reviewers: Adrian Achong — VP Human Resources; Nicole Lange — Head of Internal Audit & Risk Assurance; Sasha George — VP Supply Chain Management; Teresa Daniel — Chief Financial Officer; Rodney Garcia — VP Communications & Corporate Services
docs.applies: All ACE activities, sites, employees and contractors
docs.subtitle: The standards of honest, fair and lawful conduct ACE expects of everyone who works for or with it, and the freedom to speak up.

blocks.t: This policy sets the standards of conduct ACE expects of everyone who works for or with it: honesty, fair dealing, no bribery or corruption, conflicts declared, and the freedom to speak up without fear. The detailed rules are in the Code of Conduct (ACE-LDR-STD-001), which this policy governs.
It applies to every ACE director, employee and secondee at every site, and to contractors, suppliers, agents and partners when they act for ACE. Its parent is ACE-LDR-POL-001.
Each commitment names the ACE values it serves, as set in ACE-LDR-POL-001 section 1. The steps that deliver the commitments are in the governed processes and implementing documents in section 6.

In line with our value Integrity in everything, ACE does business honestly and within the law. We do not offer, give, ask for or accept bribes or facilitation payments of any kind, directly or through others, and we deal fairly with customers, suppliers, partners, competitors and public officials.
No person acting for ACE shall offer, give, request or accept a bribe, a facilitation payment or any other improper advantage.

sections.title: 2.2 Conflicts of interest are declared before decisions

blocks.t: In line with our value Integrity in everything, anyone with a personal interest that could affect, or appear to affect, a decision declares it before the decision is made and steps aside from it. This declaration is a check step in tendering and award, recruitment and promotion, and other approvals.

Each person taking part in a tender evaluation, contract award, recruitment or approval decision shall declare any conflict of interest before the decision and shall take no further part in it if a conflict exists.

In line with our value Integrity in everything, gifts and hospitality are modest, occasional and open, never cash, and never given or received when they could influence a decision. The limits are set in section 4.2.

In line with our values Integrity in everything and Learn and improve, anyone may raise a concern about conduct, safety or the law, openly or anonymously, and ACE protects them from retaliation. Every concern is acknowledged and answered within the times in section 4.3. Concerns that point to a better way of working are passed, with the originator's consent, to the CI register as staff ideas under ACE-OMS-POL-001.
No person shall retaliate against anyone who raises a concern in good faith.
In line with our values Care for people and places and One team, one way, everyone at ACE is treated with respect, free from harassment, bullying and unfair discrimination.

docs.title: Equipment Criticality and SCE Maintenance Practice
docs.author: Nadira Ramsaran — Reliability & Maintenance Lead
docs.reviewers: Marc Gomes — Maintenance & Integrity Manager; Sunita Seepersad — Maintenance Superintendent; Sharon Alexander — Rotating Equipment Lead; Akilah Noel — Fire & Gas and Safety Systems Lead
docs.applies: PAP, CHB, SAP, CPF, LND, PLB
docs.subtitle: Ranking equipment by risk, selecting maintenance strategies and assuring Safety-Critical Elements.

blocks.t: This Practice defines ACE’s equipment criticality ranking and maintenance strategy method, including identification and maintenance assurance for Safety-Critical Elements (SCEs). It supports the Maintenance Management Standard and links to Asset Integrity, Risk, Control of Work and ONE deviation controls.
Applies to equipment and maintainable assets at the CPF, Pommerac A, Chenet B, Sapodilla C, land leases, shore base and supporting infrastructure.

Parent Standard: ACE-MNT-STD-001 Maintenance Management Standard. This Practice turns its requirements into the method ACE uses to rank equipment, select strategies and assure Safety-Critical Elements. It applies at PAP, CHB, SAP, CPF, LND and PLB.

Recognised practice applied: ISO 14224 Collection and exchange of reliability and maintenance data for equipment; IEC 60300-3-11 Reliability centred maintenance; ISO 55001 Asset management systems; Energy Institute guidance on the management of SCEs.

Reliability & Maintenance Lead owns criticality methodology and strategy consistency. Maintenance & Integrity Manager assures cross-functional alignment. Maintenance Superintendent coordinates execution and backlog. Equipment discipline leads advise failure modes and strategy. Operations confirms operating context and access, and accepts operational handover.

SCE designation and performance requirements are endorsed through integrity and technical authority arrangements. Operations and Maintenance must jointly resolve maintenance deferral or impairment decisions.

rows: Approves the method; accountable for SCE maintenance performance across operated sites.
Owns the criticality method, strategy library and reliability reviews.
Assures alignment between maintenance, inspection and SCE performance standards.
Plans and schedules work; manages backlog and overdue SCE reporting.
Failure modes and strategies for pumps, compressors and turbines.
Akilah Noel — Fire & Gas and Safety Systems Lead
Performance standards and test methods for fire and gas, ESD and SIS elements.

blocks.t: The Reliability & Maintenance Lead shall maintain the criticality method and the strategy library, and shall present the criticality coverage report to the Technical Leadership Council every six months.
The Maintenance Superintendent shall report overdue SCE work to the Area Authority and the Maintenance & Integrity Manager every week.

Maintain a consistent equipment hierarchy from site/system to functional location, equipment and maintainable component. Unique equipment IDs connect CMMS, integrity registers, ONE, drawings and maintenance history.

Rank equipment A/B/C using ACE risk criteria: safety/environment consequence, production impact, escalation potential, repairability, redundancy, detectability and failure history. Document rationale and uncertainty; avoid assigning criticality solely by equipment type.
Every maintainable item shall have a unique equipment ID in the ISO 14224-aligned hierarchy, and the same ID shall be used in the CMMS, the SCE register and ONE (C-MNT-001).

A-critical equipment has high consequence or essential barrier/function significance and requires enhanced strategy, planning and assurance. B-critical equipment has material consequence requiring managed preventive or condition-based maintenance. C equipment has lower consequence where a justified run-to-failure strategy may be acceptable.
Review ranking after failure, significant change, barrier role change, operating context change, redundancy loss, new risk assessment or reliability trend.
Every equipment item shall carry an A, B or C criticality ranking assessed against the ACE Risk Matrix, with the rationale recorded and reviewed after each trigger listed above (C-MNT-002).

Identify SCEs through risk and barrier analysis and maintain the SCE register linked to AIM-REG-001 and performance standards. Each SCE has a defined safety function, required performance, verification method, maintenance tasks, test interval, failure criteria and impairment response.
SCE maintenance is not merely a work-order frequency: the task and test must verify the required function and preserve evidence of acceptance.
Every SCE shall be listed in the SCE register (ACE-AIM-REG-001) with a current performance standard that defines its function, required performance and verification test (C-MNT-003).

Choose preventive/time-based, predictive/condition-based, functional testing, corrective or run-to-failure strategies according to failure modes, consequence, detection, degradation, data availability and lifecycle cost.

For A-critical assets, use an RCM-light review: function, functional failure, credible failure modes, consequence, effective task, task interval and residual risk. Run-to-failure requires documented justification and confirmation that failure consequence is tolerable.

The maintenance strategy for each A and B item shall be selected from its credible failure modes and recorded, and a run-to-failure strategy shall only be applied to C items with documented justification (C-MNT-004).

sections.title: 7 Work order priority, backlog and planning

blocks.t: Prioritise work by risk, SCE status, operating impact, defect severity, overdue exposure, resource and access constraints. Priority is not a substitute for approved risk classification.

Maintenance planning confirms scope, materials, isolation needs, competency, vendor support, test requirements, permits, work packs and schedule dependencies. Backlog ageing and risk-weighted overdue work are reviewed.
Preventive and test work on A-critical equipment shall be scheduled in the CMMS with a planned date, and completion against plan shall be monitored every month (C-MNT-005).
The Maintenance Superintendent shall review the risk-weighted backlog every week and escalate any A-critical or SCE item older than its backlog limit (C-MNT-006).

rows: SCE failed or loss of containment
B-critical defect; preventive work on A items

sections.title: 8 SCE overdue, impairment, bypass and deviation

blocks.t: An overdue SCE maintenance or test task is treated as a deviation and raised under ACE-OMS-STD-002. The record includes risk, expiry, approval, interim measures and visible ONE tracking. No overdue task is silently rescheduled to conceal the exposure.

Defeat, bypass, inhibit or impairment of an SCE requires Control of Work authorization, affected barrier identification, risk assessment, duration, compensating measures, communication, restoration checks and override-log entry. Escalate if conditions or time limit change.
An overdue SCE maintenance or test task shall be raised as a deviation under ACE-OMS-STD-002 before its due date passes, with interim measures and an expiry date (C-MNT-007).
Any defeat, bypass or inhibit of an SCE shall be authorised under ACE-COW-STD-001 and entered in the override log with its duration and compensating measures (C-MNT-008).
SCE work orders shall only be closed when the function test result and the restoration to service are recorded against the performance standard (C-MNT-009).

Capture equipment ID, criticality, SCE flag, failure mode, symptom, cause, downtime, repair, parts, task history, test results and recurrence. Preserve links between work order, defect, risk, SCE register and performance standard.
Failure data is reviewed for repeat failures, task effectiveness, bad actors, spare strategy and criticality assumptions. CMMS data must be complete, consistent and auditable.
The Reliability & Maintenance Lead shall review failure data every quarter and update the criticality ranking or strategy where repeat failures show the current task is not effective (C-MNT-010).
Failure records shall capture the ISO 14224 failure mode, cause and downtime against the equipment ID in the CMMS.

Reliability & Maintenance Lead reviews criticality coverage, preventive compliance, risk-weighted backlog, overdue SCE work, repeat failures, maintenance effectiveness and bad actors. Assurance samples SCE work orders for task quality, test acceptance, restoration and record completeness.

Leading: SCE preventive and test work completed on time (target ≥ 98%); A-critical backlog older than limit (target 0); open SCE deviations past expiry (target 0). Lagging: SCE test failures on demand; repeat failures on bad-actor equipment.
These planned processes execute this Practice. Process maps must show Operations, Maintenance Planning, discipline Technical Authorities, Supply Chain and Integrity handovers.

docs.title: Maintenance Management Standard
docs.author: Nadira Ramsaran — Reliability & Maintenance Lead
docs.reviewers: Sunita Seepersad — Maintenance Superintendent; Rohan Ali — Plant Manager - Central Processing Facility; Garvin Mark — Integrity Engineer
docs.endorser: Sharon Alexander — Rotating Equipment Lead (Technical Authority)
docs.applies: All ACE operated offshore and onshore assets, plant, pipelines, buildings and support facilities, including contracted maintenance.
docs.subtitle: Asset maintenance strategies, planning, execution, safety-critical tasks, materials and reliability improvement across ACE operations.

blocks.t: This standard establishes how ACE selects, schedules, executes, verifies and learns from maintenance on all managed assets. It brings preventive, predictive, statutory, corrective and safety-critical tasks under one controlled operating process, using the approved equipment hierarchy and work-order record as the common trace from the engineering basis to field execution and return to service.

The required outcome is equipment that remains capable of its approved duty, predictable operation within defined limits, effective safeguards against major accident hazards and an auditable record of what was done, what was found and what was restored. Work completion is a physical and technical outcome, not merely a closed work-order status.

All maintainable ACE equipment shall have an accountable asset owner, a documented maintenance strategy proportionate to its risks, and a means of recording history in the approved computerised maintenance management system (CMMS) or authorised linked application.

This standard applies to the Central Processing Facility (CPF), tank farm, loading jetty, Gulf of Paria platforms Pommerac A, Chenet B and Sapodilla C, subsea and land pipelines, Tamarind/Pawpaw/Soursop leases, Point Lisas Shore Base, workshops and support equipment. It covers ACE technicians, supervisors, specialist vendors and contractors working under ACE operational control.

The Well Integrity Standard governs well barriers, the Asset Integrity Management Standard governs integrity and safety-critical performance standards, and the Control of Work Standard governs worksite permits, energy isolation and interfaces. Maintenance personnel remain subject to all three; this document does not supersede them.

Governing documents: ACE-OMS-MAN-001; ACE-RSK-STD-001; ACE-AIM-STD-001; ACE-MOC-PRC-001; ACE-COW-STD-001; ACE-DOC-STD-001; ACE-DOC-STD-002. Associated planned documents: ACE-AIM-STD-002 Inspection Management; ACE-COW-PRC-001 Permit to Work; ACE-COW-PRC-002 Isolation and Reinstatement.

rows: Owns system performance, resources and material risks; decides escalation and cross-site priorities.
Owns implementation, budget, integrated schedule, competence and CMMS data stewardship.
Maintains strategies, criticality, failure history, reliability review and technical effectiveness.
Controls execution resources, work-pack quality, supervision and work completion verification.
Authorises access and area work; confirms plant status, SIMOPS, safe handover and return to service.
Owns technical criteria, SCE endorsement, engineering dispositions and risk-based deferral advice.
Coordinates approved stock, preservation, availability and transport from Point Lisas.

blocks.t: The Maintenance & Integrity Manager is accountable for ensuring that the maintenance plan implements the relevant Technical Authority performance standards and that Operations can verify the status of impaired or overdue safety-critical safeguards.
Protect people and major accident barriers before production or schedule efficiency.
Use the ACE Risk Matrix to choose priority and treatment; do not substitute work-order categories for risk assessment.
Do work only to an approved scope, on identified equipment, with the necessary permits, isolations, competence and quality checks.
Treat unexpected condition, failed tests, repeat faults and missing evidence as potential defects requiring disposition.
Use formal MOC when a change to design, safeguards, operating limits, procedures, intervals or equipment strategy is proposed.

A maintenance planning or scheduling decision shall not authorise a deviation from an approved engineering limit, safety-critical performance standard, statutory requirement or the Control of Work requirements.

The maintenance strategy is established at the correct functional level by considering failure functions, credible failure modes, causes and consequences, detectability, protective barriers, operation duty and cost of failures. Sources include hazard studies, original equipment manufacturer instructions, inspection findings, reliability history, regulatory duties, environmental exposure and verified operating experience.

For each failure mode, the selected intervention has to be technically effective: condition monitoring if degradation provides useful warning; scheduled restoration or replacement if failure behaviour warrants it; proof testing for hidden protective functions; failure finding or run-to-failure only where consequences are demonstrably tolerable. Risk assessment must take account of multiple items sharing the same failure cause.

The Reliability & Maintenance Lead shall document and approve maintenance strategies with the relevant Technical Authority for safety-critical or discipline-controlled equipment; changes affecting function, task intervals or protection shall follow MOC.

rows: Performance standard, barrier function, proof-test coverage, allowable impairments, prescribed task due date.
SCE identifier, performance requirement, test method and result.
Reliability-centred analysis; condition-based work; consequence of prolonged outage; spares.
Criticality assessment, failure history, strategy basis.
Preventive/condition monitoring matched to failure mode and manufacturer guidance.
PM task, condition trend, work-order close-out.
Proportionate inspection or run-to-failure where assessed as acceptable.
Approved selection rationale and repair response plan.

blocks.t: Criticality is assigned using the ACE Risk Matrix for credible failure consequences, distinguishing effects on personnel, process safety, the environment, production, legal obligations and customer delivery. Assess independence, standby availability, shared utilities and recovery time. A second compressor is not redundant if both machines depend on a common cooling-water system with no alternative.

The criticality review is triggered by MOC, major failure, material service change, new hazard-study findings and asset acquisition; not every task needs a full new analysis, but the parent criticality and assumptions must remain traceable.

Any equipment identified as safety-critical by the hazard and barrier register shall be flagged in the CMMS as SCE and linked to the currently approved performance standard; maintenance criticality alone shall not change its barrier status.

Each preventive or predictive task specifies the equipment boundary, purpose, frequency or condition trigger, acceptance criteria, work steps or linked instruction, competence requirements, tools, spares, isolation and access conditions, quality evidence and escalation if the test fails. Task packages distinguish between a successful test, a test not performed and an unsuccessful test restored after repair.

A time-based task frequency is set against the risk and degradation rate, not an automatically inherited calendar interval. Where running-hour cycles or starts are material, scheduling logic uses those measures and defines fallback controls when the measurements fail. Fixed statutory or performance-standard frequencies are protected from local schedule optimisation.
Each new or revised maintenance task shall retain a strategy reference, task version, approving role, equipment applicability, acceptance values, mandatory evidence and effective date.

Condition-monitoring routes for pumps, compressors, motors, electrical switchgear and corrosive services capture comparable measurements, normalise for duty when necessary and differentiate warning limits from trip and operating limits. Results need trend context; a green current reading does not extinguish a documented persistent adverse trend.

In the CPF, compressor vibration and lubricant results are reviewed together with seal leaks, bearing temperatures and machine duty. On Pommerac A, valve function test results are compared with recorded stroke times and partial-test histories. On land gathering stations, repeated motor starts and power interruptions may indicate problems outside the failed component.

Condition monitoring findings outside approved warning or action criteria shall generate a traceable defect record with screening, owner, due date and follow-up verification; they shall not be treated as completed routine inspections without disposition.

ACE maintains a common hierarchical record from company to site, unit, functional location, maintainable equipment and component. Functional location identifies duty and place; equipment identifier identifies a physical item that may be removed or replaced. Equipment movements maintain history rather than overwriting it. Tags used by the CMMS must agree with engineering drawings, P&IDs, safety-critical registers and asset handover documents.

The CMMS is the execution system of record for maintenance. The controlled repository stores approved source instructions, engineering justifications and formal close-out documents. The ONE portal provides navigation to these sources; it is not a substitute for transactional task history.

rows: Location authority, area risk and worksite interfaces.
Process boundary, system, parent drawings and duty.
Manufacturer, model, commissioning date, service status.
Replacement history, test or calibration record.

blocks.t: The Equipment Master holds active/inactive status, physical location, parent hierarchy, duty, criticality, SCE flag, Technical Authority, drawings, maintenance tasks, vendor information, spares links and applicable warranty or certification. Data cannot be marked verified merely because a field is populated. Verification must compare the record with the asset and approved baseline.

Each equipment or functional-location change is processed through a controlled request with old and new values, supporting evidence, change basis, reviewer and effective date. Duplicate records are reconciled before open work orders are migrated. Data fields used for ONE role/process navigation must use approved controlled values.

Equipment master changes resulting from projects, modifications, replacements or asset transfers shall be accepted by the Maintenance & Integrity Manager or delegate and synchronised with relevant drawings, SCE records and active work plans before operational handover.

Data checks compare the SCE register against overdue proof tests, ensure every active PM is attached to a valid equipment record, detect work orders without closure findings and check task frequencies against current approved versions. Data quality reports are corrected at source by assigned stewards. Import scripts and mobile data capture must not bypass required approval fields.

When historical task data are incomplete, ACE records the uncertainty and the interim safeguards. An unknown last test cannot be treated as evidence that a test passed. Missing acceptance values trigger a strategy review rather than an invented default value.

Monthly master-data scorecard: active equipment with complete critical fields; SCE-to-performance-standard reconciliation; orphan work orders; duplicate tags; maintenance tasks with overdue review; work orders closed without findings.

Work originates from planned tasks, operator rounds, monitoring alarms, condition findings, integrity assessments, regulatory inspections, incidents, MOCs and improvement projects. A request describes the observed symptom, location, operating context, hazard or affected barrier and urgency; the planner separates fault diagnosis from a premature prescriptive solution.

Requests that may involve loss of containment, protection failure or unsafe operation are immediately referred to the Area Authority and relevant Technical Authority. An urgent verbal work request still requires a recorded work order and required Control of Work authorisation prior to execution except under emergency arrangements permitted by the applicable emergency plan.

Every request shall be screened for immediate operational risk and SCE impact before it enters the routine backlog; emergency and impairment cases shall be escalated without waiting for the next planning cycle.

rows: Uncontrolled hazardous condition, failed critical safeguard or unsafe state.

blocks.t: Priority codes facilitate scheduling but do not constitute risk acceptance. The asset owner uses the ACE matrix to justify work that must be executed or a restriction that must be imposed. Backlog ageing is reviewed by risk class, not only total count; a low number of work orders can conceal overdue protective function tests.

A work order is “Ready to Schedule” only when its safe method, resources, parts, tooling, access, permits, constraints and evidence requirements are sufficiently specified. A work order awaiting a spare is not a schedule-ready task, and an SCE due date does not extend because its material is late.

The planner combines the work description, operating conditions, equipment data, drawings and approved job instruction; identifies task and isolation boundaries; estimates competent labour and duration; confirms plant status and any simultaneous activities; and specifies the tests that determine acceptance. Complex scopes include a hold-point and inspection-test plan.

The maintenance supervisor reviews practicality with the site team; the Area Authority checks conflicts with production, marine transfers, loading operations and well work. Work packs reference controlled documents by identifier and revision. Only the latest approved revision is used for execution.

Work packs shall identify equipment unambiguously and state the means of verifying successful work and safe reinstatement; a general instruction such as “repair as necessary” is not an adequate completion criterion for an SCE.

rows: Safe execution sequence, urgent repairs, permits, isolations and handovers.
Frozen weekly plan, work-package readiness, lifting/access and contractor support.
SCE compliance, backlog risk, budget, turnarounds and reliability actions.
Campaign windows, capital replacement, failure trends and capacity constraints.

blocks.t: The integrated schedule draws on operations availability, contractor mobilisations, marine/weather constraints, CPF process campaigns and statutory inspection windows. The same equipment cannot simultaneously be unavailable for maintenance and promised as a live standby control without explicit operational assessment. Schedule changes with risk or barrier implications are re-approved at the appropriate level.

Break-in work is recorded separately so ACE can distinguish inevitable emergency response from weak planning, recurring failures or improper schedule discipline. The Maintenance Superintendent assesses whether another planned task must move and whether that move causes an overdue SCE or statutory task. Safety or reliability rationale is recorded and, when necessary, escalated.

The work-order category is corrected after investigation if the root cause shows the task was planned maintenance, predictive intervention or recurring defect elimination. This prevents the reactive maintenance measure from being improved by recoding work retrospectively.

Weekly plan changes shall record the removed work, substituted task, reason, approving role, any altered risk and the new commitment date; SCE deferrals require the separate authorisation process in section 6.

sections.title: 5 Execution, verification and return to service

blocks.t: The supervisor confirms the work pack is current and executable; the Performing Authority accepts the work scope and applies the Control of Work requirements. A toolbox discussion reviews the task risk assessment, line-of-fire hazards, simultaneous activities, lifting, stored energy, hazardous substances, access, weather and emergency response. The Area Authority retains control of the site and plant state.

Specialist maintenance requires demonstration of competence and tools fit for purpose. Manufacturer instructions and standards are available at the point of work. The permit, isolation, test instrument and job pack must identify the same equipment and boundaries; mismatches stop the job pending correction.
Work shall not begin until the required permit, risk assessment, isolations, competency checks, site coordination and work-package acceptance are complete.

Technicians record as-found observations before resetting, replacing or recalibrating equipment. Any unexpected defect or change in scope is assessed and, where necessary, the work paused while the supervisor and Technical Authority determine the safe disposition. Removed safeguards, protective covers, drains and temporary lifting points are tracked until restored.

Mandatory inspection or independent hold points prevent concealment of defects, as with pressure test witness requirements, final checks on ESD valves, alignment verification of a critical pump or electrical protection relay testing. Photographs or readings support but do not replace the acceptance decision.

A change to an approved maintenance task, acceptance criterion or engineered configuration shall not be implemented solely by modifying the work order; use the approved MOC or deviation route as applicable.

The job is tested in a controlled order: confirm installation against drawings, inspect workmanship, verify correct tools and calibrated instruments, perform functional/proof tests, remove temporary isolations and reinstatement devices in the authorised sequence, complete operational checks and obtain the Area Authority’s acceptance. Function tests record measured result against a stated limit.

A task remains technically incomplete when the physical job is finished but the required test cannot be performed. The Area Authority decides whether the equipment can remain isolated or run under a formal restriction; the Technical Authority assesses any affected barrier. Administrative closure cannot imply restored function before verification.

Return to service after work affecting an SCE, pressure boundary, interlock, safety system or operating envelope shall require documented verification of acceptance criteria, resolution of impairments and Area Authority release.

The technician enters labour, installed parts and serial numbers, as-found and as-left readings, test instruments, faults, photographs where relevant, unresolved follow-up requirements and links to permit/isolation records. Supervisor review checks adequacy and resolves missing findings, repeat failures and obligations for strategy improvement. The planner updates the next due date under the approved frequency logic, not simply from whichever day data entry was completed.

Work orders closed as “No fault found”, “Unable to access”, “Deferred”, “Cancelled” or “Not performed” are distinguished from completed successful maintenance. The reason and consequence are retained. Safety-critical tasks cannot be falsely counted compliant due to a closed status when no successful performance evidence exists.

For proof tests and other acceptance-critical tasks, the CMMS record shall retain the approved procedure revision, test conditions, instrument identity and calibration state, measured results, failed items, restorative work and authorised acceptance.

Contract maintenance is controlled through technical scopes, mobilisation checks, interface plans and the same permit system as ACE work. Qualified vendor status does not waive site-specific induction, competence verification or an ACE witness point. Where vendor software holds detailed test results, a controlled record is transferred into the ACE repository with identifiers and access safeguards.

ACE’s accepting engineer verifies as-built configuration, material certification, component traceability and test evidence. Outstanding punch items carry owner, risk and due date; safety-critical exceptions follow deviation control. The contractor handover must identify temporary devices, outstanding isolations, open leaks and warranty-related obligations.

A safety-critical element is maintained to its performance standard: functionality, availability/reliability, survivability, dependencies and evidence method. The SCE register identifies accountable Technical Authority, inspection/test tasks and impairment logic. CMMS activities are traced to this register and to the major accident hazard for which the safeguard is credited.

Examples include emergency shutdown valves at Pommerac A, CPF fire and gas detection and shutdown systems, high-integrity pressure protection, selected relief systems and structural or containment barriers. The classification is determined by the approved hazard study and register rather than by a generic list in this standard.
A failed or overdue SCE task shall be evaluated as a potential impairment of the credited barrier, including whether other safeguards share the same failure cause or are simultaneously unavailable.

A proof test is planned with adequate plant access and competent personnel before its approved due date. Operations is advised early if shutdown or isolation is necessary. When a test cannot be completed, the site team records the reason and estimates the risk of the unverified function; it does not silently move the task date.

A failed test is recorded as a failure even if a repair and successful retest occur within the same shift. Failure analysis considers the as-found fault, duration of unknown failure, associated demands, common causes and similar devices. The corrective action may include interim compensating measures and a wider population review.

No SCE proof-test or inspection interval shall be extended without the Technical Authority’s written technical basis, an approved risk decision by the designated risk acceptance authority and a time-limited deviation where required.
