blocks.t: ACE separates the authority that specifies an engineering boundary from the authority that operates a site. The Process Engineering Lead is the technical custodian of the envelope. The Area Authority accepts the operational implementation and controls people and work in the location. The technical authorities establish discipline-specific constraints and endorse changes within their scopes.

blocks.t: ACE distinguishes the design/verified boundary from the operating boundary used in day-to-day work. Limit categories are not interchangeable; each entry must state its nature and consequence if breached. Where operating margins are required, the margin must account for instrument uncertainty, response time, process dynamics and the demand on protective systems.

blocks.t: Each limit record shall identify its class, measurement basis, units, measurement source, margin and tolerance, deviation response, controlling technical reference and responsible owner.
No limit, alarm or trip setting shall be raised or removed solely to improve production continuity or suppress a recurrent nuisance alarm.

Example interface: a pressure separator at Pommerac A has a process operating band, a documented safe pressure ceiling, alarm setpoints and a protective shutdown function. Different records may supply the design rating and current operating restriction. The local approved envelope identifies which is governing; the process engineer reconciles the technical basis with the I&C and Process Safety leads.

A limit is an engineering decision supported by traceable evidence, not merely a chosen control-room number. The starting information includes design dossiers, P&IDs, equipment certificates, hazard studies, relief and disposal system capacity, SIL or barrier performance standards, OEM manuals, inspection findings, process simulations and previous incident lessons.

rows: Equipment, tag and operating-mode scope; interfaces and utility dependencies.

blocks.t: The Process Engineering Lead shall prepare and maintain the technical basis for safety-critical process limits; the relevant Technical Authority shall endorse restrictions within their discipline.
Changes affecting a protection-layer design assumption, instrument setpoint, trip logic, equipment rating or operating envelope shall be assessed through ACE-MOC-PRC-001 before implementation.
For operating modes outside the verified design case, the Area Authority shall prohibit routine operation until a justified, approved temporary operating envelope is in place.

The envelope should be built at useful operating-mode resolution: normal operation, start-up, ramp-up, planned shutdown, emergency shutdown, post-trip restart and abnormal utility loss. A limit valid in one mode is not automatically valid in another. A single register record can identify mode-dependent values and the transition rules between them.

The operating-envelope register is the controlled source for each site. It points to design and hazard evidence and must support a query by equipment tag, system, operating mode and limit class. A controlled operating instruction translates the register into plain language for a shift; a control-system display provides the current measured condition. All three must be mutually consistent.
The Area Authority shall ensure that safety-critical limits and their immediate responses are accessible at the control point, including a degraded-communications fallback where necessary.

The controlled register shall record unique limit ID, asset/system/equipment tag, parameter, units, limit class and value, mode, basis, owner, reviewer, approved revision, alarm/trip links, normal response, escalation authority and next review trigger.

Disagreement between the DCS configuration and the approved register is treated as a controlled discrepancy, not corrected by undocumented field edits.

An alarm exists to trigger an operator action within an available response time. Rationalisation must connect the cause, credible consequence, operating limit, action, time to respond and possible automatic safeguard. Alarms without a timely response are better represented as condition indicators, maintenance alerts or event logs rather than safety-critical operator demands.

blocks.t: Safety-critical alarm rationalisation shall document the associated operating limit, priority, response time, operator action and protective function relationship.
The Instrumentation & Control Lead shall maintain the alarm and setpoint technical basis; Operations shall own the human response instructions and competence verification.

The alarm lifecycle and the operating envelope support each other: an integrity restriction can temporarily narrow the permissible operating range without changing the certified design rating. Such a restriction must be visible to the operator and protected against accidental overwrite in a system configuration update.
External reference: IEC 62682, Management of alarm systems for the process industries; adopted editions are identified in the ACE Engineering Standards Register.

An exceedance is a recorded event in which an approved operating limit is crossed, even if equipment damage or loss of containment does not occur. Operators first establish safety, then preserve evidence and report. The seriousness of an event is determined by actual and potential consequences, barrier condition and duration rather than production loss alone.
Figure 2. Area Authority-led exceedance and restart process.
All safe operating limit exceedances shall be reported in the incident system and assessed for possible impact on safety-critical equipment and major accident hazard barriers.
The Shift Supervisor shall secure the plant when the approved response requires shutdown or when the remaining protection against escalation cannot be demonstrated.

A temporary restriction or departure from an approved limit shall be processed through the relevant deviation and MOC requirements, with explicit expiry, safeguards, communications and restart authority.

The exceedance record shall contain event time, operating mode, tags and trends, duration beyond the limit, alarm/trip state, immediate actions, personnel notified, barrier effects, associated MOC/deviation and technical release evidence.

blocks.t: Operating-envelope information changes when plant is modified, hazards are revalidated, inspection reveals damage, an instrument is re-ranged or an alarm is reconfigured. The change package must identify affected limits, source drawings, operating procedures, training and safe start-up checks. The revision of an engineering document must not silently alter the live control-system configuration.

A limit revision shall identify affected documents, alarm settings, control logic, operating instructions, training and integrity records and shall not be considered complete until all affected controlled sources are aligned.

blocks.t: Site scenario — CPF compressor discharge pressure: an operating trend approaches its approved boundary during increased gas sales demand. The Shift Supervisor verifies indication, applies the control-room response and records the event. If a safe operating limit is crossed or protective function trips, the Plant Manager controls restart; the process engineer investigates the limit relationship; I&C verifies measurement and trip evidence; integrity input is requested if mechanical condition may be affected.

No operator should infer a new limit from remote instrumentation alone.

blocks.t: Operating scenario — CPF tank transfer: a transfer line is being prepared for crude loading while a temporary integrity restriction is active on a downstream segment. Before opening the route, the Plant Manager confirms the line-up, approved reduced envelope, transfer protection, alarm displays and communication with the loading function. A revised transfer rate is not applied solely because the jetty schedule is constrained. The restriction remains attached to the asset tag and the shift handover until technically closed.

Operating scenario — planned offshore start-up: Pommerac A restarts after an ESD valve intervention. Operations confirms the isolation and reinstatement evidence, verifies any affected trip proof test, checks the register revision for start-up mode and follows the ramp-up instruction. I&C verifies the live configuration; the OIM releases the operating mode; the Process Engineering Lead resolves any inconsistent limit sources.

docs.title: People and Competence Policy
docs.author: Damian St. Hill — Competence Assurance Coordinator
docs.reviewers: Sophia Hosany — VP Operations; George Habib — VP HSE & Compliance; Gary Ho Sing — Manager, Strategy & Planning; Paul Fernandes — Industrial Relations Specialist; Richard Ng Wai — HR Business Partner
docs.applies: All ACE activities, sites, employees and contractors
docs.subtitle: How ACE makes roles clear, proves competence before people work alone, and builds OMS duties into every job.

blocks.t: This policy sets ACE's commitments for recruiting, developing, authorising and managing the people who do ACE's work, so that every role is clear, every safety-critical task is done by someone proven competent, and OMS duties are part of the job.

It applies to all ACE employees and secondees at every site, and to contractors where they fill an ACE role or perform a safety-critical task at an ACE site. Its parent is ACE-LDR-POL-001. Financial delegation is set by ACE-FIN-POL-001; this policy covers role authority.
Each commitment names the ACE values it serves, as set in ACE-LDR-POL-001 section 1. The steps that deliver the commitments are in the governed processes and implementing documents in section 6.

In line with our value One team, one way, every ACE role has a profile that states its OMS duties and the process steps the role performs. Because the lanes in ACE process maps are roles, a person can see from their role profile where they act in each process, and ONE links role pages, process lanes and steps.

In line with our value Safety above all, no one performs a safety-critical role or task unsupervised until they have been assessed against the role profile and authorised in writing (ACE-PPL-STD-003). This authorisation is a pre-condition check in permit to work, isolation, offshore travel and other processes.
No person shall perform a safety-critical task unsupervised unless they hold a current, recorded authorisation for that task.

sections.title: 2.3 Role authorities are appointed in writing

blocks.t: In line with our values One team, one way and Integrity in everything, the OMS role authorities (Area Authority, Technical Authority, Performing Authority, Isolating Authority and Process Owner) are appointed in writing by the person named in section 4.1, with a defined scope, and the appointment is recorded so that anyone can check who holds it.

sections.title: 2.4 Process owners trained and lanes briefed

blocks.t: In line with our value Learn and improve, a new process owner completes process owner training within 60 days of appointment (C-BPM-040 in ACE-BPM-PRA-003), and the people in each lane of a revised process are briefed before the revision takes effect (C-BPM-045).

sections.title: 2.5 We consult the people who do the work

blocks.t: In line with our values Learn and improve and Care for people and places, ACE consults its workforce and their representatives on changes to work, procedures and organisation that affect them, and uses what they tell us.

In line with our values Integrity in everything and Safety above all, ACE recognises people who work safely, speak up and improve the way we work, and deals fairly and consistently with behaviour that puts people or plant at risk. Honest mistakes reported openly are treated as chances to learn.

In line with our value Integrity in everything, people are recruited and promoted on merit against the role profile, with credentials verified and conflicts of interest declared, and every new starter is inducted before starting work.

docs.title: Competence Assurance Standard
docs.author: Andrea Farfan — Learning & Competence Manager
docs.reviewers: Richard Ng Wai — HR Business Partner; Paul Fernandes — Industrial Relations Specialist; Shane Isaac — Operations Training & Competence Coordinator
docs.applies: ACE employees, secondees, agency personnel and contractors in roles under ACE operational control, at all ACE locations
docs.subtitle: Role-based competence, practical verification and authorisation for work throughout ACE operations.

blocks.t: This standard establishes a single process for defining, developing, demonstrating and maintaining competence to perform ACE work. It is applicable to roles in the Head Office, Point Lisas Shore Base, the Central Processing Facility (CPF), Pommerac A, Chenet B, Sapodilla C, the Tamarind, Pawpaw and Soursop land leases, and to Wells and contracted work under ACE control.

Competence is demonstrated ability to apply relevant knowledge, practical skill and behaviours to a defined role or task under real operating conditions. Training completion, tenure, qualifications and professional registration may support an assessment, but none alone constitutes authorisation to undertake a safety-critical task.
Every ACE role shall have a current competence profile approved by its functional owner before unrestricted appointment or deployment.
Personnel shall not perform a safety-critical task unsupervised until the specified evidence has been assessed and a line manager has recorded the appropriate authorisation.
Fitness for work, professional licences, permit issuer appointment and authorisation for specialist equipment are additional gates where relevant. A competence approval does not override any of them.

Human Resources controls the assessment framework. Functional managers own role suitability, training provision and release for work. Technical Authorities control discipline criteria and technical assessment standards. Area Authorities control access to sites and operational work. The same person may hold more than one role, but required independent endorsement remains independent.
Andrea Farfan — Learning & Competence Manager: maintains competence profiles, assessor criteria, the central register and assurance programme.
Adrian Achong — VP Human Resources: accountable system owner and approver of material changes to the competence assurance framework.
Line managers and Area Authorities: confirm task assignment, work restrictions, supervision arrangements and release to operational duties.

rows: ACE-PPL-STD-001 Roles, Accountabilities and Delegated Authority Standard

blocks.t: Figure 1. Functional interfaces that produce a valid task authorisation.

A competence profile is a role-controlled set of task units and the evidence required to show satisfactory performance. Units distinguish awareness, working knowledge, supervised practical capability and independent execution. Every unit references the controlling standard or procedure and identifies any required permit, licence or Technical Authority endorsement.
The functional owner shall define each role profile with the Learning & Competence Manager and consult the relevant Technical Authority for discipline-controlled work.
Profiles for safety-critical roles shall specify task-level performance criteria, assessment method, reassessment triggers, independent verification needs and authorised scope.

blocks.t: A safety-critical task is one where incorrect execution or omission can defeat a major-accident barrier, cause uncontrolled energy release or prevent timely emergency response. Examples include permit and isolation authorities, well-control personnel, operators managing process-safety limits, safety-instrumented-system testers and emergency command roles.
Task criticality shall be established using the ACE Risk Matrix and the associated barrier function; a job title alone is not sufficient to classify risk.

blocks.t: A profile is reviewed whenever the role, equipment, process controls, legal requirements, work instruction or relevant hazard study changes. Cross-functional profiles must be reviewed by both the receiving function and the technical owner. Superseded profile versions remain retrievable against historical authorisations.
The Learning & Competence Manager shall control profile revisions in the central register and identify all existing authorisations affected by a revision.
The approved profile, change justification, assessor sign-off and affected-person list shall be retained as controlled competence records.

Screening establishes whether entry qualifications, experience, legal credentials and capability evidence are suitable for a proposed job. HR verifies personal and employment evidence, while the hiring function and Technical Authority assess specialist competence claims. Verified prior experience may reduce training needs but does not remove the requirement for assessment of ACE-specific tasks.
A hiring or transfer decision into a safety-critical role shall include documented verification of credentials and a gap assessment against the ACE role profile.

Induction proceeds in stages: corporate ONE introduction, function induction, location and emergency induction, task familiarisation and supervised work. An individual can move between stages only after the designated accountable person closes the relevant gate. Site induction for Pommerac A does not automatically authorise work at CPF or on the land leases.

blocks.t: People newly assigned to a work area shall complete location-specific induction before receiving unsupervised access to operational work.
Do not confuse a visitor induction or site access pass with permission to operate equipment.

Transfers between Offshore Operations, Land Operations and the CPF create new task and site differences even when a role title is unchanged. Prior evidence is mapped unit-by-unit. Temporary cover, acting appointments and leave relief use written scope and duration, including supervision and any restricted duties.
An acting appointment in a safety-critical role shall be authorised by the receiving line manager only after required competence and local command arrangements have been confirmed.

Annual function training plans are compiled from competence gaps, critical-task forecasts, new equipment, audit findings, incident learning, planned turnarounds and upcoming campaigns. The Line Manager funds and schedules the plan; HR consolidates and challenges priorities. Wells campaigns and offshore rotations need forward planning so critical positions are covered before mobilisation.
Each functional manager shall approve an annual training plan that prioritises outstanding safety-critical competence gaps and links every course or supervised task to a role unit.

Delivery may comprise instructor-led learning, mentored work, equipment simulations, scenario drills, procedure briefings, manufacturer training and external certification. Provider selection is proportional to the risk and skill being taught. The training record identifies the provider, learning objectives, evidence of completion and applicability to the ACE task.

The assessor uses an approved task-unit checklist to select a representative task or scenario, review baseline evidence, observe critical decisions, test response to abnormal conditions and record the result. Safety-critical outcomes are verified by performance, not by a signature collected after the fact.
Assessment decisions shall be supported by identifiable, contemporaneous evidence that can be traced to the profile version, assessor, work setting and acceptance criteria.

An assessor is technically competent in the task, trained in assessment methods and free from material conflict. For critical work, the independent verifier may be another suitably qualified employee or Technical Authority representative outside the direct task performance line. A line manager can authorise release but cannot replace an independent verification when the profile requires it.
A safety-critical competence assessment requiring independent verification shall not be accepted until that verifier records a distinct judgement.

blocks.t: The line manager issues the authorisation, with task-code, plant/site scope, conditions, verifier and expiry. The role register and competence register are linked; the employee does not self-authorise.
The relevant line manager shall issue, vary, suspend and close authorisation in the competence register and communicate restrictions to the work planner and Area Authority.
A complete assessment file shall include task criteria, evidence, assessor and verifier identities, result, gap closure, manager decision and expiry or review date.

An employee may request a technical reassessment. The Learning & Competence Manager appoints a different assessor and involves the Technical Authority where technical interpretation is disputed. The individual remains under the existing work restriction pending the outcome.

Periodic re-verification is based on role risk and exposure. Safety-critical task units require documented review at intervals recorded in the competence profile; re-verification can include observation, scenario assessment and review of performance evidence. The schedule below sets programme maximums; a Technical Authority can require a shorter period for a particular task.

Safety-critical competence shall be re-verified no later than the applicable profile date and after any defined event-triggered reassessment.

The register notifies line managers of upcoming expiry at 90, 60 and 30 days. Any lapse changes the authorisation status to expired; work planning must not silently assume continuation. In exceptional cases the function may nominate a supervised temporary arrangement, but it does not convert expired evidence into current competence.
Where competence has expired or been suspended, independent task execution shall cease until reassessment and recorded release are complete.

Field verifications, incident investigations, drill observations, permit audits and supervisor checks provide continuing evidence. Patterns in deficiencies are evaluated as a possible failure of role profile design, training effectiveness, assessment integrity or supervision, not only as an individual training gap.

The contract owner defines contractor competence expectations in the scope of work and obtains verifiable evidence before mobilisation. Contractors engaged in safety-critical tasks shall be checked against ACE-approved role or task criteria before mobilisation or permit-role appointment.

A contractor competence deficiency affecting a major-accident barrier shall be escalated to the Area Authority and task execution suspended pending a documented safe alternative.

Field performance, assessment rework, incidents, expired training and failed verification inform contract performance reviews. The contract owner records feedback for the supplier and the competence profile owner; repeated failures trigger supplier qualification review.

The master register is controlled by Human Resources. It links the organisation person ID, role ID, task unit, competence profile revision, assessment evidence, assessor, authoriser, expiry, restrictions and records location. Work planners and Area Authorities receive a current authorisation view, not unrestricted access to private training or personal information.

docs.title: Assurance and Audit Standard
docs.author: Edward Low Chew — HSE Auditor
docs.approver: George Habib — VP HSE & Compliance (system owner); Nicole Lange — Head of Internal Audit & Risk Assurance (audit authority)
docs.custodian: Nicole Lange — Head of Internal Audit & Risk Assurance
docs.reviewers: Marissa Bobb — OMS Manager; Dillon Haddad — Compliance & Assurance Manager
docs.func: HSE & Compliance / Internal Audit & Risk Assurance
docs.applies: All ACE OMS elements, sites, assets, functions, controlled standards, key contractors and business processes
docs.subtitle: Risk-based, independent assurance of ONE controls, the ten OMS elements, corrective action and sustained operating effectiveness.

blocks.t: This standard sets one risk-based assurance method for assessing the design, implementation and effectiveness of ACE controls and the ten elements of ONE. It defines clear ownership of line checks, management-system conformance and independent internal audit; evidence quality and independence; annual planning; finding decisions; corrective action verification; and reporting to the Executive Leadership Team (ELT) and Board Audit Committee.

Assurance is not a search for a document that contains the right OMS tag. It must determine whether the requirement exists, is understood by the relevant duty holder, is implemented where the hazard arises and performs under credible operating demand. The audit record links each conclusion to identifiable evidence and accountable roles.
ACE shall operate a risk-based annual assurance plan approved by the Executive Leadership Team, with each of the ten OMS elements independently audited at least once in every three-year period.

sections.title: 1.2 Scope, exclusions and relationship to other systems

blocks.t: The programme applies to ACE-operated sites and functions, including Head Office, Point Lisas Shore Base, the Gulf of Paria assets, land leases and CPF; the relevant governance and support processes; critical contractors; and technical disciplines whose standards provide cross-functional assurance. Partner-controlled activities are included to the extent required by applicable interfaces and contractual rights.

This standard does not substitute for statutory inspection, engineering design approval, individual SCE proof testing, incident investigation or contractor supervision. Findings from these activities may be evidence to the assurance programme but require their own authorising processes. Corporate Internal Audit retains its independent reporting relationship and annual-plan ownership.

Governing: ACE-OMS-MAN-001 (Elements 9 and 10; Part D); ACE-DOC-STD-001; ACE-DOC-STD-002; ACE-RSK-STD-001; ACE-PSM-STD-001; ACE-AIM-STD-001; ACE-MOC-PRC-001; ACE-COW-STD-001; ACE-MNT-STD-001; ACE-INC-STD-001. Planned related: ACE-PRF-STD-001 KPI; ACE-PRF-STD-003 Management Review; ACE-OMS-STD-003 OMS Plan.

The VP HSE & Compliance remains the PRF system owner under the OMS Manual and approves controlled PRF standards. The Head of Internal Audit & Risk Assurance owns the independent assurance plan, independent audit methodology and reporting to the Board Audit Committee. Joint document approval records both authorities without allowing the operational system owner to change an independent audit conclusion.

The OMS Manager manages framework mapping and conformance assessments; the Compliance & Assurance Manager coordinates second-line programme delivery; the HSE Auditor performs assigned reviews; first-line operational managers remain responsible for their own control performance.

Nicole Lange, Head of Internal Audit & Risk Assurance, owns the independent assurance plan and safeguards the independence of audit scope, evidence, findings and reporting to the Board Audit Committee.
No audited function shall approve, suppress or unilaterally downgrade the independent assessment findings concerning its own controls.
Follow risk and material operational exposure before convenient document availability.
Use objective, traceable evidence with clear sampling boundaries and quality limitations.
Evaluate both design adequacy and operating effectiveness of preventive and mitigating controls.
Triangulate records, interviews and direct observation; do not treat policy existence as implementation.
Challenge cross-system interfaces such as PSM–AIM–MNT–COW and MOC–Document Control.
Protect confidential personal, commercial, privileged and security-sensitive evidence.
Report failure mechanisms, systemic weakness and practical corrective requirements without negotiating away facts.

Area Authorities, site supervisors, system owners and Technical Authorities verify daily conformance where work happens: permit checks, isolations, SCE status, maintenance task quality, contractor controls, shifts, barrier demands and change release. Routine evidence is generated by the operating process, not by a separate paperwork exercise.

First-line verification includes the controls that prevent work continuing when an unacceptable condition is found. It is especially important to distinguish successful task completion from the proof that an approved safety or integrity criterion was met.
Each Area Authority shall retain evidence of planned field verification, timely response to failed controls and escalation of material risk beyond local delegated authority.

The OMS Manager, Compliance & Assurance Manager and functional specialists perform systematic checks against approved standards, OMS expectations and risk controls. These reviews may sample documents, registers and implementation. They must distinguish a metadata fault, a procedural weakness and a field-control failure because the response, authority and residual risk differ.

Second-line work complements first-line checks, challenges cross-site consistency and maintains a view of conformance trends. It does not substitute for independent third-line assurance; a review team should avoid validating the effectiveness of corrective work it directly implemented.
Marissa Bobb, OMS Manager, owns framework and expectation mapping and the schedule for OMS conformance assessments; Dillon Haddad coordinates second-line delivery and action follow-up.

Internal Audit independently assesses governance, the sufficiency of key controls and the quality of evidence on which management relies. It reports through its authorised oversight arrangements to the Board Audit Committee and maintains an audit universe spanning all ten OMS elements and their significant interfaces.

The scope may test the adequacy of first- and second-line reviews rather than repeating their entire sample. In high-risk areas the audit may directly verify field evidence, including safeguards that are marked healthy in registers but have not been challenged under operating conditions.
The independent audit programme shall retain an auditable link between the three-year coverage map, annual approved plan, completed engagements, findings and reported exceptions.

sections.title: 3 Risk-based annual and three-year assurance plan
3.1 Audit universe and annual planning factors

blocks.t: Maintain a rolling audit universe covering ten OMS elements, defined systems within each element, major facilities and key process interfaces. Plan engagements using credible consequence, major accident hazard exposure, SCE or other barrier status, recent changes, event and repeat-finding history, legal duties, assurance age, contractor performance, control complexity and available independent evidence.

Risk-based selection changes audit depth and frequency, but not the minimum coverage. Independent assurance of all ten elements is mandatory within each three-year cycle. The Head of Internal Audit maintains a coverage forecast and explicitly identifies any planned exception, resource deficiency or pending scope limitation.
The annual assurance plan shall be risk-based, formally approved by the Executive Leadership Team and updated through recorded change control where material scope or timing changes arise.

rows: Risk matrix decisions to work authorisation; MOC to field control; process safety safeguards.
Technical Authority to SCE integrity; maintenance proof tests; controlled documents and role competence.
External interfaces, incident learning, action effectiveness and management review.

blocks.t: This is an illustrative rolling distribution for scheduling purposes; actual risk may require the same element to be sampled in more than one year. An element is counted as independently covered only when the audit scope tests material expectations and representative implementation, not when its name appears in a document audit.
Coverage control: number of OMS elements with completed qualifying independent audits within the rolling three-year window / 10, with aging and justified exceptions separately visible.

The annual plan records engagement title, asset/function, tested risks, elements/expectations, assurance line, responsible leader, expected evidence, timing, resources and recipient. An approved budget or workforce allocation does not by itself demonstrate competence or independence.

Changes arising from a serious incident, regulatory development, new CPF project, well intervention campaign, high-impact MOC or a deteriorating barrier may trigger re-prioritisation. The Head of Internal Audit proposes amendments with reasons, effect on the three-year coverage obligation and governance approval.
Plan changes shall preserve the earlier approved baseline, originating risk or trigger, decision authority, deferred coverage, revised completion date and communication to affected management.

sections.title: 3.4 Audit planning risk score and escalation

blocks.t: 1. Identify the business risk and approved criteria: specific ONE requirement/OMS expectation, law, technical performance standard, contract or defined control objective.
2. Define sites, period, systems, asset/equipment populations, contractor interfaces, evidence sources and known exclusions.
3. Declare and resolve competence, independence, conflict and resource concerns before sampling.
4. Agree site access, safety arrangements, auditee contacts, evidence-security rules and opening meeting.
5. Record sampling plan, tests, materiality basis, findings threshold and reporting route.
Auditors shall identify the explicit criteria and sample boundary against which each conclusion is reached, including any significant information gaps or restrictions on access.

Evidence comprises approved source documents, register records, system transaction history, interviews with accountable people, field observations, equipment condition, tests, independent measurements and third-party records where valid. Prefer a mix of methods: interviews alone show understanding, while records and physical tests show implementation and operating outcome.

Define the population and selection method. For example, testing permit controls requires a sample from the full issue register (including cancelled, extended and contractor permits), not only permits presented by a supervisor. Sample across high-risk shifts, remote platforms, urgent work and representative trades. For a safety-critical maintenance sample, trace each selected SCE from hazard analysis through performance standard and CMMS work order to as-found/as-left evidence.

blocks.t: The opening meeting confirms the objective, criteria and safety arrangements and provides a route for emerging critical risks. During fieldwork the audit team maintains a working-paper index, documents facts before conclusions, re-tests inconsistent data and gives management a fair opportunity to clarify factual errors.

Where a hazardous uncontrolled condition is discovered, the auditor immediately tells the Area Authority. The auditor does not personally authorise a plant change or override an operating decision; the relevant duty holder manages the risk and records the disposition. Audit findings must still report the issue independently.
Evidence access must not interfere with isolation boundaries, control-room duties, live emergency response or legally restricted records.

sections.title: 4.4 Exit meeting, factual review and report issuance

blocks.t: At the exit meeting the leader explains objective findings and evidence limitations. Management may provide missing records or challenge incorrect facts; the audit leader distinguishes a factual correction from a disagreement over risk grading. The signed final report states decisions on disputed evidence and any unresolved management response.

The report is issued under the independent audit function’s authority. Findings are added to the corporate action tracker and the audit universe receives a completed-coverage record once qualifying work has been finalised.
The independent audit leader and Head of Internal Audit & Risk Assurance shall retain authority over final findings and scope limitations; management agreement is not a precondition for reporting.

sections.title: 5.1 Linking IOGP expectations to ONE controls

blocks.t: The OMS wheel provides an authoritative taxonomy for navigation: the ten elements and numbered expectations from the ACE expectation register. Under ACE-DOC-STD-002, each document title and section may carry a comma-separated list of expectation numbers, most relevant first, held in editable OMS-tag controls. These tags support a search and planning index, not a finding by themselves.

A conformance assessment starts with the expectation and its intended control outcome, identifies accountable owners and supporting standards, then samples implementation at one or more relevant operating sites. Auditors record whether the requirement is designed adequately, actually deployed and demonstrably effective; they explain gaps, compensating controls and residual exposure.
A conformance conclusion shall not be based solely on the existence of an OMS tag, a published document, a training attendance record or a self-reported checklist.

sections.title: 5.2 Evidence thread from requirement to effective control

blocks.t: These are programme reporting categories, not IOGP certification labels. Rating decisions include scope, sampling limitations, risk implications, and differences between sites. Inability to show records does not automatically prove that no work occurred, but it fails the documented-control criterion where records are mandatory.

For each expectation assessed, retain document number/revision/heading reference, relevant tagged content, functional owner, site/sample, evidence IDs, design and effectiveness conclusion, rating rationale and follow-up reference.

The highest-value ONE tests follow a hazard and its safeguards across several systems: HAZOP/LOPA or bow-tie to SCE register and technical performance standard; maintenance/inspection strategy to work orders and deferrals; permits, isolations and operating limits to field execution; MOC to updated documents, competence and pre-start-up checks; incident to corrective action and reverified barrier.

A sample must include both the nominal normal path and meaningful exceptions such as overdue proof tests, temporary bypasses, unclosed MOCs, incomplete contractor checks or rejected document-gateway entries. A fully green dashboard without sampled exceptions is weak assurance.

The audit leader must understand the relevant management systems, risk controls, evidence practices, interviewing, report writing and graded findings. Specialist team members may provide process safety, integrity, functional safety, well, marine, environmental or information management knowledge. A qualified auditor without domain competence should not independently conclude that a complex SCE test is technically adequate.

The Head of Internal Audit maintains a competence and development record covering training, supervised audits, technical exposure, continuing learning and performance feedback. External providers are evaluated for conflicts and scope qualification.
Audit-team appointments shall identify the competence needed by the risk under review, the named leader and any technical specialist whose evidence or endorsement is required.

blocks.t: An auditor shall disclose any conflict of interest before commencing work, and the Head of Internal Audit shall approve the mitigation or reassignment.

Maintain respectful, accurate and confidential conduct. Ask factual questions rather than manufacturing agreement. Record quotations accurately, avoid broad conclusions from limited samples and permit management to correct objective factual errors. Maintain the evidence file with limited rights and preservation requirements.

Auditors should state a conclusion as a conclusion, not as proof of causal certainty beyond the tests performed. A control failure can be well-evidenced without full certainty about why it arose. Further investigation or technical review can be an appropriate action when a causal explanation remains unresolved.

Working papers shall preserve engagement identity, evidence source, sample method, notes, reviewer, finding, management response, conclusion and report version under the approved audit retention schedule.

Each finding states criterion, observed condition, source evidence, cause where supported, current or credible consequence, weakness of control, and a corrective requirement proportionate to risk. Audit recommendations should identify the control outcome and its necessary verification, while allowing the accountable business owner to design the technically appropriate solution.

Where a finding involves serious safety or regulatory exposure, record its immediate protective escalation separately from the published report. Do not delay action because wording is under discussion.
Every finding shall cite an identifiable approved requirement or control objective and objectively verifiable evidence, together with the significance and recommended corrective outcome.

blocks.t: Grades require traceable risk rationale and are not identical to the ACE Risk Matrix score; however, the matrix informs consequence and escalation. An isolated missing tag may be a publishing-gateway failure; repeated untagged safety requirements that render control inaccessible can indicate a systemic management-control weakness.

A final report shall record purpose, scope and criteria; sites/period; audited owners; audit team and independence declaration; approach and sample; evidence and limitations; findings with grading; immediate escalation; agreed actions and dissent; overall conclusion; distribution and report approval.

Internal Audit reports material issues to the responsible executive, CEO and Board Audit Committee under the approved governance route. The OMS Manager receives appropriate findings for the improvement programme and quarterly performance pack. Operational recipients are restricted to the data needed to manage the control; personal, commercial or sensitive details are safeguarded.

sections.title: 7.4 Factual disagreement, dissent and scope limits

blocks.t: The audit leader logs a contested finding, reviews new factual evidence and documents a reasoned disposition. Where management remains in disagreement, the final report includes the concern and audit response without treating disagreement as proof the issue is resolved. Scope limitation is an explicit finding about the reliability of the conclusion, not a reason to mark the process “green”.
Serious unresolved interference, denial of records or obstruction is reported to the Head of Internal Audit and the Board Audit Committee as appropriate.
An audit report shall not be represented as complete for a material control area when critical evidence or site access was denied without a documented scope limitation and escalation.

sections.title: 8.1 Action ownership and single corporate register

blocks.t: Findings become action records in the common corporate tracking system. One finding may need multiple deliverables across Operations, Engineering, HSE and Document Control; each deliverable has a named owner, due date, linked risk disposition, required Technical Authority review and measurable evidence. The finding remains open until all critical outcomes and effectiveness checks are satisfied.

Action owners are responsible for implementation, while audit or assurance personnel determine verification scope appropriate to significance. Repeat or overdue issues are visible to the element owner and in the performance review rather than hidden by closing the report.
Actions from audits, investigations and management reviews shall be tracked in one action system with named owners, approved dates, risk-based priorities and objective closure evidence.

rows: Finding and control objective accepted for tracking; owner and due date assigned.
Technical approach, risk, milestones, evidence and resource needs agreed.
Deliverables completed with traceable controlled records; not equivalent to verified effective.
Independent verifier tests the relevant operating exposure or sample.
Evidence reviewed; control behaves as intended; audit conclusion updated with trace.
Failed verification or past due; escalation, risk disposition and revised plan preserved.

blocks.t: An action owner shall not approve an extension that accepts additional risk outside their delegated authority or self-certify effectiveness of their own significant corrective action.

Verification is chosen to test the original failure mechanism: witness a permit or isolation at worksite; sample complete SCE proof-test results; trace a revised MOC through field handover; or review whether an overdue task trend has measurably improved. A training attendance list or revised document proves implementation only where it does not establish behaviour or performance.

Record whether the test was representative, the operating exposure since implementation, known limitations, and any new weakness requiring further action. For major findings, revisit risk rating and barrier effectiveness with a relevant Technical Authority or HSE lead.
Significant action closure shall be independently verified and the verification evidence retained with the originating finding and approved source revision.

Critical and major findings receive risk-appropriate visibility immediately and in the next regular assurance pack. Overdue action age, accepted extensions, repeat exposure and root-cause recurrence are tracked. If the same underlying control fails despite prior closure, reopen the previous effectiveness conclusion and reassess assumptions or incentives rather than issuing another identical action.
Lessons learned are fed into the annual OMS improvement plan, revised source documents through ACE document control and, where needed, new functional or cross-site audit coverage.

rows: Completed approved engagements / engagements due; manual target 90%, with scope exceptions reported.

Recurrence by underlying control failure and site, not merely a reissued finding count.
Number and age by significance, interim safeguards and approval of risk disposition.
Frequency of invalid tags, unstyled mandatory text, missing bookmarks or approval records.
Internal file review: criteria clarity, sample basis, evidence sufficiency and defensible rating.

blocks.t: The OMS Manual sets a 90% assurance-plan completion target. Management must also see deferred high-risk coverage and quality of findings; meeting a numeric completion measure does not override missing three-year element coverage.

Quarterly OMS reports consolidate independent coverage, plan completion, findings by severity and element, significant action age, thematic weaknesses, barrier and SCE assurance status, incident recurrence, document-control gateway performance and resourcing concerns. The OMS Manager prepares the management-system pack; the Head of Internal Audit reports independent matters through the audit governance channel.

Where assurance indicates the formal source requirement itself is inadequate, initiate an owner-led revision under ONE document control rather than relying on a memo or dashboard annotation. Retain prior findings and record which approved revision remedied the failure.

sections.title: 9.3 Annual trend and management review interface

blocks.t: Each element owner produces an annual trend assessment combining performance, incidents, audits, weak controls, new risks, stakeholder feedback and prior management review actions. The annual CEO-led management review uses this evidence to set OMS improvement priorities, allocate resources and assess maturity.

The Head of Internal Audit assesses the reliability of management assurance and reports persistent systemic weaknesses directly to the authorised oversight body. Next year’s planning uses verified evidence of risk reduction rather than counts of actions closed.
An annual analysis of trends across incidents, audits and KPIs shall be completed for each OMS element and material weaknesses assigned to an improvement action.

The master Standard is maintained in Word under the controlled repository and published through ONE with numbered headings, persistent bookmarks and OMS-tag controls. It is reviewed at least every three years, and earlier after significant audit/incident learning, governance change or revisions to the Manual. Audit records are stored in approved repositories, with ten years as the minimum retention for audit reports and management reviews.
Audit reports and management review records shall be retained for at least ten years, subject to any longer legal or contractual requirement and hold.

docs.title: Process Safety and Hazard Study Standard
docs.author: Stephanie Boissiere — Process Safety Engineer
docs.reviewers: Michelle de Verteuil — Process Engineering Lead; Rohan Ali — Plant Manager - Central Processing Facility; Akilah Noel — Fire & Gas and Safety Systems Lead
docs.endorser: Damian Daniel — Process Safety Lead (Technical Authority)
docs.applies: All ACE functions, assets, sites, projects, staff and relevant contractors
docs.subtitle: Major accident hazards, HAZID, HAZOP, LOPA, bow-tie, study governance, barriers and technical close-out.

blocks.t: This standard governs the identification, systematic analysis, independent challenge and control of major process hazards at ACE. It establishes the requirements for HAZID, HAZOP, Layer of Protection Analysis (LOPA), Safety Integrity Level (SIL) determination, bow-tie analysis and the use of results in engineering design, operations and asset integrity.

A hazard study is successful only when the credible scenarios are understood, actions are traceable, barriers are assigned and fit for duty, and required changes are incorporated into the approved plant, procedures and competence system. A completed workshop report is not proof of risk reduction.

ACE projects, assets, changes and operations with credible major accident hazards shall be assessed through the methods and lifecycle gates defined in this standard and linked to the ACE Risk Management Standard.

The requirements cover the Pommerac A manned production platform, Chenet B and Sapodilla C normally unmanned wellhead platforms, the offshore export pipelines, Tamarind, Pawpaw and Soursop field installations, the Central Processing Facility (CPF), crude storage and loading facilities, and the relevant project, marine, contractor and well-service interfaces.

Hazard studies consider hydrocarbon loss of containment, fire, explosion, toxic or oxygen-deficient atmospheres, pressure excursions, structural and marine events, mechanical failure, environmental releases, emergency response limitations and loss of utilities or protective systems. Well-specific subsurface barriers are managed with the Well Integrity Management Standard; shared interfaces remain in scope.
VP HSE & Compliance: Accountable for this standard and for assurance that major accident risks are systematically identified, reduced and reported.

Process Safety Lead (Technical Authority): Endorses study selection and technical method; approves facilitator competence; challenges safeguard credit and SIL recommendations; approves technical close-out evidence.
Area Authority: Owns the operating risk at the site, verifies the installed barrier condition, and coordinates operational actions and pre-startup readiness.
Project / MOC owner: Initiates the right studies at the right project stage, supplies a controlled design basis and closes findings before the defined decision gate.
Discipline Technical Authorities: Accept the performance and design basis of barriers within their disciplines and record any unresolved technical limitations.
Use the ONE Risk Matrix for qualitative categorisation and company-level risk acceptance; supplementary quantitative analysis supports, rather than silently replaces, these controls.
Treat major accident hazard analyses as multi-disciplinary studies. Record scenarios, assumptions, safeguards and disagreements explicitly.
Separate the initiating event, top event, consequence and protective function so a credited barrier cannot be double-counted.
Carry study actions and safety-critical element performance requirements forward into MOC, commissioning, maintenance, inspection, training and operational procedures.
Where the study is conducted for a partner or contractor interface, identify ACE’s boundaries and the bridging standard applied.

A major accident hazard (MAH) is a potential event with the capacity to cause multiple fatalities, substantial loss of containment, significant environmental harm or major damage to facilities. ACE identifies such scenarios from facility inventories, process conditions, energy sources, location and population exposure, historical incidents, technical studies and relevant industry lessons.

The assessment examines escalation paths as well as initial events. For example, a CPF overpressure incident may start with a control failure, proceed to containment rupture, generate a flammable cloud and threaten multiple processing trains or the jetty. Loss of platform utility services can disable protection functions while an upstream event continues.

rows: Hazard ID, installation, top event, escalation pathway and consequence groups
Latest HAZID/HAZOP, bow-tie, LOPA where required, assumptions and revision
Barrier IDs, safeguarding functions and performance standards
SCE register, maintenance tasks, inspection, proof testing and impairment status
Current/residual risk, actions, risk acceptance and exposure restrictions

blocks.t: The MAH register shall preserve scenario IDs across revisions and link to the controlled study, risk register, safety-critical element register and action records.

At Pommerac A, critical scenarios include hydrocarbon release with ignition in a manned environment, emergency shutdown failure, collision or marine impact and evacuation impediments. Chenet B and Sapodilla C require scrutiny of remote isolation, wellhead pressure containment and delayed access. At land leases, unattended releases, ignition sources, public interface and flowline integrity are material. At the CPF, gas compression, tank farm inventories, gas conditioning, loading operations, process isolation and emergency response resources are central.

Threat frequency and the adequacy of independent safeguards are facility-specific. A generic bow-tie copied from one asset cannot be deemed complete for another without site-specific verification and documented endorsement.

sections.title: 2.4 Relationship to operating envelopes and barriers

blocks.t: The study identifies key operating parameters and failure paths. Operations translates validated limits into the approved operating envelope; Engineering assigns design limits and protection requirements; Asset Integrity manages safety-critical performance standards and maintenance. Instrumented protective functions subject to SIL requirements follow the functional safety lifecycle, including proof-test and modification control.
A credited barrier that is unavailable, inhibited, overdue for required testing or outside its performance standard invalidates the previous risk conclusion until its impact has been assessed.

Principal hazards and fatal flaws visible before option selection.

Recommendations incorporated or justified for design freeze.

sections.title: 3.2 Hazard study schedule and critical triggers

blocks.t: Each asset maintains a study schedule showing due dates, risk priority, responsible owner, study method, previous study date, expected design inputs and action status. For a material change to the process, equipment configuration, operating envelope, chemicals, control logic, staffing or emergency capability, the MOC screen determines whether part or all of a hazard study must be repeated.

ACE establishes a maximum HAZOP revalidation interval of five years for operating process facilities; earlier review is required following material changes, a major incident, new evidence of failed barrier assumptions or a significant period of deferred actions. A five-year calendar interval is not authority to defer a known material change until the next cycle.
Each operating asset shall have a controlled five-year maximum HAZOP revalidation programme, with documented triggers for earlier revalidation and ownership of overdue study actions.
Approved process descriptions, material and energy balances, inventories, PFDs and marked-up P&IDs at the correct revision.
Design and operating pressures, temperatures, relief basis, trip settings, alarm philosophy, hazardous area classification and equipment data.
Equipment layout, occupancy and escape routes, fire and gas coverage, utilities and ESD cause-and-effect information.
Previous studies, incident and failure history, operating lessons, maintenance and inspection anomalies, temporary deviations and barrier impairments.
Project scope, contractor interfaces, site constraints, HAZOP assumptions and unresolved technical queries.
The Process Safety Lead may postpone or limit the study when critical technical information is absent or uncontrolled; deficiencies and the resulting release restrictions are recorded.

HAZID is a structured, multi-disciplinary exploration of major hazards and interfaces when the design or activity is not yet mature enough for node-by-node process deviation analysis, or when facility-wide events need wider consideration. It covers operations, logistics, human interaction, environment, security and emergency response and develops the basis for more detailed studies.

The leader establishes a defined boundary and separates external initiating threats from system vulnerabilities. A Shore Base marine transport HAZID includes quay, lift, deck, voyage, offshore transfer and emergency response interfaces; a CPF HAZID includes upstream supply, compression, tank farm, loading and nearby work activities.
1. Agree scope, asset boundary, operating states and technical inputs; allocate a unique study and scenario register identifier.

2. Select guide categories: hydrocarbons, loss of containment, pressure, ignition, mechanical, marine, weather, environment, simultaneous operations, utilities, human factors, security and emergency response.
3. Define each credible threat and top event; capture consequences to people, environment, asset and reputation.
4. Record actual safeguards, uncertainty, gaps and risk ranking using ACE-RSK-STD-001; distinguish proposal from existing control.
5. Identify mandatory deeper analyses: process HAZOP, LOPA, consequence modelling, bow-tie, marine assessment, escape/evacuation review or specialist studies.
6. Assign actions and accountable owners; review the complete scenario set with the asset/project owner and Process Safety Lead.

rows: Unique ID, facility, study date, assumptions and asset boundaries
Physical or organisational cause; failure mode
Loss-of-control event and credible impact for each domain
Identified barriers, evidence and named owner
Consequence, likelihood and ACE matrix rating, with rationale
Actionable, measurable outcome, accountable owner and due date
Technical response, close-out evidence and residual decision

blocks.t: Inherently safer alternatives identified by HAZID are evaluated before major design commitments. Recommendations such as inventory reduction, safer layout, remote isolation or segregation of ignition sources are not automatically deferred as “operational improvements” if design can eliminate the underlying hazard. The design decision includes cost, feasibility, residual exposure and Technical Authority endorsement.

HAZOP examines deviations from the intended process behaviour using a disciplined guide-word and parameter approach. The facilitator divides the process into nodes with defined boundaries and design intent, documents normal/abnormal states and examines deviations that could create a hazard or cause loss of operation.

Node drawings must be legible and at an approved or formally controlled mark-up revision. Where an open project query could change the process, the HAZOP records the assumption and routes a hold point for resolution before design freeze or commissioning.

The core team ordinarily includes an independent or suitably separate facilitator, trained scribe, Process Engineer, Operations representative, Instrumentation/Controls Engineer, Mechanical/Integrity representative and appropriate Technical Authorities. Project, Maintenance, Wells, HSE, Human Factors and contractor expertise are added for affected nodes. The Area Authority provides operational challenge even when site staff cannot attend every session.

The facilitator establishes meeting rules: examine one deviation at a time, avoid crediting unsupported safeguards, record minority technical objections, distinguish design actions from operating recommendations, and agree exact wording of each study record before moving to the next node.

sections.title: 5.3 Guide words, deviations and causal analysis

rows: No flow to gas compression stage
Higher pressure from blocked downstream path
Delayed ESD actuation on gas detection

blocks.t: For each credible deviation, identify independent causes, a reasonably foreseeable top event and consequences before listing safeguards. Record preventative safeguards and mitigative measures separately. An alarm credited as a barrier needs a defined detection element, alarm management, human availability, response time, competence and an effective action; a generic phrase such as “operator awareness” does not establish a barrier.

The team evaluates the risk using the ACE matrix and recommends additional controls proportionate to the outcome. When specialist quantified analysis is required, the HAZOP record identifies the corresponding LOPA or SIL action and the assumptions to be transferred. Design safety actions have a release gate, not only a due date.
HAZOP records shall identify node, design intent, guide word, parameter, credible cause, consequence, existing safeguards, risk rating, recommendation, owner and final close-out evidence.

The five-year maximum revalidation includes review of as-built drawings, actual alarm/trip settings, changed operating conditions, incident reports, maintenance deferrals, temporary bypasses, modification history and outstanding study recommendations. The team does not merely reread the prior worksheet: it checks whether previous assumptions remain valid at the facility.

Where the facility has operated outside the earlier study boundary, the review identifies missing nodes and deviations and initiates additional study. The Process Safety Lead may require partial revalidation sooner based on trend evidence.

sections.title: 6 LOPA, independent protection layers and SIL determination

blocks.t: LOPA is a semi-quantitative method to test whether the combined frequency of a defined scenario and the credited independent protection layers meets the approved tolerability basis. It is applied where high-consequence HAZOP scenarios demand a defensible risk reduction claim, where design choices depend on safeguard integrity, or where SIL determination is required for a safety instrumented function.

LOPA is not a substitute for identifying the hazard. The initiating event, consequence boundary and safeguard list must first be established in a sound HAZOP or equivalent process study. The calculation records all assumptions, units and dependencies, and the output is interpreted alongside the ACE matrix acceptance requirements.
Independence: the protection function is not vulnerable to the same initiating event, common utility loss or shared component failure that defeats another credited layer.
Specificity: it prevents the defined event or mitigates the stated consequence, within the required time window.
Auditability: it has an assigned owner, functional basis and evidence of proof testing, inspection or performance verification.
Reliability: the claimed probability of failure on demand is supported by design, operating data or valid standard methodology.
Availability: the layer is not currently bypassed, inhibited or in a known degraded condition.
Human response: an operator response is credited only when detection, alarm, diagnosis and action time are demonstrably adequate.

sections.title: 6.3 Calculation requirements and safeguards against double counting

blocks.t: For a simple independent-layer model, scenario frequency is calculated from initiating-event frequency adjusted for enabling conditions and conditional modifiers and multiplied by the probability of failure on demand for each genuinely independent protection layer. The team records the source of every numerical value, the operating exposure and the scenario scope; values are not adopted merely because they appear in an example worksheet.

A BPCS control loop that fails as the initiating cause cannot also receive independent protection credit in the same scenario. Two shutdowns sharing the same sensor, logic solver, power supply or final element are not automatically independent. Common-cause vulnerabilities and maintenance or testing outages may eliminate intended numerical reductions.

Never count the same physical function twice under different names such as “high-pressure trip”, “ESD logic” and “instrumented shutdown”. Independence must be demonstrated for the defined initiating event.

sections.title: 6.4 SIL determination and functional safety lifecycle

blocks.t: Where the analysis demonstrates a need for a safety instrumented function, the team documents the hazardous scenario, safe state, initiating event, required response time, target risk reduction and the derived SIL requirement. The SIL target is then carried into a Safety Requirements Specification and the IEC 61511 functional safety lifecycle, including architecture, verification, factory/site acceptance, validation, proof testing, operation and modification.

This standard governs the process-hazard justification of the requirement. It does not replace the detailed SIS specification, hardware/software verification or performance testing required under ACE-ENG-SPC-410 and the relevant functional safety standards.

The Process Safety Lead and Instrumentation & Control Technical Authority shall endorse SIL determinations before release of the Safety Requirements Specification or changes to safety-critical trip functions.

Review LOPA when initiating event frequency, occupancy, demand rate, trip setpoint, bypass arrangements, proof-test interval or barrier architecture changes materially. Findings from proof-test failures, spurious trips and functional safety assessments must inform the credited performance assumptions. Significant revisions are controlled under MOC, with the impact on associated bow-ties, risk acceptance and operating procedures checked.

A bow-tie visually links hazardous threats to a single top event, then to credible consequences. Prevention barriers sit between threats and the top event; mitigation barriers sit between the top event and each consequence. Escalation factors are the conditions that can weaken a barrier, with controls specifically intended to prevent those weaknesses.
The diagram is a communication and assurance tool, not a replacement for HAZOP worksheets or LOPA calculations. The source analysis and assumptions remain traceable through reference IDs.

Rated duty, design basis, verification and maintenance.

blocks.t: A barrier is assigned a unique barrier ID and owner, with reference to the corresponding Safety-Critical Element where relevant. Each such element has a performance standard capturing functionality, reliability, survivability, dependencies, inspection/test requirements and failure response. Links extend to maintenance plans and work orders, inspection findings, test results, impairments and deviations.

For Pommerac A, ESD valve close-on-demand performance may support several threats in the hydrocarbon release bow-tie. The element is managed once in the register but each scenario retains the intended barrier function and technical assumptions. A failed valve test therefore triggers review of every dependent scenario.

Barrier health is reported from objective data: required maintenance and proof-test compliance, known defects, overrides and inhibits, overdue repairs and verification findings. Barriers may be classified healthy, degraded, unavailable or unverified against the agreed performance standard. A status of unknown is not counted as healthy.

The Area Authority establishes operating restrictions in response to significant impairment; the Technical Authority assesses engineering adequacy; the relevant VP accepts any elevated exposure under ACE-RSK-STD-001 and ACE-OMS-STD-002 where deviations apply.

Facilitators require a demonstrated ability to apply the specific method, lead multidisciplinary challenge, recognise major accident scenarios, manage technical disagreements and write auditable findings. Scribes must accurately record cause, consequence, safeguards, decisions and actions at the pace of a session without silently altering meaning. Competence may be established through suitable training, supervised studies and previous performance review.

An independent facilitator is preferred for major HAZOP/LOPA decisions and for studies with significant contractor, project or commercial pressure. Where the facilitator has design involvement, the Process Safety Lead evaluates the conflict and specifies a compensating independent review. A project manager does not assume technical facilitation solely because of seniority.

rows: Actual use, abnormal events, maintenance and shift interface
Design intent, flows, relief and process envelopes
Trips, alarms, logic and instrument architecture
Detection, deluge, evacuation and emergency consequence
Marine, wells, human factors, civil/structural and contractor risk

blocks.t: Facilitator confirms scope, node list or hazard category list, design maturity and approved input document revision.
Team receives the technical pack early enough for review; missing inputs and open design queries are tracked.
Study agenda has realistic node coverage and recording resources; fatigue and meeting duration are managed.
Independent technical challenge is explicitly included for high-consequence scenarios and layered safeguards.
The final report states participants, dates, method, exclusions, assumptions, studies to follow and release gates.

The facilitator records unresolved technical differences rather than averaging them away. The Process Safety Lead assigns a technical challenge and nominates the appropriate Technical Authority or study review panel. Where the disagreement affects the adequacy of a major accident barrier or a High/Very High risk, the decision remains open until an authorised technical conclusion and risk acceptance are recorded.
Commercial and schedule constraints are legitimate project inputs but are not substitutes for documenting the technical risk basis.

Recommendations describe the outcome needed to control a specific scenario, rather than a vague instruction such as “review the system”. They identify the study and node, the risk affected, action owner, supporting Technical Authority, required evidence and date. Where the recommended action is rejected, an approved alternative and its basis are documented with an equal or stronger risk control argument.

Actions to prevent a major accident are prioritised by the risk consequence, barrier importance and project gate. Some findings are mandatory for design freeze, pre-commissioning or safe startup regardless of their administrative target date.
1. Register each action under a permanent study/action identifier, link to the initiating scenario and nominate owner and required completion gate.
2. Action owner develops a response and evidence plan; the relevant Technical Authority confirms the proposed solution meets the technical safety intent.
3. Implement the action through controlled design, construction, operations or procedural work, following MOC and document control where applicable.
4. Provide evidence such as accepted calculation, updated P&ID, functional test, approved instruction, inspection record or verified training.
5. Process Safety Lead checks that the original scenario has been adequately addressed; the risk owner updates current/residual risk and affected barrier records.
6. Close with a dated decision, evidence index and any continuing restrictions; independent assurance samples high-criticality closures.

A plant or modified system is not released merely because the HAZOP report was issued. The Project/MOC owner reconciles study findings with as-built documents, cause-and-effect, safety instrument testing, pressure system verification, operational procedures, competence, spares and emergency plans. The Area Authority verifies plant and personnel readiness; Technical Authorities endorse critical technical items.

Open actions are classified as pre-startup critical or deferrable only on an accepted risk and technical basis. A temporary operating restriction has an owner, expiry and monitoring evidence; it is not a hidden open item.
No new or materially modified process shall enter operation with an unresolved major accident hazard study action that compromises required barriers or exceeds the authorised risk acceptance basis.

blocks.t: Early warning signs are changes in protective function, integrity or operating behaviour that may precede a process safety event. The asset process safety review seeks both visible events and failure of the underlying barrier system. Examples include repeated high-high alarms, isolation failures, temporary inhibits, unexpected hydrocarbon leaks, relief system demands, overdue safety-critical tests and recurring abnormal operating modes.

A weak signal is acted on according to its significance; it is not dismissed solely because it has not produced a recordable injury. The review considers whether multiple signals share a common cause, such as instrument supply quality, maintenance strategy or a control system change.

blocks.t: Asset leaders set justified thresholds and escalation rules consistent with the applicable equipment and hazard basis. A rising trend, repetitive near misses, multiple degraded barriers or a cluster of trips can trigger immediate technical review even when a formal corporate numerical threshold has not yet been exceeded. The Process Safety Lead documents the trigger, investigation, interim operating position and corrective-action effectiveness.

sections.title: 11 Study records, revalidation and management of change

blocks.t: Controlled records include study terms of reference, input register, attendance and competence evidence, approved worksheets, calculations, revised drawings, recommendations, challenge decisions, technical endorsement, approval and close-out evidence. Each report names the exact as-studied configuration and cites document revisions; a controlled revision is created for a subsequent revalidation rather than silently replacing the original.

The source Word files and related engineering records reside in the approved document repository. ONE may extract tagged sections and provide navigation to the relevant study and barrier records, but cannot replace the authoritative approved files or guarantee that a study was technically adequate merely because its metadata passed the publishing gateway.

When operations propose a change to equipment, process chemistry, control philosophy, trip logic, facility occupancy, maintenance basis or emergency response capability, the MOC reviewer checks whether the change invalidates the study assumptions. Depending on its magnitude, the action may require focused HAZOP nodes, LOPA recalculation, bow-tie update or an entirely new study. The technical response links the affected hazard and barrier IDs and identifies new required records.

Controlled PSM reports and technical standards shall meet ACE-DOC-STD-001 and ACE-DOC-STD-002 requirements, including revision history, owner, approval, stable section bookmarks and relevant OMS tags where the document is published through ONE.

Study packs shall be retained under the approved retention schedule for the life of the relevant asset and thereafter as required by the records owner, Legal and the retention schedule; legal holds override scheduled disposal.

sections.title: B.1 Miniature CPF compressor node example

blocks.t: Design intent: maintain compressor discharge pressure within approved operating envelope. Deviation: “More pressure” caused by downstream isolation while compression continues. Potential consequences include containment rupture and an ignitable gas release. Study safeguards may include high-pressure trip, pressure relief and operator alarms, but each is credited only after duty, independence, configuration and maintenance status are verified.

The action register may require checking relief discharge destination, shutdown response time, safe-state logic, alarm setpoints, spurious-trip history and proof-test evidence. A LOPA action is created if the team cannot substantiate that the credited independent protection reduces the scenario to the corporate tolerability criterion.

sections.title: C.1 Illustration only — not a pre-approved target

blocks.t: Assume for illustration a particular initiating event frequency of 1 × 10⁻¹ per year and two demonstrated independent protection layers with probability of failure on demand of 1 × 10⁻¹ and 1 × 10⁻². If the layers are genuinely independent and no further conditional factors apply, the estimated scenario frequency is 1 × 10⁻⁴ per year (0.1 × 0.1 × 0.01). These figures are instructional, not ACE design values or risk tolerance criteria.

Before any actual SIL or operating decision, the team must use the approved ACE risk criterion, validate all quantitative inputs, account for common-cause failure and test intervals, and obtain Process Safety and Instrumentation Technical Authority endorsement. Without these steps the arithmetic cannot substantiate acceptance.
Do not use this example as a safety instrumented function SIL determination or as acceptance of a real ACE scenario.

sections.title: D.2 Linking the example to ACE systems

blocks.t: The Process Safety Lead owns scenario method integrity, while the CPF Plant Manager owns live operating risk. The Instrumentation Technical Authority owns trip and detector performance criteria, the Mechanical Technical Authority owns pressure containment and relief criteria, and Maintenance & Integrity delivers planned tests and anomaly correction.
