docs.subtitle: How ACE assesses, accepts, changes and learns from operational risk, and prepares for and responds to emergencies.

blocks.t: This policy sets how ACE understands, accepts, changes and learns from operational risk, and how it prepares for and responds to emergencies. It brings together risk assessment, barriers, Management of Change, deviations, incident learning, emergency response, crisis management and business continuity under one set of commitments and decision rules.

It applies to all ACE sites (HOF, PLB, PAP, CHB, SAP, CPF and LND), all functions, all phases of the asset life, and to contractors working on ACE activities. Its parent is ACE-LDR-POL-001. The detailed rules are in the implementing standards listed in section 6.2; where this policy states a band or a number, it is the one set in those standards.
Each commitment names the ACE values it serves, as set in ACE-LDR-POL-001 section 1. The steps that deliver the commitments are in the governed processes and implementing documents in section 6.

In line with our values Safety above all and One team, one way, ACE assesses risk before it acts, using one ACE Risk Matrix for every kind of risk: people, environment, asset and production, and reputation (ACE-RSK-STD-001). A risk is accepted only by the person with the authority for its band, and only once it is as low as reasonably practicable.

sections.title: 2.2 Barriers are identified, owned and verified

blocks.t: In line with our value Safety above all, every significant risk has prevention and recovery barriers that are identified, have an owner and are tested to show they work. A barrier that has not been verified is not counted as available (ACE-RSK-PRA-001).

In line with our values Safety above all and One team, one way, no change to plant, process, people, procedures or organisation that could affect risk is made without Management of Change. Each change is classified by its most significant credible impact, assessed, approved at the right level, and verified before it is put into use (ACE-MOC-PRC-001).
A change to plant, process, people, procedures or organisation that could affect risk shall not be implemented until it has been approved under ACE-MOC-PRC-001.

In line with our values Integrity in everything and Safety above all, a departure from an ACE requirement is a temporary, controlled condition and never a quiet new normal. Every deviation has an expiry date, compensating measures and a named approver; at expiry without a replacement approval, the affected work stops or the equipment goes to its safe state (ACE-OMS-STD-002).

In line with our value Learn and improve, every incident, near miss and non-conformance is reported, investigated in proportion to its actual and potential consequence, and closed with actions whose effectiveness is verified. Lessons are shared across sites. Actions that change a process are handed to the improvement arrangements of ACE-OMS-POL-001 and recorded in the CI register with the source "incident and near-miss actions".

In line with our values Safety above all and Integrity in everything, weak signals are acted on before they become events: repeated alarms, overdue safety-critical work, growing action backlogs, repeated deviations and workarounds. A risk that moves to a higher band is escalated to the acceptance authority for the new band without waiting for the next scheduled review.

In line with our values Safety above all and Care for people and places, every site has a tested emergency response plan, ACE has an oil spill contingency plan for the Gulf of Paria and its land operations, and critical business functions have tested continuity arrangements. When an emergency happens we protect people first, then the environment, then the asset, and we keep communities, regulators, partners and customers informed (ACE-EMR-STD-001).

blocks.t: This Practice sets how ACE defines, identifies, links and monitors the controls that manage its risks. It makes the control the hinge of the OMS: the one item that connects a risk to the document that requires the control, the process step that performs it, the role that owns it, the equipment it depends on and the evidence that proves it works.

Parent: ACE-RSK-STD-001 Risk Management Standard, which sets the ACE Risk Matrix, risk acceptance and the Risk Register. This Practice applies to every significant risk at every ACE site (PAP, CHB, SAP, CPF, LND, PLB, HOF) and to every controlled document that establishes a control.

Recognised practice applied: ISO 31000 Risk management — Guidelines; IEC 31010 Risk assessment techniques (bow-tie analysis); IOGP Report 415 Asset integrity — the key to managing major incident risks; Energy Institute guidance on barrier management.

docs.title: Risk Management Standard
docs.author: Christina Bain — HSE Manager
docs.reviewers: Nicole Lange — Head of Internal Audit & Risk Assurance; Damian Daniel — Process Safety Lead; Teresa Daniel — Chief Financial Officer
docs.applies: All ACE functions, assets, sites, projects, staff and relevant contractors
docs.subtitle: The single ACE Risk Matrix, accountability, tolerability and barrier-based decision rules for operating and business risk.

blocks.t: This standard establishes the single approach ACE uses to identify, evaluate, reduce, accept, monitor and communicate risk. It provides the company Risk Matrix used by operations, wells, engineering, projects, contractors, corporate functions and assurance. Technical discipline standards may use specialist analyses, but their risk conclusions return to the common ACE risk categories and acceptance authorities.

A decision is complete only when its assumptions, barriers, residual exposure, owner, competent review and acceptance evidence can be reconstructed. A register entry or coloured matrix cell alone does not demonstrate that a risk has been controlled.

All ACE activities, MOCs, deviations, barrier impairments, major projects, task risk assessments and business risk reviews shall use the ACE Risk Matrix in this standard when a categorical risk rating is required.

This standard applies at Head Office, Point Lisas Shore Base, Pommerac A, Chenet B, Sapodilla C, the Gulf of Paria pipelines, Tamarind, Pawpaw and Soursop leases, and the Central Processing Facility (CPF). It also applies to services performed on ACE’s behalf where operational or enterprise risk is transferred through a contractor or partner interface.

The framework supports hazards to people, environment, assets and production, reputation, legal and regulatory duties, supply continuity, security and commercial performance. Separate statutory and technical obligations continue to apply even when the matrix indicates a Low rating.
VP HSE & Compliance: Owns the risk methodology, controlled matrix, overall performance expectations and management escalation to the Executive Leadership Team.
Area Authority: Owns safe operation of the location, verifies the real barriers present before work and may stop activities when exposure exceeds the authorised basis.
Technical Authority: Owns technical assumptions and acceptability of specialist barriers, engineering solutions and technical deviations.
Risk owner: Is a named ACE role with the authority and resources to act on the exposure; owns action completion and review of the residual risk.
A likelihood label describes the credible frequency of the defined hazardous event at ACE or a comparable operation; it is not a substitute for evidence of barrier performance.
Consequence is assessed separately for each domain; the most severe credible domain is used for the headline rating. Other domains remain recorded, not erased.
Current risk is assessed with verified controls that are in place; planned improvements do not lower the current rating until the controls have been installed and verified.
Residual risk is the estimated position after the proposed or verified additional actions. Current and residual values remain visible in the record.
Numerical risk methods, where used, must disclose assumptions, units, uncertainty, dependencies and the relationship with the categorical decision.

The assessment leader defines the decision being made, the plant or business activity, operating state, interfaces, affected people, hazards, time horizon and foreseeable abnormal conditions. Work at the CPF may involve compressor trips, gas release, fire, loading and simultaneous maintenance. Offshore work includes helicopter and marine transfer, platform isolation, confined spaces and pipeline interfaces. Land activities include road transport, unmanned sites and third-party access.

The boundary must not omit a contracted activity, shared utility or neighbouring site merely because it falls outside the reporting line of the nominated owner. The team records relevant drawings, operating limits, incident history and assumptions, including quality limitations in the data.
1. Identify the operational or business decision and the risk owner; define the asset, location, lifecycle phase and affected interfaces.
2. List hazards and credible initiating causes for normal, start-up, shutdown, maintenance, emergency and degraded conditions.
3. Identify consequences separately in People, Environment, Asset/Production and Reputation; record legal or stakeholder obligations.
4. List existing preventive and mitigative barriers; distinguish demonstrably effective controls from assumed or proposed controls.
5. Determine consequence and likelihood categories; read the rating directly from the controlled matrix in section 3.
6. Select additional controls; determine whether the remaining risk is tolerable and ALARP; assign an acceptance authority.
7. Record actions, owner, due date, interim arrangements, residual assessment and approval; communicate operational constraints.
8. Verify implementation and periodically reassess; reopen the analysis when conditions, assumptions or barrier health change.

Use a method suited to the decision: structured checklists for simple tasks, HAZID for broad interfaces, HAZOP for process deviations, bow-tie for major accident hazards and LOPA where independent protection layers need quantitative evaluation. The method selected is recorded and justified by the leader. A single checklist is not an acceptable substitute for a multi-discipline assessment of a credible major accident hazard.

Ask deliberately about interacting failures, loss of utilities, common-cause events, human performance, SIMOPS, weather, marine transfer, contractor handovers, maintenance deferrals, cyber or instrumentation failures and the possibility that a safeguard is unavailable during an abnormal state.
When a safety-critical element is bypassed, failed or overdue, assess the exposure on the impaired condition, not on the assumption that the element will perform to its nominal performance standard.

Acceptance records the decision, not an instruction to live indefinitely with a known deficiency. Each decision identifies the exposure period, scope, maximum operating conditions, temporary measures, action dates and the next review. Work supervisors brief the affected crew using task-specific controls and do not substitute a general risk acceptance for a permit to work, isolation or operating envelope requirement.
A revised assessment shall be completed before a material change in scope, operating conditions, barrier availability or risk consequence is implemented.

The approved assessment pack shall contain the defined scenario, version-controlled inputs, matrix selections, safeguards, current and residual ratings, ALARP justification, required approvals, implementation evidence and review history.

The ACE matrix has five consequence levels and five likelihood levels. It produces one of four qualitative ratings: Low, Medium, High or Very High. Matrix cells are categorical controls, not calculated risk scores; do not substitute likelihood × consequence arithmetic where it would produce a different band.

Consequences are assigned on the credible outcome before the likelihood dimension is applied. Consider reasonably foreseeable escalation and safeguards whose independence and availability have been established. Where one event produces several domain consequences, use the highest domain level for the headline cell and show each domain in the supporting analysis.
This is the controlling ACE matrix reproduced from Appendix 2 of ACE-OMS-MAN-001. Colours in a portal view are only a presentation layer; the cell label is authoritative.

rows: Expected — several times a year at ACE
Demonstrated recurring exposure; recent ACE events, operating history or credible repetitive conditions.
ACE experience supports recurrence under comparable conditions.
Possible — has happened in the industry
Relevant industry history establishes a credible event despite no known ACE example.
Unlikely — heard of in the industry
Known but uncommon industry experience, with suitable barriers in place.
Rare — not heard of in the industry
Very exceptional event for which the team has little comparable experience; not automatically impossible.
Small spill outside containment; cleaned within days
Spill reaching land or sea; short-term effect
Major spill; long-term effect in Gulf of Paria or on land

sections.title: 3.4 Rules for multi-domain and uncertain outcomes

blocks.t: A risk evaluation must identify the credible outcome, not the average expected loss. For example, a small compressor release may produce an equipment-only cost in one scenario and a potential fatality in a separate ignited scenario. These are distinct scenarios requiring separate likelihood selections. Do not hide the second scenario by merging it into the first.

Where a consequence straddles definitions, the assessment team documents its reasoning and uses the more conservative applicable category unless a more specific approved technical criterion governs. Quantitative analyses may refine likelihood but do not authorise unreviewed remapping of the matrix.

Any change to the category definitions, cell assignments or acceptance levels shall be managed as a controlled revision of this standard, approved by the VP HSE & Compliance after affected-system review.

sections.title: 4 Risk tolerance, ALARP and hierarchy of control

rows: Tolerable subject to controls being maintained
Local owner accepts and monitors; retain required statutory or company controls.
Manager verifies control adequacy, actions and review period.
VP acceptance needed, documented ALARP case, interim restrictions and dated reduction plan.
Not acceptable as ordinary ongoing operation
Stop or prevent exposure; CEO decision on exceptional recovery plan only after VP and TA review, not permission to bypass absolute requirements.

blocks.t: ALARP requires a reasoned review of reasonably practicable risk reduction, not merely a declaration that the matrix cell is acceptable. The team identifies further controls, estimates their effectiveness and implementability, records alternatives and shows why any rejected option would be grossly disproportionate to the benefit. There is no simple fixed ratio that automatically proves a rejected safeguard is unreasonable.

For major accident hazards, preference is given to inherently safer design, reliable prevention barriers, engineered detection and shutdown, emergency mitigation and verified emergency response capability. Administrative controls and personal protective equipment support, but are not equivalent to, engineered protection against catastrophic process outcomes.
High-risk acceptance shall include a written ALARP demonstration endorsed by the relevant Technical Authority and linked to the risk register and any required deviation.

sections.title: 4.3 Hierarchy of controls and interim arrangements

blocks.t: Eliminate the hazard or avoid the activity where feasible; substitute lower-hazard materials or methods where possible.
Use engineered isolation, containment, equipment design, interlocks and instrumented protection before relying on procedural measures.
Provide detection, emergency shutdown, relief, fire and gas protection, spill containment and response arrangements for credible escalation.
Use work planning, authorisations, supervision, competence, maintenance, inspection, operating limits and emergency drills as supporting controls.
Record barrier impairment, compensating measures, expiry date and restoration owner; do not count a proposed control as available until verified.

Risk reduction decisions may consider disruption to the Gas Buyer gas deliveries, loss of crude loading windows, contractual exposure, community relationships and asset life. Economic analysis informs options but cannot displace non-negotiable life-safety, environmental or legal duties. Financial values in the consequence table are in Trinidad and Tobago dollars and are used consistently across ACE functions.

rows: Task controls verified and recorded by the work supervisor.
Documented safeguards, control owner, action dates and permitted conditions.
Technical Authority endorsement where technical barriers affected; ALARP case and defined expiry or review.
Chief Executive Officer (L1), for managed exceptional recovery decisions
Normal activity prohibited; operations remain stopped unless reduction to an authorised level is verified and formally released.

blocks.t: The acceptance authority is the higher of the function accountable for the consequence and the location accountable for the exposure. Cross-functional High risks are escalated to affected VPs. A VP cannot delegate formal High acceptance to the work supervisor. The CEO is notified of every Very High exposure and significant impairment of a major accident barrier.

sections.title: 5.2 Risk acceptance and technical endorsement are distinct

blocks.t: The Technical Authority assesses whether the proposed technical condition is defensible against engineering standards and barrier performance requirements. The line or executive risk acceptor decides whether ACE can operate within the proposed conditions. An Area Authority remains responsible for the immediate field safety and may stop the job regardless of a previous corporate acceptance.

An exemption from a mandatory technical requirement is handled under ACE-OMS-STD-002. Risk acceptance is not an exemption; both controls are required where the proposed decision departs from an approved standard.

No manager may accept an unassessed or inadequately understood risk, authorise breach of law, waive a safety-critical performance standard without approved deviation, or use an expired acceptance record to continue work.

Work shall cease where a foreseeable fatality, major spill or loss of containment lacks the prescribed prevention or mitigation barrier, or where the assessed condition is outside the authorised acceptance envelope.

The supervisor makes the area safe, informs the Area Authority, contacts the Technical Authority where required, opens an impairment or incident record and requests reassessment before restart. The restart decision records actual conditions and any compensating measures; verbal reassurance is not evidence of barrier restoration.

blocks.t: Selection is based on complexity, hazard magnitude, novelty and available knowledge. Routine low-risk jobs use a trained supervisor-led task assessment. Unusual conditions, new equipment, failures of significant controls or concurrent operations trigger a team review. Major accident hazard work requires independent facilitation appropriate to the risk and linkage to ACE-PSM-STD-001.

The method record identifies facilitator, participants, source documents, version status, assumptions, outcomes and any unresolved points. For process modifications, study close-out is an input to MOC and pre-startup readiness; it is not a substitute for either.

Before a permit-controlled task, the performing team walks down the location to compare the proposed work against actual plant condition, isolation state, simultaneous activities, environmental conditions and nearby personnel. The briefing explains significant hazards, the control that prevents each credible outcome and what changes require the job to stop. A change in weather, line contents, test boundary or crew composition is a trigger to revisit the assessment.
A dynamic assessment can stop or adjust a job within an existing authorised method, but cannot bypass a formal MOC, approved isolation design or barrier impairment decision.

A barrier is a preventive or mitigative control with a defined safety function. Hardware, instruments, structural containment, trained operator action and emergency response may all serve barrier roles when their effectiveness is defensible. Barriers for major accident hazards are traced from the hazard study through the bow-tie to the Safety-Critical Element register and to the relevant functional performance standard.

Performance standards describe function, availability or reliability targets, survivability and dependencies, test and inspection requirements, failure response and the Technical Authority responsible. Maintenance and inspection requirements are derived from these standards, not selected solely from historic work orders.
Place the top event at loss of control (for example, loss of hydrocarbon containment) rather than at the final injury or environmental consequence.
Record independent initiating threats on the left and credible escalated consequences on the right.
Identify prevention barriers for each threat and mitigative barriers for each consequence, including common-cause vulnerabilities.
Nominate a barrier owner, performance evidence and impairment response. Avoid generic entries such as “training” without a defined competency or action.
Use audits, inspections, tests and events to update the barrier health record and revisit residual risk.

An impairment includes failure, bypass, inhibit, overdue mandated test, unresolved anomaly or unavailability of an element relied on by a major accident scenario. It triggers reassessment of the affected threats and consequences; this may move likelihood into a less favourable cell even if the original consequence remains unchanged. A controlled, time-limited deviation and approved temporary measures are required before continued exposure where permitted.

Engineering design changes, modifications to trip settings, performance standard changes, material substitutions and changes to prescribed inspection intervals are reviewed through MOC. Assurance that maintenance has been planned is not proof that the barrier meets its standard.

An administrative restriction cannot be assumed to fully replace a failed safety instrumented function; the Technical Authority must assess common-cause, human response time and the actual protected scenario.

ACE maintains local work and activity assessments, asset risk registers and an enterprise risk register. Site risks reside with the responsible Area Authority, system risks with the accountable owner and cross-business threats with the assigned Executive Leadership Team member. The enterprise register includes material exposures escalated from the assets, but its inclusion does not transfer operational ownership away from the site.

Each register entry has a stable risk identifier, sufficient scenario definition, current and residual ratings, barrier owner and action trail. Historical ratings are preserved so trends cannot be concealed by overwriting earlier assessments.

blocks.t: Register history shall preserve the approved risk statement, previous ratings, approval evidence, barrier changes, completed actions, review decision and any linked document revision.

An overdue action does not automatically mean the risk remains acceptable. The owner evaluates the effect of delay, verifies compensating controls, requests revised acceptance if the authorised basis changes and escalates to the approving authority. Closure requires objective evidence such as a test result, approved drawing, trained crew or formally commissioned safeguard; a completion assertion is insufficient.

The common matrix also applies to financial, supply, stakeholder and regulatory scenarios, provided the adverse event is defined and consequence categories are stated explicitly. Examples include interruption to the Gas Buyer gas sales, delayed crude liftings at the CPF jetty, loss of a critical marine supplier, contractor capacity gaps, cyber disruption to operations and community concerns near land leases.

A cross-functional assessment includes the commercial, legal, HSE, operational and technical representatives needed for the scenario. Business Development & Markets owns sales interfaces; Supply Chain owns materials and contracts; Legal & Government Affairs owns legal interpretation; Communications & Corporate Services coordinates external stakeholders. Each retains a linked risk entry where responsibilities overlap.

Joint venture agreements, contracted rigs and chartered marine services create interfaces between ACE acceptance authority and third-party systems. Bridging documents identify which party owns permits, control barriers, maintenance, incident response, emergency mobilisation and approval of changes. A contractor statement that its own risk is “accepted” does not discharge ACE of its duty to understand exposure at an ACE-operated site.

High and Very High risks involving partner activities, public exposure or off-site consequences shall be referred to the responsible ACE VP and to Legal & Government Affairs or Communications where the consequence domain requires it.

blocks.t: Asset and function reviews provide current exposures, movement in risk, weak barrier trends, action backlog and matters requiring executive decisions. The VP HSE & Compliance consolidates the quarterly significant-risk report. Internal Audit & Risk Assurance periodically checks completeness of registers, existence of approvals, treatment effectiveness and whether the rating is supported by actual operating evidence.

The management review considers new enterprise exposures, lessons from incidents and regulatory changes, system improvement proposals, and whether the corporate matrix and tolerability rules remain suitable. Findings are assigned to named roles with due dates and tracked through the assurance system.
High and Very High risk positions and material changes to barrier health shall be reported with current and residual ratings, risk owners, acceptance status, interim controls and overdue actions.

blocks.t: Describe the initiating event, the top event and credible outcome in plain language. For example, “loss of compressor seal containment during CPF operation leading to an ignited gas release and serious injury”, rather than the ambiguous label “compressor failure”. Identify the operating state and the safeguards being credited. If a scenario can produce both an injury and a major spill, assess both domains and retain the larger consequence in the headline selection.

sections.title: Appendix B — Worked ACE risk assessments

blocks.t: Scenario: a seal failure at the CPF gas compression train results in an ignitable gas cloud during operation. The team judges a credible outcome of one fatality (People level 4). Existing protective functions comprise isolation, gas detection, emergency shutdown, hazardous-area controls and emergency response, subject to verified performance. If the team can justify likelihood C (Possible), the matrix result is High (row C, consequence 4).

A degraded gas detector cannot be credited as fully available. The team rechecks likelihood on the impaired basis, considers reduced operating envelope or shutdown, and obtains VP acceptance for any authorised High exposure after Technical Authority endorsement. Replacement and functional test evidence, not delivery of the spare detector, closes the barrier-restoration action.

sections.title: B.2 Pommerac A ESD valve test deferral (example)

blocks.t: Scenario: a mandated ESD valve proof test is overdue on Pommerac A and the risk study relies on that valve to limit escalation after a process release. The overdue condition is an impairment. The Area Authority records the valve, protected scenarios, isolation capacity, additional controls and period of exposure. The Technical Authority checks whether a credible alternative barrier exists and whether the offshore operating envelope needs restriction.

If risk remains High, approval is a VP-level decision with a defined expiry; a maintenance work-order date alone does not justify continued operation. The record links to the SCE performance standard, deferral decision, risk register and valve test certificate after restoration.

Scenario: transfer of a load from the Point Lisas Shore Base to a supply vessel during deteriorating weather risks a dropped load and serious injury. The lifting supervisor defines crane capacity, load condition, deck movement, line of fire, exclusion zones and the weather stop criterion. A task risk assessment alone is insufficient if the vessel, lifting appliance or lift configuration introduces major new hazards; a lifting specialist review is then required.
The dynamic briefing confirms actual conditions. If wind or deck motion exceeds the approved lift plan, the lift stops even if the original matrix result was Medium.

sections.title: B.4 Gas sales continuity and storm exposure (example)

blocks.t: Scenario: tropical weather and marine access restrictions delay corrective maintenance on the Gulf pipelines, affecting Gas Buyer gas delivery and crude processing capacity. Operations, Supply Chain, Finance and Business Development assess duration, alternatives, contractual impacts and spill or loss-of-containment possibilities. Business interruption and process safety outcomes are recorded separately; the most severe applicable consequence domain determines each headline rating.

The action plan considers spare parts positioning, access windows, maintenance priority, customer communication and fallback operating arrangements. The relevant VPs jointly review material cross-functional exposures each quarter.

sections.title: Appendix D — Assessment quality and ALARP checklist

blocks.t: Scenario definition: Is cause–event–consequence separation clear, including abnormal and degraded conditions?
Inputs: Are drawings, asset condition, incident history and specialist analyses current and traceable?
Affected parties: Have contractors, shore/sea interfaces, neighbouring communities and concurrent tasks been addressed?
Barrier evidence: Is each credited barrier owned, available and tested or justified? Are dependencies understood?

ALARP: Are reasonable further measures compared and rejections justified, not merely asserted?

docs.author: Dillon Granger — Security Coordinator
docs.custodian: Jenelle Paul — Emergency Response & Security Manager
docs.reviewers: Marvin Williams — VP IT, Data & Knowledge; Kevin Mohammed — Telecoms & OT Cyber Security Lead; Imran Singh — IT Infrastructure & Operations Manager; Lisa Williams — Logistics & Materials Manager; Sophia Hosany — VP Operations
docs.applies: All ACE activities, sites, employees and contractors
docs.subtitle: How ACE protects its people, sites, control and safety systems, and information against deliberate harm, physical and cyber.

blocks.t: This policy sets ACE's commitments for protecting its people, sites, control and safety systems, and information against deliberate harm: theft, intrusion, sabotage and cyber attack. It covers physical security, information technology (IT) security and operational technology (OT) security, the control and safety systems that run the plant.

It applies to all ACE sites, with particular attention to the Point Lisas Shore Base (PLB) port facility and the offshore installations, to every ACE information and control system, and to every employee, contractor and visitor. Its parent is ACE-LDR-POL-001.
Each commitment names the ACE values it serves, as set in ACE-LDR-POL-001 section 1. The steps that deliver the commitments are in the governed processes and implementing documents in section 6.

sections.title: 2.1 Access by need and authorised role

blocks.t: In line with our values Safety above all and Integrity in everything, access to ACE sites, systems and information is given only to people who need it for an authorised role, only for as long as they need it, and is removed promptly when they no longer do.
Access to ACE sites, systems and information shall be granted only for an authorised role and shall be removed within one working day of the role ending.

sections.title: 2.2 Control and safety systems are protected

blocks.t: In line with our value Safety above all, every change to a control or safety system, including software, configuration and network connections, goes through Management of Change. There is no standing remote access to OT: each remote session is approved, time-limited and logged.
No change shall be made to a control or safety system, its software, its configuration or its network connections without an approved Management of Change.

In line with our values Integrity in everything and Learn and improve, every security incident or suspected incident, physical or cyber, is reported straight away and handled through the incident system (ACE-INC-STD-001). One that affects a control or safety system is also treated as a process safety matter.

sections.title: 2.4 Port and marine security at Point Lisas

blocks.t: In line with our values Safety above all and One team, one way, the Point Lisas Shore Base meets the port facility security requirements that apply to it: controlled entry for people, vehicles and cargo, screening, a security plan agreed with the port authorities, and coordination with vessels calling at the base.

sections.title: 2.5 Security risk is assessed and planned for

blocks.t: In line with our value Safety above all, ACE assesses security threats to each site and system every year using the ACE Risk Matrix, and its emergency plans cover security events and cyber attacks on control systems.

docs.applies: All ACE activities, sites, employees and contractors
docs.subtitle: How ACE knows, engages and listens to the communities around its sites and in the Gulf of Paria, and answers their grievances on time.

blocks.t: This policy sets how ACE knows, engages and listens to the people affected by its work: neighbours of the Point Lisas Shore Base, the CPF and the land leases, fishing communities in the Gulf of Paria, landowners, local authorities and regulators. It sets clear times for answering grievances.
It applies to all ACE sites and activities and to contractors working for ACE in the community. Its parent is ACE-LDR-POL-001. Customer relationships for gas and crude are covered by ACE-HMA-POL-001.
Each commitment names the ACE values it serves, as set in ACE-LDR-POL-001 section 1. The steps that deliver the commitments are in the governed processes and implementing documents in section 6.

In line with our value Care for people and places, ACE keeps a current map of the people and groups affected by each site (PLB, the CPF and the land leases) and by its marine activity, and meets them regularly so that relationships exist before they are needed.

In line with our values Care for people and places and Integrity in everything, every grievance or complaint is logged, acknowledged and answered within the times in section 4.1, and escalated if it is not resolved. No one is disadvantaged for raising a grievance.
Every grievance shall be logged in the grievance register with the date received, the acknowledgement, the response and the outcome.

sections.title: 2.3 Fishing communities are consulted before marine activity

blocks.t: In line with our value Care for people and places, fishing communities in the Gulf of Paria are consulted before marine activity that affects them, such as rig moves, pipeline work, surveys and exclusion zones, with the notice set in section 4.2.

In line with our values Safety above all and Care for people and places, ACE prepares nearby communities and local authorities for how we would respond together in an emergency, and keeps them informed during one (ACE-EMR-STD-001).
In line with our value Integrity in everything, what ACE says to communities is accurate and timely, including when the news is bad.

docs.subtitle: Establishing, verifying, monitoring and handing over well barriers through every well state.

blocks.t: This Practice defines ACE’s technical method for establishing, verifying, monitoring and handing over well barriers in drilling, completion, production, suspension, intervention and abandonment states. It applies to wells at Pommerac A (PAP), Chenet B (CHB), Sapodilla C (SAP), and land leases Tamarind, Pawpaw and Soursop (LND). It serves ACE-WEL-STD-001 Well Integrity Management Standard. Well-specific barrier schematics, status records and acceptance evidence are mandatory parts of the well file.

blocks.t: The Well Integrity Lead shall maintain the well integrity register, the barrier methodology and the integrity category of every ACE well.
The wellsite or intervention supervisor shall keep the barrier status current during operations and record every barrier test.

ACE applies a two-independent-barrier philosophy for activities and well states where required by the well design, risk assessment and applicable standards. The primary and secondary barrier envelopes are identified on a well-specific schematic. Independence is assessed for common failure modes, shared components, pressure sources, control dependencies and exposure to the same threat. Barrier selection is state-specific; a barrier configuration acceptable for production may not be acceptable for intervention, suspension or abandonment.

blocks.t: Category assignment is based on the well-specific risk and barrier evidence, not solely on a colour label. The Well Integrity Lead shall assign each well a category with recorded rationale, and every category change shall be communicated to Operations within 24 hours (C-WEL-004).
A well in Red category shall have the affected operation stopped and the well secured before any further work, with escalation to the VP Wells (C-WEL-005).

Annulus pressure is monitored against the well-specific maximum allowable annulus surface pressure (MAASP), pressure source assessment, thermal effects, fluid level and annulus configuration. MAASP is calculated and approved from the well design and weakest exposed element; it is not copied from another well. Monitoring frequency is risk-based and increased for unexplained pressure, sustained trends or integrity-category changes.

blocks.t: Handover is a formal transfer of well status, operational responsibility and surveillance expectations. The receiving role confirms that the information pack is complete, barrier status is understood, outstanding actions are accepted and the operating surveillance plan is available.

docs.title: Well Integrity Management Standard
docs.author: Shalini Jaggernauth — Well Integrity Lead
docs.reviewers: Arjun Ramlal — Drilling Engineering Lead; Kathy-Ann Simmons — Completions Lead; Nazim Bailey — Completions & Well Intervention Manager; Arjun Gittens — Offshore Operations Manager (Gulf of Paria)
docs.applies: All ACE producing, shut-in, suspended, appraisal, injection, intervention and abandonment wells on land and offshore, including contracted activities under ACE control
docs.subtitle: Well barriers, operating limits, surveillance, handover and lifecycle integrity control for ACE wells.

blocks.t: This standard governs the integrity of all wells operated by Acme Caribbean Energy Limited, from initial design and drilling to suspension and permanent abandonment. It applies to the Gulf of Paria wells on Pommerac A, Chenet B and Sapodilla C, and to wells on the Tamarind, Pawpaw and Soursop leases. It also applies to ACE-directed work carried out by drilling, workover, completion and well-services contractors.

The objective is to prevent uncontrolled flow of formation fluids and loss of containment by establishing, verifying and maintaining effective well barriers, managing operating pressures and temperatures, responding to anomalies and preserving reliable well records. Site-specific limits and barrier schematics are maintained in the approved well file rather than being generalized in this company-wide standard.

Every ACE-operated well shall have an identifiable well integrity custodian, a current barrier status and a controlled life-cycle record before it is placed in operation, shut in or transferred between accountable operating groups.
Joanne Ho Sing — VP Wells: accountable for the well integrity management system across the well life cycle and for approving this standard.
Shalini Jaggernauth — Well Integrity Lead: maintains barrier criteria, well status classification, anomaly review, verification basis and well integrity reporting.
Arjun Ramlal — Drilling Engineering Lead and Kathy-Ann Simmons — Completions Lead: Technical Authorities for drilling and completion design criteria within their discipline scopes.

Arjun Gittens — Offshore Operations Manager (Gulf of Paria) and Luis de Verteuil — Land Operations Manager: accountable for operational surveillance, worksite controls and release of work in their areas.

blocks.t: The mandatory basis consists of ACE engineering standards, approved well programmes, hazard studies, applicable licence conditions and adopted external well integrity codes. Where requirements differ, the more restrictive applicable requirement is identified and referred to the relevant Technical Authority. An external code does not remove the obligation to document the ACE well-specific design and acceptance basis.
The Well Integrity Lead shall maintain a register of adopted technical references, approved editions, applicability and authorised deviations in accordance with ACE-ENG-STD-901.
ACE-ENG-STD-901 — Engineering Standards Framework and Technical Authority Standard
ACE-RSK-STD-001 — Risk Management Standard
ACE-PSM-STD-001 — Process Safety and Hazard Study Standard

The well barrier philosophy uses independently effective primary and secondary barrier envelopes, where required by the operating phase and well-specific risk assessment. A barrier envelope is a verified combination of barrier elements and interfaces that together prevent uncontrolled flow along a defined path. Equipment counted in two envelopes is reviewed for common cause and shared-failure vulnerability.

The well design and operational programme shall identify the required barrier envelopes, their functions, verified elements, credible flow paths, acceptance tests and applicable exceptions for each phase.

blocks.t: Barrier element performance standards define functionality, integrity, reliability and testability. The design dossier identifies rated pressure and temperature, service fluids, material compatibility, operating environment, intended duty, potential failure modes and proof of suitability. Barrier elements that are safety-critical elements are registered under ACE asset integrity controls.
Every safety-critical well barrier element shall have an approved performance standard and traceable inspection, test or verification evidence for its intended operating duty.
A degraded barrier shall not be treated as available solely because a second barrier exists; operability depends on the documented remaining envelopes and approved risk decision.

A controlled schematic identifies flow paths from reservoir to environment, primary and secondary barrier elements, interfaces with surface systems, pressure reference points and the last verified condition. It is updated after completion changes, intervention, integrity repair and abandonment. The schematic is a technical control, not a decorative drawing.
Barrier schematics and related status records shall be version-controlled in each well dossier and cross-referenced to the applicable completion and intervention programmes.
Stop the job if a required barrier cannot be demonstrated or its condition conflicts with the approved barrier schematic.

sections.title: 3 Well integrity through the life cycle
3.1 Basis of design and drilling programme

blocks.t: At concept and design, Wells establishes hazards, pore and fracture pressure windows, corrosion and erosion threats, casing and cement design, completion philosophy, availability of isolation barriers and credible future interventions. The design basis records uncertainties, design margins and the authority for acceptance. Technical Authority endorsements are required at defined well programme gates.
Each well programme shall include a documented barrier plan and acceptance criteria for its planned drilling, completion, testing, suspension and emergency configurations.

During drilling and construction, the Wellsite Supervisor verifies critical installation and test records against the programme and ensures deviations are controlled. Essential evidence includes pressure-test charts, cementing reports, equipment traceability, material certificates, dimensional checks and as-built schematics. Missing or contradictory evidence is an integrity anomaly requiring resolution, not a documentation task to defer without assessment.

rows: Approved well design basis, hazard review, barrier plan, equipment selection
Formation programme, centralisation, cement design, batch and QA records
Accepted casing and wellhead pressure integrity, as-built barriers
Completion test evidence, barrier schematic, operating envelope, emergency closeout
Current well dossier, barrier status, intervention programme and risk assessment
Approved suspension or P&A programme, verified barriers and residual risks

blocks.t: Once released to Operations, routine monitoring includes tubing and annulus pressures, pressure trends, temperature and relevant flow performance, corrosion indicators, safety-device tests and visible leakage. Operating anomalies are reported to the Well Integrity Lead and linked to the well status and action register. Operations cannot make an integrity classification change without the designated technical review.

The Area Authority shall maintain well surveillance records and promptly escalate abnormal pressure, barrier-test failures, loss of communication or suspected containment defects under the approved trigger criteria.

Well interventions can remove, substitute or temporarily alter barriers. The intervention programme identifies every transition in barrier configuration, the testing needed to regain verified status and any competent authority needed to approve hold points. Suspended wells require a documented inspection and monitoring plan; the required level reflects pressure, fluids, environment and abandonment intent.
Figure 1. Lifecycle phases and cross-functional evidence transfer.

Each well has an approved operating envelope based on its design, completion, casing loads, formation pressure, pressure-containing equipment, temperature, service environment and expected transient conditions. The record identifies maximum and minimum allowable parameters, assumptions, calculation revision, escalation threshold and credible failure consequences. The standard does not prescribe one annulus pressure limit for all ACE wells.
A well shall not be operated outside its approved well-specific pressure, temperature, flow and annulus operating envelope without an approved and technically endorsed risk decision.

blocks.t: Monitoring distinguishes sustained annulus pressure, thermal pressure effects, pressure communication, trapped fluids and instrumentation error. Trends are reviewed against the well-specific allowable band and response triggers, including changes following shut-in, startup or workover. Operations records enough time-series context to distinguish an isolated reading from a developing integrity condition.
Active annuli shall have a documented monitoring schedule, alert limits and escalation criteria traceable to the current approved well operating envelope.

The first response to an abnormal reading is to verify instrumentation, check related wells or surface interfaces, confirm current barrier conditions and notify the Area Authority. Controlled bleeding, pressure management and diagnostic tests require an approved work plan, because uncontrolled pressure manipulation can change barrier loading or conceal deterioration.
Personnel shall not bleed or pressure-cycle an anomalous annulus as a routine corrective action without a reviewed diagnostic plan and Area Authority permission.

If pressure or barrier criteria require shut-in, Operations records the safe state and controls permits and isolations. Wells assesses repair or testing requirements. Return to service is contingent on documented technical evidence, updated limits and manager/Area Authority release; a temporary deviation cannot automatically extend beyond its expiry.

Verification establishes that an installed or restored barrier meets the defined performance requirement under representative conditions. Test selection may include pressure testing, negative testing, function testing, inspection, cement evaluation and independent witness. Acceptance criteria derive from the approved well design, operating programme and adopted technical standards.

Barrier verification shall use written acceptance criteria approved before the test, including fluid, differential direction, hold period, tolerance, instrumentation accuracy and required witnesses appropriate to the barrier.

blocks.t: Testing is planned as a controlled activity under applicable permits and energy isolation. Equipment traceability and calibration are checked; test boundaries and communication requirements are understood. A failed or inconclusive result is recorded in full, investigated and linked to the anomaly register. Repeating a test does not erase an earlier failure.
Unsuccessful barrier tests shall be recorded and classified before any retest; the revised test plan and acceptance decision shall be approved by the responsible technical authority.

Inspection programmes account for material compatibility, produced fluids, corrosion mechanisms, vibration, fatigue and historic anomalies. The Well Integrity Lead coordinates with the Materials & Corrosion Lead and Inspection Lead when integrity mechanisms overlap tubing, wellhead, connected flowlines or structures. Work orders and observations flow into the well-level barrier assessment.
Degradation mechanisms affecting well barriers shall be included in the well integrity surveillance basis and linked to the relevant inspection, maintenance or monitoring programme.

Tests, failed results, calculations, as-built changes, calibration records, approvals, photographs and intervention reports shall be retained against the unique well identifier in the controlled well dossier.

Well integrity status is classified from the available barrier evidence and ACE risk assessment, not inferred solely from whether a well continues producing. The following categories are internal operating states; they are not a universal external code and must be reconciled with well-specific technical limits. A higher urgency can always be assigned based on credible escalation.

blocks.t: A well classified W3 shall be prevented from normal production or injection pending a verified safe state and approved recovery plan.

Typical triggers include uncontrolled annular pressure growth, pressure communication, failed wellhead valve test, evidence of corrosion penetration, unexpected fluid discharge, sustained external leakage or damaged barrier instrumentation. Operations protects personnel and establishes a safe site condition; Wells diagnoses and classifies the well; Technical Authorities endorse a repair or restriction.
An integrity anomaly shall receive a unique register entry with first detection, well ID, suspected failed element, available barrier envelope, risk, restrictions, owner and closure evidence.

Risk evaluation uses the ACE Risk Matrix and considers credible loss-of-containment consequences, potential escalation, well location, gas/oil inventory and available independent barriers. The first assessment is revisited when diagnostics add evidence. A lower-risk classification requires a documented technical basis rather than assumptions about production value.

A temporary continuation or restricted operation with an impaired barrier shall be approved through ACE-OMS-STD-002 at the applicable risk authority and endorsed by the Well Integrity Lead and relevant Technical Authority.

blocks.t: Figure 2. Operating anomaly response from detection to verified restoration.

A handover is an explicit acceptance of responsibility for a defined state and operating envelope. It is not completed by emailing a drilling report or announcing first flow. The receiving Area Authority has the right to refuse a well whose records, controls or credible barrier state are incomplete. A conditional acceptance is a controlled, time-bound decision with named restrictions.

Prior to release for production, injection or routine surveillance, Wells shall present a controlled well dossier and Operations shall sign the acceptance record with all open restrictions identified.

blocks.t: Offshore Operations receives Gulf of Paria well status and coordinates Pommerac A and unmanned platform access and work control. Land Operations performs the equivalent role for Tamarind, Pawpaw and Soursop leases. CPF operations receive relevant flowline, processing and isolation constraints when a well condition affects delivery or receiving capacity.
Arjun Gittens — Offshore Operations Manager (Gulf of Paria): accepts Gulf of Paria well operational releases and ensures offshore monitoring and work control.
Luis de Verteuil — Land Operations Manager: accepts land-well operational releases and coordinates land well surveillance and response.

Before a workover or intervention, the receiving Wells team obtains the current operating condition, live trends, applied overrides, pressure history, tests, recent anomalies, well fluids and pending production constraints. Wells accepts and documents the changed worksite status; after intervention the well is re-released through the same formal gate.
Intervention work shall not start until the receiving Wells authority and the Area Authority have agreed and recorded barrier ownership, worksite control and emergency responsibility.

Changes to completion configuration, barriers, pressure envelopes, well control systems, operating philosophy, chemicals, monitoring or permanent operating restrictions are screened under ACE-MOC-PRC-001. Replacement in kind is demonstrated against approved design and service criteria, not assumed because equipment is similar. Relevant Technical Authorities review changes to drilling and completion design bases.

Changes to well barrier functions, associated operating limits or technical standards shall be assessed through MOC before implementation, except where an approved emergency response arrangement permits immediate safeguarding actions.

A deviation is an explicit approved departure from a requirement, not a means to conceal a failed barrier or extend operating life without engineering basis. Requests specify the precise requirement, existing condition, risk assessment, compensating measures, Technical Authority review, approval authority, monitoring, duration and recovery plan.
Any temporary deviation involving a safety-critical well barrier shall have documented Technical Authority endorsement, time-bounded risk acceptance and an expiry date in the deviation register.

Repair scope and verification requirements are defined before execution. The repair programme identifies which existing barriers remain effective, which are intentionally removed and the hold points for restoring normal configuration. Operations is involved before well return to production, including changed limits and revised emergency response instructions.
The MOC number, deviation, technical assessment, approved programme, work execution evidence, barrier tests and final acceptance shall be linked in the well dossier.

Deferred actions remain visible in both the integrity status and organisational action registers. A deferral includes consequence of non-completion, interim safeguards, approval authority, monitoring and planned close-out. Expiry is an active management decision; silence is not approval to extend.

Permanent plug and abandonment (P&A) removes a well from service and establishes durable isolation against formation-to-formation and formation-to-surface communication. Design considers geology, pressure sources, produced fluids, corrosion potential, barrier material longevity, shallow hazards, future access and environmental conditions. The approved plan identifies barrier placement, verification and documentation methods.
Each well to be permanently abandoned shall have a Technical Authority-endorsed P&A programme demonstrating the intended permanent barrier envelopes, placement basis and verification requirements.

Planning includes well condition assessment, pressure and fluid data review, logistics, well-control provisions, permit/isolations, service company qualification, contingency arrangements and required approvals. Field execution records barrier installation depth, volume, material batch, equipment, pressure response, verification method and unexpected conditions. Deviations are assessed before proceeding past a hold point.

blocks.t: Temporarily suspended wells have defined barrier configuration, preservation, access control, pressure surveillance and a recorded inspection schedule appropriate to their risk. Surveillance accountability stays with the named operator; any change in future use or planned time to abandonment triggers review.
A suspended well shall retain a documented barrier and monitoring basis and shall not be left without an identified accountable custodian.
P&A evidence, permanent barrier schematic, approved deviations, regulatory submissions and as-left well condition shall be archived in the controlled well dossier with a stable well identifier.

The master inventory links each ACE well to its field or lease, physical location, drilling and completion identifiers, owner, producing/suspended/abandoned state, barrier classification, operating limits, test history, active anomalies, deviations and next review. One accountable well integrity state is used across Operations, Wells and the assurance dashboard to prevent contradictory local spreadsheets.

The Well Integrity Lead shall publish a current well integrity status report and maintain a controlled register that identifies every open impairment, restriction, expired control and required action.

blocks.t: Assurance samples trace the chain from well design basis through field evidence to verified operating state. Independent review tests completeness of barrier schematics, calculation basis, test evidence, status decisions, permit interfaces, deviations and closure effectiveness. Findings feed the ACE assurance and corrective action system.
Integrity assessments, challenge records, field verification, action owners, close-out evidence and management review outputs shall be stored in the approved controlled repository.

Wells leadership reviews integrity performance quarterly and following a significant barrier event. Reviews examine common causes, site trends, ageing wells, contractor performance, inspection effectiveness, recovery actions and design improvements. Decisions affecting production or major operating constraints involve the relevant Operations and Technical Authority representatives.
Measure: No well operates with an unacceptable barrier classification, and no safety-critical impairment continues beyond its authorised expiry without a new technical decision.

docs.author: Marissa Bobb — OMS Manager
docs.reviewers: George Habib — VP HSE & Compliance; Gary Ho Sing — Manager, Strategy & Planning; Sanjay Jagessar — Information Management Lead
docs.applies: All ACE activities, sites, staff and contractors
docs.subtitle: One Management System — how ACE works, every site, every day

rows: ONE MANAGEMENT SYSTEMOne framework. One source. One way of working — on every platform, every lease, every shift.
IMAGE IMG-01Pommerac A at first light, supply vessel alongside, crew on the cellar deck. Wide, warm, optimistic. 16:9.

blocks.t: Every day, about three hundred of us and many more contractors produce oil and gas from the Gulf of Paria and our land leases, process it at the Central Processing Facility, and deliver it to the Gas Buyer and to the market. Our work is valuable and it is hazardous. The difference between a good day and a terrible one is almost always a barrier that held, a procedure that was followed, or a person who stopped the job.

OMS — our One Management System — is how we make sure those things happen every time. It is not a binder on a shelf or a programme run by the HSE department. It is how ACE works: one framework, one Risk Matrix, one set of documents and one way of checking that we do what we say.

This fourth revision takes OMS a step further. It makes our processes visible — who does what, in what order, across functions — and gives each one an owner who is accountable for making it better. It connects every control that protects us to the risk it addresses, the document that requires it, the step that performs it and the evidence that it works. And it introduces Standard Practices: the way each of our disciplines does its work, written down by the people who know it best.
Figure 1. The OMS wheel: ten elements in three groups — Lead, Control and Learn

1 We know our hazardsEvery task starts with understanding what could go wrong — from a toolbox talk to a HAZOP.
2 We look after our barriersSafety-critical equipment is maintained, tested and never bypassed without approval.
3 We follow the procedure — or we change itNever work around a procedure. Raise it, fix it through the proper route, then use it.
4 We stop when it is not safeEveryone has the authority and the duty to stop work. No one is ever criticised for it.
5 We learn and shareWe report every incident and near miss, find the real causes and act on the lessons.
…and we keep getting betterEvery process has an owner whose job is to make it simpler, safer and more reliable.

blocks.t: OMS is only real at the worksite. Here is what it means, in practice, for the people who make ACE work.

rows: Operators and techniciansYou have the current procedure at the point of use, you know the limits of the plant you run, and you can stop the job. If a procedure does not match reality, tell your supervisor — fixing it is part of OMS.
Supervisors and Area AuthoritiesYou plan and release work safely through permits, check that barriers are healthy before work starts, and verify the job is done as planned.
Engineers and Technical AuthoritiesYou own the technical standards and Practices of your discipline, endorse changes and deviations, and make sure our barriers perform as designed.
Managers and leadersYou own the processes, standards and risks in your area. You visit the work, listen, remove obstacles and judge success by how well risk is controlled.
Office and support staffFinance, supply chain, HR, IT and communications all carry OMS duties: the right contractor, the right competence, the right data, the right message.
Contractors and visitorsYou work to OMS, or to your own system where ACE has bridged it. You have the same right and duty to stop unsafe work as any ACE employee.
Standard Practices join Standards at Level 2
Each discipline writes down how ACE does its work — methods, criteria and technical rules — in one place.
Cross-functional work is drawn as swimlanes in ONE, so you can see who does what, in what order, and which documents and controls apply at each step.
Every process has a process owner
One person is accountable for how well each process performs and for improving it.
Controls get an ID and a home
Each control is linked to its risk, the document section that requires it, the step that performs it and the evidence that it works.
Three new systems: BPM, LOG, HMA
Business Process Management, Marine and Aviation Logistics, and Hydrocarbon Measurement and Allocation are now part of OMS.
The rules for writing and publishing documents are clearer and are checked automatically by the ONE gateway.

sections.title: Part A — Our One Management System

rows: PART AOne system, built around our assets and our people — not a shelf of separate systems.
IMAGE IMG-02The Central Processing Facility at dusk: lit columns and tanks, a small flare, two operators walking the plant. 16:9.

blocks.t: OMS — One Management System — is the single framework ACE uses to manage everything that affects safety, health, environment, integrity, reliability and performance. It covers our policies, standards, practices, processes, procedures, people, plant, and the way we check and improve them.

OMS replaced a set of separate systems that grew up as ACE grew. There is no separate HSE system, integrity system or quality system: each is now a system within OMS, using the same framework, Risk Matrix, document standard and assurance programme.
All ACE activities shall be planned, carried out and checked in line with OMS.
OMS applies to all ACE activities, at every stage of the asset life cycle:
Head Office in Central Trinidad and the Point Lisas Shore Base;
the Gulf of Paria platforms — Pommerac A (manned), Chenet B and Sapodilla C (normally unmanned) — and their pipelines;
the Tamarind, Pawpaw and Soursop land leases, well pads, flowlines and gathering stations;
the Central Processing Facility, its tank farm and export systems;
drilling, workover and well services, projects, marine and aviation logistics.
Contractors working on ACE sites or on ACE's behalf shall work to OMS, or to their own system where ACE has formally bridged it to OMS.
Where ACE is not the operator, or shares facilities with partners, the Joint Venture and Partner Interface Standard sets out how OMS applies.
OMS rests on four foundations that run through every element:

rows: Leaders own OMS, are visible at the worksite, and judge themselves by how well risks are controlled, not only by production.
One way of identifying and controlling risk, using one Risk Matrix, from a toolbox talk to a major accident hazard study.
Plan, do, check, act: objectives are set, work is done, measured and audited, and the system is improved — process by process.
Every requirement has an owner, a document that delivers it, a process step that performs it and a way of checking it is done.

blocks.t: Everything in OMS traces back to why ACE exists. Our mission, vision and values shape our strategy and objectives; policies state our commitments; standards and practices set what must be true and how our disciplines work; processes and procedures make it happen; and records prove it did.
Figure 2. The golden thread from mission to evidence
The ten elements follow the structure of the industry framework published by IOGP and IPIECA. ACE groups them as Lead (elements 1–4), Control (elements 5–8) and Learn (elements 9–10).

Each system within OMS has a three-letter code, an owner on the Executive Leadership Team and a set of documents. The code is used in document numbers (see Part D). Revision 04 adds three systems: BPM, LOG and HMA.
