VP Business Development & Markets (Technical Authority: Metering & Measurement Lead)

blocks.t: System owners are accountable for the design, documents, performance and improvement of their system, and for its fit with the rest of OMS.
The value of one system is in its connections. The chain below is the backbone of OMS: it runs from understanding hazards to doing the work safely and learning from the results.
Figure 3. The OMS risk thread: how the systems inside OMS connect

rows: The ACE Risk Matrix is defined once and used by HAZOP, MOC, deviations, incident classification, contractor risk rating and audit planning.
HAZID, HAZOP, LOPA and bow-tie studies identify the barriers each major accident hazard needs. Hardware barriers become safety-critical elements.
Each safety-critical element has a performance standard owned by a Technical Authority: what it must do, how reliably, and how it is tested.
Maintenance and inspection turn performance standards into scheduled tasks, with safety-critical work given priority.
Permits, isolations and operating limits protect barriers during work. Overrides of safety systems need explicit approval.
Any change to plant, process, people or documents is checked for its effect on hazards, barriers, documents and competence before it is made.
Investigations, KPIs and audits show where barriers are weak, and the findings feed back into risk assessments and standards.

blocks.t: A control is anything that prevents a hazardous event or limits its consequences. In OMS, each control is the hinge that joins everything else: the risk it addresses, the bow-tie barrier it forms, the document section that requires it, the process step that performs it, the role that owns it, the equipment it depends on and the record that proves it works. Each significant control carries an ID, such as C-AIM-014, so ONE can follow every one of those links.
Figure 4. One control, linked to everything that depends on it
What this means for you When you see a control ID in a document, it tells you that paragraph is protecting someone. Do it exactly as written — and if you cannot, stop and raise it.
ACE-RSK-PRA-001 Controls and Barrier Linkage Practice

rows: Oversees ACE's risk and OMS performance through the Board Audit Committee
Owns OMS; approves the OMS Policy and this Manual; chairs the annual management review
Executive Leadership Team members accountable for the performance and improvement of an element across ACE
Accountable for a system within OMS: its standards, practices, processes, performance and interfaces
Accountable for the content of a controlled document and for keeping it current
Accountable for how well a process performs end to end, across functions, and for improving it
Discipline lead who owns the technical standards and Practices of a discipline and endorses designs, changes and deviations
The discipline leads, chaired by the VP Engineering & Projects, who endorse engineering standards, Practices and technical deviations
Custodian of the OMS framework, its mapping to industry frameworks and the conformance assessment programme
Owner of the BPM system: the ACE process architecture and the Process Register
Accountable for everything that happens at a location; issues permits and releases work (OIMs, Offshore and Land Operations Managers, Plant Manager)
Gatekeeper for controlled documents; owns numbering, templates and the ONE gateway
Apply OMS in their teams; make sure people are competent, informed and supervised
Work to OMS, use current procedures, report incidents and stop unsafe work

blocks.t: Note Four owners, four questions. The document owner answers “is the text right?”. The process owner answers “does the work flow well?”. The Technical Authority answers “is it technically sound?”. The line manager answers “are my people able to do it?”.

rows: Head of Internal Audit & Risk Assurance

sections.title: A.7 Industry frameworks and international standards

blocks.t: OMS is built on IOGP Report 510, Operating Management System Framework (2014), published by IOGP and IPIECA. ACE uses its ten elements and the numbering of its expectations so that ACE documents, audits and benchmarking line up with industry practice. The section titles and text in this Manual are ACE's own.

ISO is developing international standards for operating management systems based on the same framework: ISO/DIS 29501 (requirements with guidance for use), ISO/DIS 29502 (conformity assessment) and ISO 29011 (maturity assessment). ACE tracks their development and keeps the indicative cross-reference below. Our process architecture is modelled on the APQC Process Classification Framework, and process maps follow a simple subset of BPMN 2.0.

rows: 6.1 Risks and opportunities · 6.3 Planning of changes

blocks.t: IOGP Report 510 (2014) and IOGP Report 511 © IOGP and IPIECA. Element titles and expectation numbering are reproduced with acknowledgement. ISO documents are referenced by title only.

sections.title: OMS at work — our core areas

rows: OMS AT WORKThis is where OMS earns its keep: in the work that produces, moves, measures and sells our oil and gas.

blocks.t: ACE's work is organised into a simple process architecture. Core areas create value; enabling areas make the core possible; governing areas set direction and check the whole. The pages that follow show, for each core area, what we do, what could go wrong, and how OMS keeps it under control — from the Standard that sets the rules, through the Practice that describes how our professionals work, to the processes and procedures used every day.
Figure 5. The ACE process architecture (level 1)

rows: OPERATE & PRODUCERun the plant inside its limits, every hour of every shift.
IMAGE IMG-03CPF control room: an operator at the console, alarm summary on screen, calm and focused. 16:9.

blocks.t: What we do. We run the Pommerac A, Chenet B and Sapodilla C platforms, the land lease gathering stations and the Central Processing Facility around the clock: separating, treating and compressing gas and crude to specification.

What could go wrong. Operating outside safe limits can damage equipment, cause loss of containment or let corrosion take hold unseen. Shift handovers, start-ups and shutdowns are the moments of highest risk.

rows: How OMS keeps it under control
ACE-OPS-STD-001 Operating Envelopes and Operating Limits Standard
ACE-OPS-PRA-001 Operating Envelopes and Integrity Operating Windows Practice

blocks.t: What this means for you Know the operating limits of the plant you run. If a reading is outside its window, respond as the limits register says — and report it, even if it recovers.
Measure Critical operating-window excursions responded to within the required time (target 100%).

rows: DELIVER WELLSTwo barriers, verified, in every well, in every state.
IMAGE IMG-04Land rig on the Tamarind lease at golden hour, crew on the rig floor, well control equipment visible. 16:9.

blocks.t: What we do. We drill, complete, intervene in and look after wells offshore and on the Tamarind, Pawpaw and Soursop leases, and hand them over safely between the Wells and Operations teams.
What could go wrong. Loss of well control is our most severe hazard. Annulus pressure, degraded barriers and poor handovers can all erode the protection we rely on.

rows: How OMS keeps it under control
ACE-WEL-PRA-001 Well Barriers and Well Handover Practice

blocks.t: What this means for you Every well has a barrier schematic and an integrity category. Before you work on a well, check both — and never accept a handover without them.
Measure Wells with a current barrier schematic and integrity category (target 100%).

rows: ASSET INTEGRITY & MAINTENANCEFind the problem before it finds us.
IMAGE IMG-05Inspection engineer taking ultrasonic thickness readings on a pipeline riser, rope-access technician nearby, sea below. 16:9.

blocks.t: What we do. We inspect, test and maintain the equipment that keeps hydrocarbons contained and our safety systems ready: pressure vessels, pipelines, rotating equipment, and the safety-critical elements on every installation.
What could go wrong. Corrosion, fatigue and wear are silent. A deferred inspection or an overdue test on a safety-critical element can leave a barrier weaker than anyone knows.

rows: How OMS keeps it under control
ACE-AIM-PRA-001 Risk-Based Inspection and Corrosion Management Practice
ACE-MNT-PRA-001 Equipment Criticality and Safety-Critical Element Maintenance Practice
ACE-AIM-REG-001 Safety-Critical Element Register and Performance Standards

blocks.t: Note Safety-critical work comes first. If a safety-critical inspection or test cannot be done on time, it is a deviation — raise it so the risk is seen and managed.
Measure Safety-critical maintenance and inspection completed on time (target 98%); overdue safety-critical inspections (target zero).

rows: MARINE & AVIATION LOGISTICSEvery trip planned, every lift controlled, everyone home.
IMAGE IMG-06Point Lisas shore base: supply vessel loading deck cargo, crew boat alongside, helicopter overhead. 16:9.

blocks.t: What we do. From the Point Lisas shore base we move people, equipment, chemicals and waste to and from our platforms by supply vessel, fast crew boat and helicopter, and our vessels patrol the pipelines in the Gulf of Paria.
What could go wrong. Personnel transfers, lifting at sea, bad weather and helideck operations carry serious risk. Visits to unmanned platforms need extra care.

rows: How OMS keeps it under control
ACE-CON-STD-001 Contractor and Supplier Management Standard
ACE-LOG-PRA-001 Marine and Aviation Logistics Practice

blocks.t: Note Never board a vessel or aircraft without the briefing and the manifest. On an unmanned platform, follow the boarding rules — two people minimum, always.
Measure Marine and aviation trips completed without incident; vessel and aircraft assurance audits completed to plan.

rows: HYDROCARBON MEASUREMENTEvery molecule measured, every barrel accounted for.
IMAGE IMG-07Fiscal metering skid at the CPF, technician with a calibration laptop beside the flow computer. 16:9.

blocks.t: What we do. We measure the gas we sell to the Gas Buyer and the crude we ship, prove and calibrate our meters, and allocate production back to every field, well and partner.
What could go wrong. Mismeasurement costs money, damages trust with customers and partners, and breaks regulatory obligations. Lost and unaccounted-for volumes can also be the first sign of a leak.

rows: How OMS keeps it under control
ACE-STK-STD-002 Customer and Product Quality Standard
ACE-HMA-PRA-001 Hydrocarbon Measurement and Allocation Practice

blocks.t: What this means for you Treat a metering or allocation anomaly like a safety observation: report it promptly. A number that does not add up may be telling you something.
Measure Fiscal meter proving and calibration completed on schedule (target 100%); monthly allocation issued on time.

rows: BUSINESS PROCESS MANAGEMENTKnow the process, know your step, make it better.
IMAGE IMG-08Process workshop at Head Office: a cross-functional team around a wall-sized swimlane map with sticky notes. 16:9.

blocks.t: What we do. We describe our cross-functional work as processes — who does what, in what order, with which documents and controls — and give each process an owner who keeps improving it. Every process is published in ONE as an interactive swimlane.
What could go wrong. Without clear processes, work falls between functions: handoffs are missed, controls are assumed rather than performed, and the same problem is fixed again and again.

rows: How OMS keeps it under control
ACE-BPM-PRA-002 Process Modelling and Process File Practice
ACE-BPM-PRA-003 Process Ownership and Continuous Improvement Practice

blocks.t: What this means for you Find your role's lane in the processes you work in. If a step does not work in practice, tell the process owner — that is how processes get better.
Measure Processes reviewed by their owner in the last 12 months (target 100%).
Figure 6. A process in ONE: swimlanes by role, steps linked to documents, orange markers for controls

sections.title: One thread: the Pommerac A export line

blocks.t: The crude export line from Pommerac A shows how the core areas work together to protect one asset. Internal corrosion is the threat; each barrier belongs to a different team, and each is written down, performed in a process and checked with evidence.

rows: Corrosion inhibitor injected within its operating window

blocks.t: Note No single barrier is perfect. OMS works because the barriers are independent, each one has an owner, and ONE shows their health side by side — so a weak barrier is seen before the next one is tested.

rows: PART BTen elements, fifty-four expectations — and for each one, exactly what ACE requires and who makes it happen.

blocks.t: Each chapter in Part B covers one element. Each numbered section addresses the expectation with the same number, and sets out what ACE requires, who is responsible, which ACE documents deliver it and how we measure it.
What this means for you You do not need to read Part B from start to finish. Use the expectation index in Appendix 1, or the OMS wheel in ONE, to go straight to what you need.
LEAD · Element owner: Chief Executive Officer

rows: OMS only works if leaders live it and everyone owns their part. This element sets out how ACE leaders show commitment, how accountability is built into every job, and how we keep the system visible in day-to-day work.

blocks.t: What this means for you You are accountable for the OMS duties in your role profile. If you are not sure what they are, ask your line manager — then hold us to them.
OMS is how ACE runs its business, not a project beside it. The Executive Leadership Team sets OMS priorities each year, assigns owners and funds the work in the business plan.
The CEO shall approve the annual OMS plan as part of the ACE business plan, with named owners, resources and dates for each priority.
Each element owner shall report progress on their element to the Executive Leadership Team at least quarterly.
The OMS Manager coordinates the annual OMS plan and tracks delivery on behalf of the Executive Leadership Team.
ACE-OMS-STD-001 OMS Governance Standard
ACE-OMS-STD-003 Objectives and Annual OMS Plan Standard
Measure Annual OMS plan actions completed on time (target 90%).

sections.title: 1.2 A culture of safe, reliable and accountable work

blocks.t: Leaders set the tone by what they pay attention to. ACE leaders visit the work, listen to the people doing it and act on what they hear, on Pommerac A, on the land leases and at the CPF.
Every member of the Executive Leadership Team shall complete at least one structured site visit per quarter and record the conversations and follow-up actions.
Managers shall include an OMS or safety topic in every team meeting.
Line managers are responsible for the safety culture of their teams and for acting on concerns raised.
ACE-LDR-STD-002 Leadership Engagement and Communication Standard
Measure Leadership site visits completed versus plan; follow-up actions closed within 30 days.
What this means for you When a leader visits your worksite, tell them what makes the job harder or riskier than it should be. That is what the visit is for.

sections.title: 1.3 Everyone committed to OMS and the law

blocks.t: Every employee and contractor commits to working within OMS and within the laws that apply to ACE's licences and sites.
All new staff and contractors shall complete the OMS induction before starting work at an ACE site.
All staff shall confirm each year that they have read the OMS Policy and the Code of Conduct.
Line managers confirm that their staff have completed the OMS induction and the annual confirmation.
ACE-LDR-POL-001 OMS Policy — Health, Safety, Environment and Operating Integrity
ACE-LEG-STD-001 Legal and Other Requirements Standard
Measure OMS induction completion before site access (target 100%).
The ACE Code of Conduct sets out how we behave: honestly, safely, fairly and within the law, including on gifts, conflicts of interest and speaking up.
All staff shall complete Code of Conduct training on joining and every two years after that.
Concerns raised under the Code shall be handled confidentially and without retaliation.
The VP Legal & Government Affairs owns the Code of Conduct and reports on concerns to the Board Audit Committee.
ACE-LDR-STD-001 Code of Conduct
Measure Code of Conduct training current (target 100%); speak-up cases closed within 60 days.

sections.title: 1.5 OMS duties built into every role

blocks.t: OMS accountabilities are written into role profiles, delegated authorities and performance goals, so that OMS is part of the job and not extra to it.
Every role profile shall state the OMS accountabilities and authorities of the role.
Annual performance goals for all managers and above shall include at least one OMS objective.
Human Resources maintains role profiles; line managers set and review OMS goals.
ACE-PPL-STD-001 Roles, Accountabilities and Delegated Authority Standard
Measure Role profiles with OMS accountabilities defined (target 100%).
We keep OMS in front of people through regular, consistent communication: shift briefings, toolbox talks, the OMS web portal, newsletters and leadership messages.
Each function shall maintain an annual communication plan that covers OMS changes, lessons and performance.
Changes to Level 1 and Level 2 OMS documents shall be communicated to affected staff before their effective date.
The Communications Manager supports functions with OMS communication materials and channels.
ACE-LDR-STD-002 Leadership Engagement and Communication Standard
ACE-DOC-STD-002 Operational Document Publishing Standard
Measure Staff awareness score in the annual OMS pulse survey.

OMS documents are controlled so that only the current approved version is in use, and records are kept, retained and archived in a planned way. Part D of this Manual sets out the ACE documentation standard.
All OMS documents shall be numbered, approved, published and revised in line with Part D of this Manual.
Records shall be retained for the periods set in the Document and Records Management Standard.
The Information Management Lead is the gatekeeper for publication of controlled documents.
ACE-DOC-STD-001 Document and Records Management Standard
ACE-DOC-STD-002 Operational Document Publishing Standard
Measure Controlled documents past their review date (target below 5%).
We actively look for lessons inside ACE and from the wider industry, and use them to reduce risk and improve how we work.
Significant industry incidents shall be reviewed by the relevant Technical Authority for applicability to ACE within 60 days.
Lessons shall be shared through the lessons learned system and reflected in documents where needed.
The Knowledge Management Specialist runs the lessons learned process; Technical Authorities assess external lessons.
ACE-INC-STD-002 Lessons Learned and Action Tracking Standard
Measure External lessons reviewed within 60 days.
LEAD · Element owner: VP HSE & Compliance

rows: Clear policies and standards tell everyone what ACE expects, and measurable objectives tell us whether we are getting there. This element covers how ACE sets them, approves them and handles the rare cases where we cannot meet them.

blocks.t: What this means for you If a standard cannot be met on your job, do not work around it. Raise a deviation so that the risk is assessed and approved at the right level.

sections.title: 2.1 Setting and sharing policies, standards and objectives

blocks.t: ACE's expectations are written down in one hierarchy of policies, standards and procedures, and shared with everyone who needs them through the OMS web portal.
Policies, standards and objectives shall be documented in the OMS document hierarchy described in Part D.
Each Level 2 standard shall name its owner, scope and the elements it supports.
System owners maintain their standards; the OMS Manager maintains the overall hierarchy.
ACE-OMS-STD-001 OMS Governance Standard
ACE-DOC-STD-001 Document and Records Management Standard
ACE-BPM-PRA-001 Business Process Management Practice
Measure Level 2 standards with current owner and review date (target 100%).
Policies are approved by the CEO, standards by system owners and procedures by managers. The approval level reflects the risk and reach of the document.
Documents shall be approved at the level set in the approval matrix in Part D.
The OMS Policy shall be reviewed and re-signed by the CEO at least every three years or after a major change.
Approvers confirm that a document is fit for purpose before signing.
ACE-OMS-STD-001 OMS Governance Standard
ACE-DOC-STD-001 Document and Records Management Standard
Measure Documents approved at the correct level (sampled in audit).

sections.title: 2.3 Risk-based standards that meet the law

blocks.t: ACE standards are based on our risks and meet or exceed the legal and other requirements that apply to us, including licence conditions and permits for the Gulf of Paria and land operations.
Each system owner shall map their standards to the Legal and Regulatory Requirements Register.
Legal requirements shall be reviewed at least annually and when legislation changes.
The Regulatory Compliance Specialist maintains the register with Legal & Government Affairs.
ACE-LEG-STD-001 Legal and Other Requirements Standard
ACE-LEG-REG-001 Legal and Regulatory Requirements Register
Measure Legal requirements with an assigned owner and compliance status (target 100%).
Every year ACE sets OMS objectives with clear targets: improvements to the system, performance targets and compliance goals. They cascade from the business plan into function and team plans.
OMS objectives shall have a measure, a target, an owner and a date.
Function plans shall show how they contribute to the ACE OMS objectives.
The Manager, Strategy & Planning coordinates objective setting within the business plan.
ACE-OMS-STD-003 Objectives and Annual OMS Plan Standard
ACE-PRF-STD-001 Performance Measurement and KPI Standard
Measure Objectives with measurable targets (target 100%).
Where ACE shares licences or facilities with partners, we agree how policies and standards apply so that people on site get one consistent message.
Joint venture and shared-facility agreements shall define which party's OMS applies and how interfaces are managed.
Interface documents shall be reviewed when operatorship or scope changes.
The Partner Relations Lead owns partner interface arrangements.
ACE-OMS-STD-004 Joint Venture and Partner Interface Standard
Measure Shared facilities with a current interface document (target 100%).

Sometimes a standard cannot be met. A deviation is a controlled, time-limited departure with the risk assessed and approved by the right authority. Working around a standard without approval is not acceptable.
Any departure from a mandatory requirement shall be raised as a deviation before the work proceeds.
Deviations shall be risk-assessed using the ACE Risk Matrix, approved at the level set by their risk, and given an expiry date.
The relevant Technical Authority endorses technical deviations; the OMS Manager maintains the deviation register.
ACE-OMS-STD-002 Deviation and Exemption Standard
ACE-RSK-STD-001 Risk Management Standard (including the ACE Risk Matrix)
Measure Deviations past their expiry date (target zero).
What this means for you A deviation is not a failure. Hiding one is.
LEAD · Element owner: VP Human Resources

rows: The right people, with the right skills and resources, in a clear organisation. This element covers roles and authorities, workforce planning, competence, resources, consultation and the contractors who do much of our work.

blocks.t: What this means for you Only do work you are competent and authorised to do. If you have not been trained or assessed for a task, stop and tell your supervisor.
ACE's organisation is designed so that every OMS accountability has an owner, including the Area Authorities who control our locations and the Technical Authorities who set our technical standards.
The ACE organisation chart, role profiles and delegated authorities shall be kept current.
Area Authorities and Technical Authorities shall be formally appointed in writing.
Every process in the Process Register shall have one named process owner, appointed in writing.
The VP Human Resources maintains the organisation design; the VP Engineering & Projects appoints Technical Authorities.
ACE-PPL-STD-001 Roles, Accountabilities and Delegated Authority Standard
ACE-ENG-STD-901 Engineering Standards Framework and Technical Authority Standard
ACE-BPM-PRA-003 Process Ownership and Continuous Improvement Practice
Measure Safety-critical roles with a current appointment letter (target 100%).
We plan ahead for the people we need: recruitment, graduate and apprentice intake, career development, retention and succession for critical roles.
Each function shall maintain a workforce plan reviewed annually with Human Resources.
Critical roles shall have at least one identified successor.
HR Business Partners support functions in preparing workforce plans.
ACE-PPL-STD-002 Workforce Planning and Succession Standard
Measure Critical roles with a ready successor.

Competence means having the skills, knowledge, behaviours and fitness to do a job safely. ACE assures competence by screening, training, assessing and re-assessing people against role competence profiles.
Every role shall have a competence profile, and people shall be assessed against it before working unsupervised.
Competence for safety-critical tasks shall be re-verified at the intervals set in the Competence Assurance Standard.
The Learning & Competence Manager owns the competence system; line managers ensure their staff are assessed.
ACE-PPL-STD-003 Competence Assurance Standard
ACE-OHH-STD-001 Occupational Health and Fitness for Work Standard
Measure Staff in safety-critical roles with current competence verification (target 100%).
We match people, equipment and budget to our objectives and risks, using in-country suppliers and services wherever practicable.
Resource plans shall be prepared with the annual business plan and reviewed when scope or risk changes.
Procurement strategies shall consider local content commitments.
Function heads secure resources; the VP Supply Chain Management owns local content.
ACE-PPL-STD-002 Workforce Planning and Succession Standard
ACE-CON-STD-002 Local Content Standard
Measure Local content spend against licence commitments.
People who do the work know where the risks are. ACE consults its workforce and the recognised union through joint HSE committees and engagement on plans, improvements and change.
Each major location shall have a joint HSE committee meeting at least quarterly.
Workforce representatives shall be consulted on changes that affect their work.
The Industrial Relations Specialist coordinates consultation arrangements with the union.
ACE-PPL-STD-004 Workforce Engagement and Consultation Standard
Measure Joint HSE committee meetings held versus plan.

Much of ACE's work is done by contractors: rigs, well services, supply boats, maintenance and construction. We select them carefully, set clear expectations, monitor them according to risk and give them feedback.
Contractors for medium and high-risk work shall pass HSE pre-qualification before award.
Contract owners shall hold performance reviews with contractors at the frequency set by the contract risk rating.
Contract owners are accountable for contractor performance; Supply Chain manages the process.
ACE-CON-STD-001 Contractor and Supplier Management Standard
Measure High-risk contracts with performance reviews on schedule.
LEAD · Element owner: VP Communications & Corporate Services

rows: ACE operates close to communities, landowners and fishers, sells gas to the Gas Buyer and crude to buyers, and works under the eye of regulators. This element sets out how we build lasting, honest relationships and manage the risks that matter to them.

blocks.t: What this means for you If a neighbour, landowner or customer raises a concern with you, log it. Every concern gets a response.
We identify the people affected by our activities across the life of each asset: communities near the land leases and the CPF, fishers in the Gulf of Paria, landowners, regulators and customers.
Each asset shall maintain a stakeholder map reviewed at least annually.
New projects shall include stakeholder engagement from the concept stage.
Community Relations Officers maintain stakeholder maps with Area Authorities.
ACE-STK-STD-001 Stakeholder and Community Engagement Standard
Measure Assets with a current stakeholder map (target 100%).
We manage the risks our activities create for stakeholders and customers, from noise and traffic near well pads to gas quality at the Gas Buyer delivery point.
Stakeholder and customer risks shall be assessed with the ACE Risk Matrix and recorded in the asset risk register.
Sales gas and crude shall meet the agreed contract specifications.
Area Authorities manage local impacts; the Marketing Manager (Gas & Crude) manages customer specifications.
ACE-STK-STD-001 Stakeholder and Community Engagement Standard
ACE-STK-STD-002 Customer and Product Quality Standard
ACE-RSK-STD-001 Risk Management Standard (including the ACE Risk Matrix)
ACE-HMA-PRA-001 Hydrocarbon Measurement and Allocation Practice
Measure Off-specification deliveries to customers (target zero).
Feedback, including complaints, is logged, assessed and answered. We tell people what we did about it.
All grievances shall be acknowledged within five working days and tracked to closure.
Trends in feedback shall be reviewed quarterly by the Communications Manager.
Community Relations Officers manage grievances; the Marketing Manager manages customer feedback.
ACE-STK-PRC-001 Grievance and Feedback Procedure
Measure Grievances closed within 30 days.
We build trust before we need it, including by preparing communities and authorities for how we would respond together in an emergency.
Communities near the CPF and the land leases shall be briefed on ACE emergency arrangements at least annually.
Major projects shall have a community engagement plan.
The Communications Manager leads engagement; the Emergency Response & Security Manager supports emergency briefings.
ACE-STK-STD-001 Stakeholder and Community Engagement Standard
ACE-EMR-STD-001 Emergency, Crisis and Business Continuity Standard
Measure Community emergency briefings held versus plan.
CONTROL · Element owner: VP HSE & Compliance

rows: This element is the heart of OMS. It covers how ACE identifies hazards, assesses risk with one common Risk Matrix, puts barriers in place, manages change and stays alert to the early signs that risk is rising.

blocks.t: What this means for you Use the ACE Risk Matrix for every risk assessment. If you see a barrier that is weak, missing or bypassed, report it the same day.

sections.title: 5.1 Assessing risk and putting barriers in place

blocks.t: ACE uses one risk management process for every kind of risk: understand the context, identify hazards, assess risk with the ACE Risk Matrix, and put prevention and recovery barriers in place until the risk is as low as reasonably practicable. Major accident hazards are studied in depth with HAZID, HAZOP, LOPA and bow-tie methods.
All risk assessments shall use the ACE Risk Matrix in the Risk Management Standard.
Every major accident hazard shall have a bow-tie showing its prevention and recovery barriers.
HAZOPs shall be completed for new facilities and modifications as set out in the Process Safety and Hazard Study Standard, and revalidated at least every five years.

Every control that prevents or limits a significant risk shall carry a unique control ID and be recorded in the Controls Register, linked to its risk, the document section that requires it, the process step that performs it and the evidence that it works.
The Process Safety Lead is the Technical Authority for hazard study methods.
ACE-RSK-STD-001 Risk Management Standard (including the ACE Risk Matrix)
ACE-PSM-STD-001 Process Safety and Hazard Study Standard (HAZID, HAZOP, LOPA, bow-tie)
ACE-RSK-PRA-001 Controls and Barrier Linkage Practice
Measure HAZOP revalidations on schedule; overdue HAZOP actions.
Significant risks are recorded in asset and corporate risk registers, with the level of management that must accept them set by their position on the Risk Matrix.
Risks rated High or Very High shall be accepted by the VP or CEO level shown in the Risk Matrix and reviewed at least quarterly.
Risk registers shall be reviewed after any significant incident or change.
Area Authorities own asset risk registers; the Head of Internal Audit & Risk Assurance maintains the corporate register.
ACE-RSK-STD-001 Risk Management Standard (including the ACE Risk Matrix)
ACE-RSK-REG-001 Corporate and Asset Risk Registers
ACE-RSK-REG-002 Controls Register
Measure High and Very High risks reviewed on schedule (target 100%).
Any change to plant, process, people, procedures or organisation that could affect risk goes through Management of Change. MOC tracks temporary and permanent changes from request to close-out.
No change shall be implemented until it has been screened, assessed and approved under the MOC process.
Temporary changes shall have an expiry date and shall be removed or made permanent before that date.
The Manager, Technical Excellence owns the MOC procedure; Area Authorities and Technical Authorities approve changes.
ACE-MOC-STD-001 Management of Change Standard
ACE-MOC-PRC-001 Management of Change Procedure
ACE-MOC-PRS-001 Management of Change Process
Measure Temporary MOCs past expiry (target zero); MOCs closed out within 90 days of start-up.
What this means for you Replacing something with an identical part is not a change. Anything else probably is. If in doubt, raise an MOC.
Serious accidents are usually preceded by weak signals: small deviations, repeated alarms, workarounds and backlogs. ACE leaders encourage a healthy unease and act on early warnings.
Each asset shall review its process safety early warning indicators monthly.
Repeated alarms, bypassed safeguards and normalised deviations shall be reported and investigated as near misses.
Area Authorities lead monthly early-warning reviews with the Process Safety Lead.
ACE-PSM-STD-002 Process Safety Leadership and Early Warning Standard
ACE-INC-STD-001 Incident Reporting and Investigation Standard
Measure Safeguards bypassed beyond their authorised period (target zero).
CONTROL · Element owner: VP Engineering & Projects

rows: ACE's platforms, pipelines, well pads and the Central Processing Facility must be fit for purpose from design to decommissioning. This element covers design standards, operating limits, safety-critical elements, maintenance and inspection, and the integrity of what we buy and sell.

blocks.t: What this means for you Safety-critical equipment comes first. Never defeat, bypass or delay a safety-critical task without an approved deviation.
Site selection, design and equipment choices are based on sound baseline data and the findings of hazard studies, from the shallow waters of the Gulf of Paria to the land leases.
Capital projects shall complete the hazard studies and baseline surveys required at each stage gate before progressing.
Design decisions shall be recorded in a basis of design endorsed by the relevant Technical Authorities.
Project Managers deliver projects through the stage gates; Technical Authorities endorse the basis of design.
ACE-PRJ-STD-001 Capital Project Delivery and Stage Gate Standard
ACE-PSM-STD-001 Process Safety and Hazard Study Standard (HAZID, HAZOP, LOPA, bow-tie)
Measure Stage gates passed with all required studies complete.

sections.title: 6.2 Engineering standards through the asset life

blocks.t: ACE engineering standards cover design, construction, commissioning, modification and decommissioning. They are owned by the Technical Authorities and assured through the Technical Leadership Council.
Work on ACE assets shall comply with ACE engineering standards and the codes they reference.
Technical Authorities shall review their standards at least every three years.
The Technical Leadership Council, chaired by the VP Engineering & Projects, oversees the engineering standards set.
ACE-ENG-STD-901 Engineering Standards Framework and Technical Authority Standard
ACE-PRJ-STD-001 Capital Project Delivery and Stage Gate Standard
ACE-ENG-SPC-410 Safety Instrumented Systems Specification
Measure Engineering standards within their review date.
Every system has an operating envelope. Operators know the limits, the consequences of exceeding them and what to do if they are approached.
Each facility shall have documented operating limits for safety-critical parameters, available in the control room.
Exceedances of safe operating limits shall be reported and investigated.
Area Authorities ensure operating limits are known; the Process Engineering Lead owns the limits.
ACE-OPS-STD-001 Operating Envelopes and Operating Limits Standard
ACE-OPS-PRA-001 Operating Envelopes and Integrity Operating Windows Practice
Measure Safe operating limit exceedances.

Safety-critical elements are the equipment and systems that prevent or limit a major accident: emergency shutdown, fire and gas detection, relief valves, well barriers and more. Each has a performance standard that says what it must do.
All safety-critical elements shall be identified in the SCE Register with a performance standard.
Any impairment of a safety-critical element shall be risk-assessed and managed under an approved deviation.
The Manager, Technical Excellence owns the SCE Register; Technical Authorities own the performance standards.
ACE-AIM-STD-001 Asset Integrity Management Standard
ACE-AIM-REG-001 Safety-Critical Element Register and Performance Standards
ACE-WEL-STD-001 Well Integrity Management Standard
ACE-MNT-PRA-001 Equipment Criticality and Safety-Critical Element Maintenance Practice
ACE-WEL-PRA-001 Well Barriers and Well Handover Practice
Measure Safety-critical elements impaired without an approved deviation (target zero).
Maintenance, inspection, testing and calibration are planned at risk-based intervals and done on time. Safety-critical tasks have priority, and any deferral is approved by the Technical Authority.
Safety-critical maintenance and inspection shall be completed by the due date or deferred only through the approved deferral process.
Anomalies found during inspection shall be assessed and tracked to resolution.
The Maintenance & Integrity Manager delivers the programmes; the Inspection Lead and Rotating Equipment Lead assure them.
ACE-MNT-STD-001 Maintenance Management Standard
ACE-AIM-STD-002 Inspection Management Standard
ACE-WEL-STD-001 Well Integrity Management Standard
ACE-AIM-PRA-001 Risk-Based Inspection and Corrosion Management Practice
Measure Safety-critical maintenance compliance (target 98%); overdue inspections.
Before ACE buys or sells an asset, lease or interest, we check its integrity, liabilities and risks so that there are no surprises.
Every acquisition or divestment shall include technical, HSE and integrity due diligence.
Findings shall be presented to the Executive Leadership Team before a final decision.
The VP Business Development & Markets leads due diligence with Technical Authorities.
ACE-OMS-STD-005 Acquisition and Divestment Due Diligence Standard
Measure Transactions with completed due diligence (target 100%).
CONTROL · Element owner: VP Operations

rows: Good procedures turn standards into safe, repeatable work. This element covers how ACE writes, approves, trains on and publishes its plans and procedures, and how we prepare for emergencies.

blocks.t: What this means for you Use the current procedure from the OMS portal, not a copy in a drawer. If the procedure does not match the job, stop and get it changed.
Procedures and plans are written for the people who use them, in ACE templates, at a level of detail that matches the risk of the task and the legal requirements.
Procedures shall be written using the ACE templates and the Operational Document Publishing Standard.
Procedures for high-risk tasks shall be reviewed with the people who perform them.
Every Standard and Standard Practice shall list the processes and procedures that put it into effect.
Document owners write and maintain procedures; the Technical Writer supports authors.
ACE-OPS-STD-002 Operating Procedures Standard
ACE-DOC-STD-002 Operational Document Publishing Standard
ACE-BPM-PRA-002 Process Modelling and Process File Practice
Measure Procedures reviewed by users before issue (sampled).
Every plan and procedure, and every revision, is approved by someone with the authority to do so.
Procedures shall be approved at the level set in the approval matrix in Part D.
Technical content shall be endorsed by the relevant Technical Authority before approval.
Approvers confirm fitness for purpose; Document Controllers check approvals before publication.
ACE-DOC-STD-001 Document and Records Management Standard
Measure Documents published with incomplete approvals (target zero).
People are trained in the procedures they use, and supported by guidance, coaching and competence checks.
New and significantly revised procedures for high-risk tasks shall be briefed to users before use.
Training on procedures shall be recorded in the competence system.
Line managers ensure their teams are briefed; the Operations Training & Competence Coordinator records it.
ACE-PPL-STD-003 Competence Assurance Standard
ACE-OPS-STD-002 Operating Procedures Standard
Measure Users briefed on revised high-risk procedures before use.

sections.title: 7.4 The current version wherever work is done

blocks.t: The current approved version of every plan and procedure is available where the work is done: on Pommerac A, at the CPF, on the land leases and at Point Lisas, through the OMS web portal and controlled copies.
The OMS web portal shall be the single source for current OMS documents.
Printed copies shall be marked uncontrolled unless registered as controlled copies.
The Information Management Lead owns the portal and controlled copy arrangements.
ACE-DOC-STD-001 Document and Records Management Standard
ACE-DOC-STD-002 Operational Document Publishing Standard
Measure Controlled copy audits with no out-of-date documents.

ACE has emergency response plans for each site, an oil spill contingency plan for the Gulf of Paria and a business continuity plan. They are resourced, exercised and improved after every drill and incident.
Each manned site shall run emergency drills at the frequency set in its emergency response plan, including at least one major exercise each year.
Lessons from drills and real events shall be recorded and plans updated within 90 days.
The Emergency Response & Security Manager owns the emergency system; Area Authorities run site drills.
ACE-EMR-STD-001 Emergency, Crisis and Business Continuity Standard
ACE-EMR-PLN-001-CPF Central Processing Facility Emergency Response Plan
ACE-EMR-PLN-002-PAP Pommerac A Emergency Response Plan
ACE-EMR-PLN-003 Oil Spill Contingency Plan
Measure Drills completed versus plan; drill actions closed.
CONTROL · Element owner: VP Operations

rows: This is where OMS meets the work. This element covers getting ready for work, doing it as planned under Control of Work, supervising it, stopping when it is not safe, and recognising the behaviours we want.

blocks.t: What this means for you You have the authority and the duty to stop any job you believe is unsafe. No one at ACE will be criticised for using Stop Work in good faith.
Before start-up, handover or a new activity, we check that equipment, people, procedures and permits are ready, and that handovers between shifts and teams are clear.
Start-up after construction, modification or turnaround shall follow a documented readiness review.
Shift handovers at manned sites shall use the ACE handover format and be recorded.
Area Authorities approve readiness; supervisors conduct handovers.
ACE-OPS-STD-003 Operational Readiness, Start-up and Handover Standard
Measure Start-ups with completed readiness reviews (target 100%).
Work is carried out under Control of Work: permits to work, isolations, simultaneous operations controls and task risk assessments, applied the same way by staff and contractors at every site.
All work covered by the Control of Work Standard shall be carried out under a valid permit.
Isolations shall be planned, verified and reinstated in line with the Isolation and Reinstatement Procedure.
Area Authorities and permit issuers are accountable for permit quality; performing authorities for doing the work as permitted.
ACE-COW-STD-001 Control of Work Standard
ACE-COW-PRC-001 Permit to Work Procedure
ACE-COW-PRC-002 Isolation and Reinstatement Procedure
ACE-LOG-PRA-001 Marine and Aviation Logistics Practice
ACE-COW-PRS-001 Permit to Work Process
Measure Permit audit compliance (target 95%).
Supervisors are present, check that work follows the plan and the permit, and confirm that it achieved what was intended.
Supervisors shall carry out and record field verifications at the frequency set for their role.
High-risk activities shall have a named supervisor present at the worksite.
Supervisors and Area Authorities are responsible for supervision.
ACE-OPS-STD-004 Supervision and Verification of Work Standard
Measure Field verifications completed versus plan.
Everyone at ACE, staff and contractors, can and must stop work when a risk is not adequately controlled.
Any person shall stop work when they believe a risk is not adequately controlled, and work shall not restart until the concern is resolved.
Stop-work events shall be recorded and recognised.
Every person at an ACE site holds stop-work authority.
ACE-LDR-STD-003 Stop Work Authority Standard
Measure Stop-work events recorded (a rising number is a healthy sign).

sections.title: 8.5 Recognising good work and correcting poor work

blocks.t: We recognise people who work safely and speak up, and we deal fairly and consistently with behaviour that puts people or plant at risk.
Recognition and consequence management shall follow the Recognition and Consequence Management Standard, including a just culture review.
Managers shall give feedback on safety behaviours as part of performance reviews.
Line managers apply recognition and consequence management with HR support.
ACE-LDR-STD-004 Recognition and Consequence Management Standard
Measure Recognition awards given; just culture reviews completed.
LEARN · Element owner: VP HSE & Compliance

rows: We measure what matters, report it honestly, investigate what goes wrong and make sure the lessons change how we work. This element covers KPIs, incident investigation, lessons learned and data quality.

blocks.t: What this means for you Report every incident and near miss, however small. Good reporting is how we see trouble coming.
We monitor operations, measure performance and verify that OMS requirements are being met, through routine checks, inspections and self-assessments.
Each element owner shall define how conformance with their element is monitored.
Self-assessments shall be completed at least annually by each function.
Element owners and function heads are responsible for monitoring.
ACE-PRF-STD-001 Performance Measurement and KPI Standard
Measure Self-assessments completed on schedule.
Incidents, near misses and non-conformances are reported, classified and investigated to find the root causes, not just the people involved.
All incidents and near misses shall be reported within the shift in which they occur.
Incidents shall be investigated at the level set by their actual and potential severity on the ACE Risk Matrix.
Area Authorities lead investigations; the VP HSE & Compliance owns the investigation standard.
ACE-INC-STD-001 Incident Reporting and Investigation Standard
Measure Investigations completed within target time; repeat incidents.
What this means for you Reporting a near miss protects the next person. It will never count against you.
Lessons from ACE incidents, audits and the wider industry lead to actions, and actions are tracked until their effectiveness is verified.
Actions from investigations, audits and reviews shall be tracked in one action system with owners and due dates.
Closure of significant actions shall be verified by someone independent of the action owner.
Action owners close actions; the Knowledge Management Specialist manages the lessons learned process.
ACE-INC-STD-002 Lessons Learned and Action Tracking Standard
Measure Overdue actions; actions verified as effective.
ACE uses lagging indicators to see outcomes and leading indicators to see whether barriers and processes are working. Part C of this Manual sets out the core indicators.
Each element shall have at least one leading and one lagging indicator.
The set of indicators shall be reviewed annually to make sure it is still relevant.
The Compliance & Assurance Manager owns the KPI framework.
ACE-PRF-STD-001 Performance Measurement and KPI Standard
Measure Indicators reviewed annually (target 100%).
Decisions are only as good as the data behind them. We check that OMS data is accurate, consistent and complete.
Owners of OMS data shall verify data quality at least quarterly using the checks in the Data Quality and Information Management Standard.
KPIs shall state their data source and owner.
The VP IT, Data & Knowledge owns data quality standards; data owners apply them.
ACE-DOC-STD-003 Data Quality and Information Management Standard
ACE-HMA-PRA-001 Hydrocarbon Measurement and Allocation Practice
Measure Data quality checks passed.
LEARN · Element owner: Head of Internal Audit & Risk Assurance

rows: Assurance tells us whether OMS is working as intended; review and improvement make sure we act on what we find. This element covers audits, management review, analysis and the cycle of improvement.

blocks.t: What this means for you When auditors visit, show them how the work is really done. Findings are how the system improves.
ACE runs a planned assurance programme across three lines: checks by the line, conformance assessments by the OMS team, and independent audits by Internal Audit.
The annual assurance plan shall be risk-based and approved by the Executive Leadership Team.
Every element shall be independently audited at least once every three years.
The Head of Internal Audit & Risk Assurance owns the assurance plan.
ACE-PRF-STD-002 Assurance and Audit Standard
Measure Assurance plan completed (target 90%).
Performance data is brought together and interpreted so that leaders can review it, compare ACE with industry peers and report to the Board, partners and regulators.
An OMS performance report shall be presented to the Executive Leadership Team each quarter.
ACE shall benchmark its HSE performance annually against industry data.
The OMS Manager prepares the quarterly OMS performance report.
ACE-PRF-STD-001 Performance Measurement and KPI Standard
ACE-PRF-STD-003 Management Review Standard
Measure Quarterly OMS reports issued on time.
We analyse indicators, incidents and audit findings together to find weak controls and opportunities to improve.
An annual analysis of trends across incidents, audits and KPIs shall be completed for each element.
Identified weaknesses shall be assigned improvement actions.
Element owners lead the annual analysis with the OMS Manager.
ACE-PRF-STD-001 Performance Measurement and KPI Standard
ACE-PRF-STD-003 Management Review Standard
Measure Weaknesses with assigned improvement actions.
Findings, lessons and good practices feed a planned programme of OMS improvements, which is communicated to the people affected.
Improvements shall be included in the annual OMS plan with owners and dates.
Significant OMS changes shall be communicated before they take effect.
Each process owner shall review the performance of their process at least once a year and record the improvements agreed.
The OMS Manager maintains the OMS improvement plan.
ACE-OMS-STD-003 Objectives and Annual OMS Plan Standard
ACE-BPM-PRA-003 Process Ownership and Continuous Improvement Practice
Measure OMS improvement actions delivered.

sections.title: 10.5 Leadership review of the whole system

blocks.t: Once a year the Executive Leadership Team steps back and asks whether OMS is still working, still suits ACE, and is getting more mature.
The Executive Leadership Team shall hold an annual OMS management review, including the results of the maturity assessment.
Actions from the management review shall be tracked to closure.
The CEO chairs the management review; the OMS Manager prepares it.
ACE-PRF-STD-003 Management Review Standard
ACE-PRF-STD-004 OMS Maturity Assessment Standard
Measure Management review held and actions closed.

Conformance tells us whether requirements are met; maturity tells us how well OMS is embedded. Each element owner assesses their element once a year on the ACE five-level scale, and each process owner assesses their process on the same scale. Process maturity results feed the element assessments. The approach follows the spirit of the maturity assessment being developed as ISO 29011.

The annual management review, chaired by the CEO, looks at the whole system: performance against objectives, audit and maturity results, control and process health, significant incidents and lessons, changes in risk and regulation, stakeholder feedback, and resources. It decides the OMS objectives and improvement priorities for the coming year.
Minutes and actions of the management review shall be recorded and kept for at least ten years.
ACE-PRF-STD-003 Management Review Standard

blocks.t: Standard documents are what make one system possible. When every document is numbered, structured, approved and tagged the same way, people can find what they need, OMS can link every document to the expectations, processes and controls it serves, and ONE can build the portal straight from the approved Word files — with nothing re-typed.
What this means for you If you write or revise an OMS document, start from the current ACE template and talk to the Technical Writer or a Document Controller early. It saves time at the gateway.

Revisions tell you at a glance whether a document is approved:
Letters (A, B, C …) are drafts. A lettered document is never used for work.
Numbers (01, 02, 03 …) are approved issues. The first approved issue is 01.
Status values are Draft, In Review, Approved, Superseded and Withdrawn. Every document carries a revision history stating what changed and why.

sections.title: D.5 Templates, styles and OMS tags

blocks.t: OMS documents are written in Word using the current ACE master template. The template carries the styles, document properties and content controls that ONE reads. Authors need no other tool: a properly prepared document is all that is required.

rows: Start every new document from the current master template. Never start from a copy of another document — its hidden properties travel with it.
The master record of the document's details. The cover, header and footer and Word's properties must all agree with it.
Title, Heading 1, Heading 2 and Heading 3 only. Each heading keeps its bookmark between revisions.
Under the title and each heading, the OMS Tags control holds the expectation numbers the section addresses: numbers only, comma-separated, most relevant first (for example 5.3, 6.4).
Title tags apply to the whole document. Heading tags apply down to the next heading of the same or higher level. Child headings do not inherit them.
ODS.Requirement, ODS.Responsibility, ODS.ApprovalRequirement, ODS.RecordRequirement and ODS.RiskControl.
ODS.Warning (written as a plain instruction), ODS.Note, ODS.Example, ODS.ProcedureStep, Normal text, lists and table cells.
Every ODS.RiskControl paragraph carries a Control ID content control, for example C-AIM-014.
Always Name — Job title, exactly as in the ACE organisation register. Committees appear only as endorsers.

23 fixed custom properties, including ODS.Parent. Word's own fields hold: Title = title; Subject = document number; Tags = title OMS tags; Categories = type and level; Company = Acme Caribbean Energy Limited.

blocks.t: The word “shall” shall appear only in the binding styles.
ACE-DOC-STD-002 Operational Document Publishing Standard
Every document passes through the same gateway before it reaches ONE:
1. The author drafts the document from the master template and requests a number (and any control ID block) from Document Control.
2. Reviewers comment; the author resolves comments and records the resolution.
3. The Technical Authority or Technical Leadership Council endorses technical content, where required.
4. The approver signs off at the level set in the approval matrix.

5. The automated ONE check runs about sixteen tests: number and codes, revision and status, properties and their agreement with the control table, title bookmark and tags, binding words in the right styles, people against the organisation register, control IDs, parent and references, process files and Word file health.
6. A Document Controller confirms the result, publishes the document to ONE and moves the previous revision to the superseded archive.
7. The document owner communicates the change to affected staff before the effective date.
A document that fails the automated check shall be returned to the author and shall not be published until the failures are corrected or a Document Controller records an accepted exception.

sections.title: D.8 Processes and the process file

blocks.t: ACE's process architecture has five levels, modelled on the APQC Process Classification Framework: 1 Category (for example Operate & Produce), 2 Process group, 3 Process — one controlled process document — 4 Activity (a step in the swimlane) and 5 Task (a procedure or work instruction).

Each process is a pair of files with the same number and revision: a Word process description (owner, scope, suppliers, inputs, outputs, customers, measures and a narrative for each step) and a process model file that ONE draws as swimlanes. Each step names its role, the document sections it relies on, the controls it performs and the records it creates. The model also carries simple timing and cost fields so that, in future, ONE can animate and simulate how work flows.
Every process shall have one process owner, one primary function and one governing policy, recorded in the Process Register.
Process owners are accountable for the performance of their process end to end and shall review it at least once a year, or sooner after an incident, audit finding or change.

sections.title: D.9 Controls and the data spine

blocks.t: ONE links the things OMS manages through a small set of registers, joined by IDs rather than re-typed text: objectives and opportunities, risks, controls, assets and safety-critical elements, processes, roles and people, events (incidents, near misses, audit findings, test failures, operating-window excursions), actions, documents and the OMS expectations. Controls sit at the centre: each event shows which controls held or failed, and each control shows how healthy it is today.

Risk is balanced against what ACE is trying to achieve. Objectives and opportunities sit on the same ACE Risk Matrix as threats, so leaders can see both sides of a decision and keep controls in proportion to risk appetite.
Each control recorded in the Controls Register shall show its current health — effective, degraded, failed or not tested — and its owner shall act on any change.

blocks.t: ALARP As low as reasonably practicable: risk reduced until the cost of further reduction is grossly disproportionate to the benefit.
APQC PCF The APQC Process Classification Framework, a widely used way of organising business processes in levels.
Area Authority The person accountable for all activities at a defined location, including issuing permits and releasing work.
Barrier A control that prevents a hazardous event or limits its consequences. It may be hardware, a human action or a process.
Bow-tie A diagram showing the threats and consequences of a hazardous event, with the prevention and recovery barriers between them.
Control Any measure that prevents a hazardous event or limits its consequences; significant controls carry an ID such as C-AIM-014.
Control health The current state of a control: effective, degraded, failed or not tested.
Data spine The linked ONE registers (risks, controls, assets, processes, events, actions, documents) joined by IDs.
Deviation An approved, time-limited departure from a mandatory requirement, with the risk assessed and accepted at the right level.
Element One of the ten parts of the OMS framework that groups related expectations.
Expectation A numbered statement of what the OMS framework expects a company to achieve, for example E5.3.
HAZOP Hazard and operability study: a structured team review of a design or operation to identify hazards and operability problems.
Integrity operating window (IOW) A limit on a process variable that, if exceeded for long enough, damages equipment integrity.
LOPA Layer of protection analysis: a method for checking whether the independent protection layers on a hazard are sufficient.
Major accident hazard A hazard that could cause multiple fatalities, major environmental damage or loss of a facility.
MOC Management of change: the process for assessing and approving changes before they are made.
OMS One Management System: ACE's single management system.
OMS tag A number in a document's OMS Tags control showing which expectation a document or section addresses.
ONE The ACE portal that publishes OMS documents, processes and controls from the approved Word sources.
Performance standard The required functionality, reliability and survivability of a safety-critical element, and how it is verified.
Process A defined, owned sequence of activities across roles and functions that turns inputs into outputs (document type PRS).
Process owner The person accountable for how well a process performs end to end and for improving it.
Process safety event (PSE) An unplanned release of material or energy from a process, classified in tiers by severity.
Safety-critical element (SCE) Equipment or a system whose failure could cause, or fail to prevent or limit, a major accident.
SIPOC Suppliers, inputs, process, outputs, customers: a one-line summary of what a process does and for whom.
Standard Practice A Level 2 document describing how an ACE discipline does its work: methods, criteria and technical rules (type PRA).
Swimlane A process map laid out in lanes, one for each role, showing who does each step and where work is handed over.
